At the receiver, a stored pool of mutually orthogonal semantic features is mixed by the received weights to rebuild the cloud. A folding decoder then bends a flat two-dimensional grid into the three-dimensional shape, keeping surfaces continuous. Training used a distance measure between point sets plus a penalty that protects orthogonality. On the ModelNet40 benchmark, quality matched a leading rival when bandwidth was generous. When bandwidth was tight, the method pulled ahead on both fidelity measures. Follow-up tests credited the orthogonal design and the folding step.
arxiv-2512-04019:
Neural video codecs that overfit a network to one video can rival traditional compression, but their entropy coding is painfully slow. Ho Man Kwan and colleagues slim down such a codec in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their NVRC-Lite extends an end-to-end neural representation codec toward lightweight models that smart devices could actually run.

Two changes carry the design. Multi-scale feature grids, including higher-resolution grids, lift quality at low complexity far beyond earlier lightweight attempts. Then an octree-based context model replaces the autoregressive entropy coder, which was accurate but impractical, and coding speeds jump. Against a leading lightweight rival, the new codec saved more than a fifth of the bitrate on standard quality measures. Encoding and decoding both ran many times faster than the baseline design. The authors promise a public implementation, making the approach testable by other compression researchers.
arxiv-2512-04119:
Two hit 2025 texts warned that AI far smarter than us will wipe us out within a decade, and Mohamed El Louadi pushes back hard. Writing in a 2025 preprint, he checks the argument chain behind those warnings: intelligence explosion, then superintelligence, then lethal misalignment. He tests each link against the record.

None of the steps, he argues, has been seen. There is no lasting self-improvement loop, no drive to plan on its own, no deadly mismatch of goals that no one can fix. Today's models stay narrow maths tools, strong yet lacking what the doom scripts need. El Louadi adds that the claim is a decoy, drawing eyes from mass spying and from who owns the big machines. He links its hype to a bubble in fast-ageing hardware. For now the claim stays a guess, boosted by money, not a shown fact.
arxiv-2512-04319:
Zixiao Zhao, Fatemeh Fard, and Jie Wu look at a quiet flaw in training code models: wrong labels in the training data. Large code stores hold many flawed or mislabeled examples. Such noise lowers accuracy and makes models brittle. Noise handling is well studied in other fields, yet it has seen little work for software tasks and code language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers a fix built into training itself.

The framework, called MANTRA, finds and treats noise in stages while a model fine-tunes. First the team tracks how loss shifts for each example as noise grows. Then a smart dropout plan, guided by loss patterns and grouping, drops examples that stay noisy. Clean data stays in. The aim is a model that learns from sound examples only, without a hand-cleaned dataset first.
arxiv-2512-04419:
Weiwei Wang, Weijie Zou, and Jiyong Min study a failure that plagues language models in live products: text that loops forever. A stuck model repeats the same lines without end, slowing service and jamming whole batches. The team met the problem in real batch work that reads code and writes reports. Their 2025 arXiv paper gathers the case, the cause, and several working fixes.

They sort the loops into three patterns: rule-writing loops, call-chart loops, and diagram-syntax loops. A Markov model analysis pins the root cause on greedy decoding, which cannot break out once a loop starts. Self-reinforcement then deepens the trap with each pass. The authors test three fixes at scale, starting with beam search, and grade each on quality and cost. Their results give product teams a playbook for spotting loops early and choosing a cure that fits.
arxiv-2512-04819:
Rodrigo de las Heras, Tim Kokkeler, and Stefan Ilić study what happens when superconductivity meets altermagnetism inside disordered materials. Altermagnets order their spins in a pattern that, like antiferromagnets, cancels overall, yet splits electron energies by direction. Superconductors carry current without resistance. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from fresh quantum kinetic equations and derives the Ginzburg-Landau free energy for the mixed system.

Beyond the usual pair-breaking term, a new coupling ties spin to how the superconducting order varies across space. Two effects follow. A flowing supercurrent can imprint a spin texture, a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect. Separately, changes in the order's size, not its phase, can magnetize the material. Around an Abrikosov vortex the two effects compete, since phase and size both vary there. Such couplings hint at devices where supercurrents write magnetic patterns.
arxiv-2512-05019:
Barnabas Porfy and Mate Csanad use computer simulations to picture the fireball made when argon nuclei smash into scandium at a European accelerator. In such collisions, pairs of pions escaping the wreck carry clues about the size and shape of the region they came from, a technique called femtoscopy. Measurements elsewhere have shown the source follows a heavy-tailed pattern named after Lévy, but mid-sized systems like this one had not been simulated.

The team generated collisions with the UrQMD event generator and checked the simulated particle output against expectations. The pion pair source fits the Lévy pattern well, and the authors read meaning into its scale, shape, and strength parameters. Their results give experimenters a baseline to compare against when real argon-scandium data arrives, helping pin down how matter behaves in systems between small and truly large collisions.
arxiv-2512-05219: Kirill Shakhmatov and Hoang Le Truong prove a flexibility result in affine algebraic geometry. A variety is flexible when its symmetries act richly enough to move points around freely, a property tied to parametrization and deformation questions. They establish flexibility for two families. One is the complement in projective space of a quadric of rank at least three. The other is affine cones over smooth complete intersections of two quadrics, in dimension at least three. The results extend the known catalogue of flexible varieties.
arxiv-2512-05319:
Marzieh Eidi, Juergen Jost, and Dong Zhang survey how the grand structures of Riemannian geometry reappear in discrete worlds: graphs and simplicial complexes. They also ask what happens when the discrete version is sampled from the smooth one. Many pillars of geometry have discrete counterparts: Cheeger inequalities, Hodge theory, Morse theory, and the spectral theory of Laplace-type operators, together with their links. The survey asks how these analogies hold together and how discrete structures converge to the manifolds they approximate.

Recent developments get a close look: Cheeger-type inequalities for the higher-dimensional geometry of simplicial complexes, Floer-type constructions where dynamical systems have periodic or homoclinic orbits, and the disorientability of simplicial complexes. The field matters wherever smooth geometry must be computed on: meshes, networks, and sampled data. The survey maps where the bridge from discrete to continuous is solid and where it is still being built.
arxiv-2512-05819:
S Vogt and a large collaboration of cosmologists test a rival theory of gravity by counting galaxy clusters. The theory, the normal branch of DGP braneworld gravity, adds a fifth force on large scales. That force speeds structure growth, so more massive clusters should exist than standard gravity predicts. Counting clusters can therefore bound the theory's key scale.

The team used about a thousand clusters found by the South Pole Telescope through their shadow on the cosmic microwave background. Masses were calibrated with weak lensing from the Dark Energy Survey and the Hubble Space Telescope. A corrected halo abundance model, tuned on simulations, translated counts into limits. The Planck satellite's newest microwave maps were also fitted inside this model, a first. Jointly, the data give a competitive upper bound on the model's strength. Cluster counting, once a standard cosmology tool, here becomes a sharp test of gravity itself.
arxiv-2512-05919:
Dominik Still and four co-authors bring a clean splitting strategy for fluid flow into the discontinuous Galerkin world. Simulating incompressible flow means enforcing, at every instant, that the fluid neither piles up nor thins out. Sloppy splitting caps accuracy and breeds edge artifacts. Liu's consistent splitting avoids both flaws, imposing divergence freedom implicitly, with physical conditions even at open edges.

The new work discretizes that scheme with DG methods, which excel at high order work. The convective term is treated semi-implicitly, loosening the time step limit without forcing nonlinear solves each step. A Leray projection guards mass conservation. Each step solves a pressure system, then one velocity equation. Tests confirm optimal convergence in space and time, and the method handles practical cases: flow around a cylinder, and the Taylor-Green vortex. It is careful numerical engineering for the equations of fluids.
arxiv-2512-06219:
Luis Octavio Castanos-Cervantes, Manuel Calixto, and Julio Guerrero propose a way to store a quantum bit inside a group of three level atoms. A lone quantum bit fades fast when it leaks energy or picks up noise from its surroundings. Their scheme hides the bit in special shared states of the whole group, shaped like the famous cat states of light, built here for atoms with three levels each.

Because these states sit still under the group's own dynamics, they shrug off energy loss and shared noise that would ruin a plain bit. The team shows how to flip the stored bit and run other basic gates, and studies a small two atom case in depth. Even there, one state form stayed immune to local noise while a sister form did not, and they found a fix. It hints at tougher quantum memory from small atom groups.
arxiv-2512-06319:
Ayan Mitra and a large team from the LSST Dark Energy Science group test whether exploding stars can map dark energy with no spectra. The Rubin Observatory's big survey will find close to a million type Ia supernovae, stars whose steady peak glow makes them mileposts for cosmic distances. Most will be too faint for the slow, costly step of taking their spectra, which gives type and distance.

The team builds a full dress rehearsal from simulated survey data, with impostor events and wrong host matches. They sort the events with a neural net, guess distances from host galaxy colors, and correct the known biases step by step. A small set of confirmed nearby events anchors the far sample. Their pipeline then fits a standard dark energy model to the cleaned distance chart. The rehearsal shows a photo only route can still squeeze real limits on dark energy.
arxiv-2512-06419:
Molla Basir Ahamed works with Sujoy Majumder and with Nabadwip Sarkar and Ming-Sheng Liu. They sharpen a classic bound on power series, Bohr's inequality, for functions of several variables at once. The classical result concerns a bounded analytic function on a disc. It says the sum of the sizes of its series terms, weighted in a set way, stays below a bound. That bound holds out to a certain radius. Extending such bounds to the polydisk, where each variable has its own disc, is delicate.

The team proves an improved form of the bound for bounded holomorphic maps on the polydisk, and shows the gain cannot be pushed further. They also prove two companion versions, one swapping the constant term for the size of the function itself, and one for its square. All three results are sharp. Sharp constants mark the exact edge where analytic control breaks down.
arxiv-2512-06519:
Thomas Wright and James Binney tackle a snag in computing the actions of star orbits that stretch far from round. Actions are the conserved quantities that label an orbit in a galaxy's gravity. When an orbit's spin about the symmetry axis shrinks toward zero, its kind is clean: box orbits wander a filled region, while loop orbits circle the center. The authors show that split survives at nonzero spin as well.

In a special family of potentials they find a threshold value of a third conserved quantity. Below it, that quantity adds nothing to the barrier that keeps an orbit from the center, and the orbit is a box; above it, a loop. They give algorithms for the threshold in any potential. Near the threshold, the standard shortcut for actions and frequencies struggles, so they offer a modified version. The work sharpens action based galaxy modeling.
arxiv-2512-06619:
Qi Song and seven co authors propose a noise fighting scheme for quantum information built on weak measurement. Noise corrupts signals as they are gathered, sent, processed, and stored, and quantum signals are frail to begin with. Their approach reads the signal gently, through measurements so weak they barely disturb it, using pairs of carefully angled reading bases as the decoding rule.

After the signal crosses a noisy channel, the best mix of those gentle readings can rebuild it with minimal distortion. The team tests the idea on signals encoded in two level quantum states and in entangled pairs, sent through flickering and decoherence noise. Distortion fell close to zero and the fault tolerant score close to perfect, with finite resources. Bench tests with ordinary laser light and with quantum coherent light back the scheme. The authors pitch it for long distance quantum links, fine sensing, and exact computing.
arxiv-2512-07119:
Hiroyuki Takamura reviews how mathematicians prove that solutions of certain wave equations must blow up in finite time. The equations are semilinear: a wave term plus a power of the solution itself, which can feed on its own growth. At the critical power, gentle methods fail, and showing that the lifespan is finite, with a sharp upper bound, takes care, especially in low space dimensions where waves decay slowly.

The survey sets out the main strategies. One compares the solution against an ordinary differential equation using pointwise bounds. Another uses a functional method with a cleverly chosen test function in the weak form of the equation. Takamura's focus is a third route built for numerical use: an iteration of pointwise estimates powered by a slicing technique.
arxiv-2512-07319:
Marius Cizauskas and co-authors build a quantum random number generator fast enough to feed high-rate secure communications. True randomness here comes from measuring vacuum fluctuations with heterodyne detection, reading both quadratures of empty light at once. The security model is source-device-independent: nothing about the source need be trusted, even if an adversary prepared it. As long as the measurement device and its calibration are honest, the entropy is genuinely quantum.

Vacuum light is split and read by two balanced detectors, digitized billions of times per second, and distilled in real time by an FPGA chip running a Toeplitz hashing extractor. Careful noise accounting confirms the quantum noise dominates the electronics within the detection band. After extraction the system sustains a rate in the tens of gigabits per second of uniform bits, passing the standard statistical test suites.
arxiv-2512-07919:
Shi Jin and Nana Liu, researchers in applied mathematics and quantum computing, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the Hamilton Jacobi equation, a nonlinear equation used for moving fronts, games with many players, control problems, and learning. They ask how a quantum computer could find its special viscosity solutions.

Their method builds on an entropy penalty idea from Gomes and Valdinoci, which extends an older transform to general convex cases. That step turns the nonlinear dynamics into linear heat like dynamics that quantum machines can simulate. The authors then give analog and digital quantum algorithms that read out values, slopes, and minima directly. Their results hold for long times, removing a major block for quantum methods on nonlinear equations.
arxiv-2512-08019: Krishnendu Gongopadhyay and Neelanjan Mondal, mathematicians who work in geometry, posted a research article on arXiv in December 2025. They extend Thurston asymmetric metric, a distance notion first defined for Teichmuller space, to the setting of Margulis spacetimes. Along with the metric, they carry over the associated Finsler norm. They also establish several convexity properties for both the metric and the norm, giving geometers new tools for studying these spacetimes.
arxiv-2512-08819:
Ferdinand Kapl and coauthors analyze why gradually growing the depth of transformer models during training can help. A prior method that stacks new middle layers over time was shown to cut training cost and improve reasoning. A clear mechanism for those gains was missing, and this study aims to supply it.

The work connects growth to a known issue called the curse of depth. In standard models, layers in the second half contribute far less to the final output than early layers. Depth wise analysis shows that grown models use their depth more evenly and reshape the residual stream. They also form computational blocks that can be permuted more freely. The authors add a light modification to the growth method that improves reasoning scores further. Overall, gradual growth seems to build distinct circuits and to overcome poor depth use in standard training.
arxiv-2512-09519:
M. Sawczuck leads the CASCADE team in a first study of gas filaments in DR20, a high-mass star-forming region in the Cygnus X complex. Filaments, long threads of cold gas, are suspected of feeding young stars by channeling material onto growing cores. The survey uses sensitive radio observations of two molecular tracers to map the region at high resolution.

The team identifies filaments with a structure-finding algorithm and measures their velocity patterns and widths with spectral fitting and a dedicated analysis package. Several filaments show steady velocity gradients along their length, directed toward star-forming cores, which reads as gas flowing along the filaments into the cores. Filament widths cluster near the value commonly found in nearby low-mass star-forming regions. The authors present this as a first look, with the full CASCADE survey set to put high-mass filament properties on firmer statistical ground.
arxiv-2512-09719:
Nilasis Chaudhuri, Christian Rohde, and Florian Wendt analyze a relaxation model for a compressible fluid with surface tension. The underlying system is the Navier-Stokes-Korteweg equations in an isothermal setting. Their model adds a smoothing mechanism governed by two positive parameters. As those parameters move to their limits, solutions of the model should approach solutions of the original equations. The authors work in three spatial dimensions and define finite energy weak solutions for the model with initial and boundary data.

Two results follow. First, a weak-strong uniqueness principle holds: if a rough weak solution and a smooth strong solution start from the same data, they agree for as long as the strong one exists. Second, the authors prove rigorously that the model converges in the relaxation limit. The results hold even for general pressure laws that are not monotone.
arxiv-2512-09919: Callum Deakin discusses a route to generating arbitrary optical waveforms, shaped light pulses. The scheme cascades phase modulators with dispersive elements. Together they carry out spectro-temporal unitary transforms, rearranging a signal jointly in spectrum and time. Two features stand out in his account. The approach is not limited by the bandwidth of the individual modulators it uses. It is also, in theory, lossless, wasting none of the light. The text is a summary of an invited talk prepared for a major optical fiber communications conference.
arxiv-2512-10119:
A. D'Agliano and colleagues compute how much a hybrid superconducting magnet's performance degrades under its own forces. The magnet, a four layer dipole built at Fermilab, combines two superconductors, niobium tin and a bismuth based high temperature compound, aiming at sixteen tesla. When powered, intense Lorentz forces strain the cables, and strain lowers the critical current a superconductor can carry, sometimes before any mechanical failure. The team modeled every Rutherford cable in the coils at strand level, using a heterogeneous cable model in engineering software.

Into that model they fed strain dependent critical current laws with parameters from experiments. They could then predict degradation for each superconductor across all possible powering configurations of the hybrid. The method gives designers a detailed integrity check: which strands, in which coil, lose how much capacity at full field. High field magnets for accelerators and fusion live or die by such margins.
arxiv-2512-10219:
Ilya Degtev leads a team measuring how covalent silver fluorides are, to test whether they can stand in for the famous cuprate superconductors. Silver difluoride shares much of its electronic structure with the copper oxides behind high temperature superconductivity. The team probed several silver compounds with X-ray absorption and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the silver edge, comparing spectra against density functional results to pin down the features. Their scattering data show charge transfer and local electronic excitations in silver difluoride closely akin to those in the canonical cuprate.

They propose a simple yardstick for covalency: the ratio of the two kinds of excitation strength in the scattering spectrum, with formulas supplied for both crystals and powders. Measured this way, the fluorides come out much like the cuprates, and slightly more covalent. That supports silver fluorides as a stand in for cuprate physics.
arxiv-2512-10419:
Phu Pham, Damon Conover, and Aniket Bera tackle a matching problem for self-driving systems. Working out where a ground vehicle is by comparing its LiDAR scans with overhead aerial images. The two views look very different, one a ground-level sweep of shapes and the other a map-like picture from above, so lining them up is hard.

Their system, TransLocNet, turns LiDAR scans into a bird's-eye view and aligns them with aerial features using attention that runs in both directions. A contrastive learning step pulls matching views closer together in a shared space, and a decoder outputs a probability map over position and heading. On the CARLA simulator and the real KITTI dataset, it cut location error sharply and reached accuracy finer than a metre and a degree.
arxiv-2512-10919:
Elena Braverman and Alexandra Rodkina study how to stabilise a population model known as the planar Ricker system. They use prediction based control, which adjusts the system based on expected future values, aiming to hold a positive equilibrium steady. Their analysis works on a closed set that stays inside the strictly positive region.

They construct a special Lyapunov function and give conditions on the control settings that keep its changes from growing on that set. Adding random noise to the parameters lowers the average control effort needed while keeping both global and local stability. Computer simulations illustrate the theory. The results speak to controlled population dynamics where keeping numbers positive and stable is essential.
arxiv-2512-11019:
Alessandro De Angelis portrays the DELPHI experiment at CERN's Large Electron Positron Collider through the life and leadership of physicist Ugo Amaldi. DELPHI was one of the major detectors that studied collisions at that machine. The article follows its work from precise studies at the Z boson peak to higher energy running.

Later work covered pairs of W bosons and increasingly ambitious searches for the Higgs boson. Amaldi's bold detector choices, organisational ideas, and support for young physicists receive special attention. His earlier work on unifying the fundamental forces also appears. The article argues that DELPHI's technology, software, governance, and data sharing habits anticipated later collider experiments and still shape particle physics culture today.
arxiv-2512-11319:
Bingyuan Huang and colleagues help self driving cars build their own high definition road maps in real time, using satellite images as a top down helper. Onboard sensors suffer from blind spots and occlusions, so live maps come out incomplete or noisy. Satellite views cover wide areas steadily, but shadows from buildings and trees degrade them too.

Their model, SATMapTR, first refines satellite features with a gated module that mixes high level meaning with low level structure to keep only map relevant signals. A geometry aware fusion step then merges satellite features with the car's bird's eye view grid by grid, limiting damage from poor inputs. On the nuScenes benchmark the system achieved the best average precision among satellite assisted methods by a wide margin. It also degraded less in bad weather and sensor failures, and kept its advantage at long perception ranges.
arxiv-2512-11619:
Mikel Garcia de Andoin and Mikel Sanz pin down the true cost of a hybrid style of quantum computing. The style, called digital-analog computing, mixes steady pulls between qubits with quick single qubit turns. Any target operation can be built this way, but past work only gave loose caps on the total pull time needed.

The pair prove a tight cap, the best that can be guaranteed. The time grows in a straight line with the number of links between qubits. That clear rule lets builders price out quantum simulations and algorithms in advance. It also makes fair side by side checks with rival quantum styles much easier.
arxiv-2512-11719:
Yilmaz Korkmaz and co-authors let users name the change they want to find in satellite photos. Standard change detection flags every difference between two dates, wanted or not. Class based versions stick to fixed label sets, so datasets and models are hard to mix.

Their Referring Change Detection task takes a plain language prompt for one kind of change. The system, RCDNet, fuses words and images to find just that change. A second part, RCDGen, forges fake after images and change maps from a before image alone, easing the shortage of labeled data. Tests on several data sets show targeted search works at scale, a boon for city planning and disaster response.
arxiv-2512-11819:
Daniil Sukhorukov and a large team built AI-Meteorologist, a language model agent that explains weather forecasts rather than just printing numbers. Forecast work is an act of reading: spotting fronts, oddities, and local quirks, then telling that story with reasons.

The system splits the job across agents, each reading one weather factor. It adds past climate context and writes a structured report with clear reasoning steps. No fine tuning is used; all skill comes from prompting. Case studies on multi city forecasts show the reports name the true drivers behind events. The authors pitch it as a helper that can grow, not replace, human forecast skill.
arxiv-2512-11919:
Junhyung Park and Yuqing Zhou look at causal effects one event at a time instead of one variable at a time. Classic studies ask how a drug dose shifts blood pressure. But in image or language data, the raw units, pixels or tokens, carry no meaning to build questions on.

Working in causal spaces, a measure based frame for causality, the pair define when an effect on an event is present. They prove links between those definitions and dependence under intervention. They also build measures for the size and kind of event level effects. Standard treatment effect measures return as special cases. The fine grained view suits modern data where meaning lives in patterns, not single columns.
arxiv-2512-12019:
T Forrest Kieffer and co-authors build a rigorous series method for nonlinear flow equations. They study advection diffusion systems, where material is carried and spread at once. A dial parameter deforms the easy linear problem into the hard nonlinear one, with zero marking the linear case.

Solutions expand as a series in that dial, each term solving a linear forced problem fed by lower terms. For the Burgers equation case they prove the series converges for any integrable start, with infinite radius. Dirac spike and periodic cases get full treatment, plus a forced case nearing turbulence. The same scheme handles p-Laplacian diffusion models. The results open a firm path for series methods in fluid physics.
arxiv-2512-12119:
Raluca M Balan and Michael Salins prove a quantitative central limit theorem for a noisy heat equation with drift. The equation spreads a random initial field under space time white noise, with a steady push from the drift term. Spatial averages of such fields tend to a Gaussian shape; the theorem prices how fast.

The setting is one dimensional, with a constant start and twice smooth drift and diffusion coefficients of bounded slope. Malliavin calculus does the heavy lifting, via the second order Poincaré inequality. A fresh bound on products of two heat kernels, of interest on its own, controls the key term. A functional version of the limit follows, completing the picture.
arxiv-2512-12219:
Zhi Chen, Jingcai Guo, Taotao Cai, and Yuxiang Cai tackle fine grained zero shot learning in a 2025 paper. A model must name new classes it never saw in training, using traits learned from known classes. The hard part is telling apart small visual details like color, shape, and texture.

Older models mix those traits into one code, so the details blur. The authors build attribute centric codes that keep traits apart during learning itself. Two expert based parts route image patches and then map traits to sparse, part aware maps. On the CUB, AwA2, and SUN data sets, their method set new best scores for this task.
arxiv-2512-12319:
Yuan Li, Shuaijie Wang, and Xiaoming Xu study linear maps that respect unitary evolution in a 2025 math paper. Such maps arise in quantum theory, where states evolve by unitary operators. The authors describe all continuous linear maps from trace class operators to operators on a doubled space that keep covariance under that evolution.

From that description, they give exact conditions for such a map to be self-adjoint or positive. One result pins down the virtual broadcasting map by three conditions alone: covariance, swap symmetry, and match with classical broadcasting. They also characterize a related class of maps defined on all bounded operators.
arxiv-2512-12719:
Anrafel Fernandes Pereira, Maria Teresa Baldassarre, Daniel Mendez, and Marcos Kalinowski explore AI agent support for framing research problems in a 2025 vision paper. Poorly framed problems can sink the practical value of software engineering studies by missing the complexity of industrial practice. The earliest project stage, problem formulation, is where agent help might matter most.

Building on the Lean Research Inception framework, they walk through a scenario based on a published study of code maintainability in machine learning systems. Agents pre fill problem attributes, align stakeholder views, refine questions, simulate assessments from many angles, and support decisions. Their scenario study suggests richer discussion and sharper thought on value and feasibility. Real world testing is still needed, they note.
arxiv-2512-12819:
M. Serra-Ricart and co-authors report telescope views of 3I/ATLAS, a comet that came from outside our solar system. They found a faint jet near the top of its inner coma, or cloud of gas and dust. The jet lined up with a broad plume seen in visible images.

The team saw the jet clearly on seven nights in August 2025. Its angle changed in a steady cycle of 7.74 hours, plus or minus 0.35 hours. That cycle may point to a spin period near 15.48 hours if the jet comes from one active spot near a pole. The work gives the first such cycle found in an interstellar comet.
arxiv-2512-13219:
Christoph Hartmann and co-authors present PyCAALP, an open-source framework that plans both the order in which parts are assembled and how work is split across a production line. It models parts and joints as a graph and checks physical limits such as collisions, handling, tolerances, and joint fit.

The system enumerates all feasible assembly sequences, then balances station times through a mixed-integer program. A path-guided reduction solves that program on a small subgraph, keeping the full optimum or near it while using a fraction of the graph. Speedups reached up to three orders of magnitude. Users can tune engineering constraints and trade planning stages against each other.
arxiv-2512-13519:
Amadou Sy and Masseye Gaye study the horocyclic flow on curved surfaces, in a paper written in French. The flow moves points along special curves on the unit tangent bundle of a hyperbolic surface. For surfaces of finite type, the flow is well known: it is either spread out or tied to closed loops.

For surfaces of infinite type, the picture is far less clear, since some orbits are neither closed nor dense. The authors show such an orbit either returns near itself or has a closure that is not minimal for the flow. Their result nearly completes the account of minimal sets for this flow.
arxiv-2512-13919:
Eugenio Varetti and co-authors show how adaptive digital twins can improve decisions in civil engineering. A digital twin mirrors a physical structure in a virtual model, but fixed transition models limit its value over time. Their work adapts the state transition models inside twins framed as probabilistic graphical models.

They model the two-way link between physical and virtual domains with dynamic Bayesian networks. Treating transition probabilities as random variables with conjugate priors allows online Bayesian learning from new data. Policies are computed by solving parametric Markov decision processes with reinforcement learning. A case study on structural health monitoring and maintenance of a railway bridge shows the gains. The authors claim better personalization, robustness, and cost-effectiveness.
arxiv-2512-14219:
Weifeng Qiu proposes one finite element method for two hard equation types in a 2025 paper. Finite element methods solve equations on a mesh of small pieces. The targets are second order elliptic equations in non divergence form and the related Hamilton Jacobi Bellman equation used in control theory.

For both problems, Qiu proves that strong solutions exist in a suitable space and that the numeric method converges at the optimal rate. The results hold on convex polyhedra in two and three dimensions, for a range of exponents. On non convex polygons the range narrows. He also relaxes common assumptions on how smooth the coefficients of the Hamilton Jacobi Bellman equation must be.
arxiv-2512-14519:
Tushar Singh, Ajim Uddin Ansari, and Shiv Datt Kumar define a new class of rings in commutative algebra. Laskerian rings are those whose ideals split neatly into simpler pieces. Their nonnil-S-Laskerian rings merge two earlier generalizations, requiring the splitting only for ideals that avoid both the nilpotent elements and a chosen multiplicative set.

The main theorem places every nonnil-S-Noetherian ring inside the new class. Under a mild extra condition, such rings also have a well-behaved prime spectrum. A final result works backward from power series: if the series ring qualifies and its nilradical splits properly, the original ring is S-Laskerian and satisfies a finite-type property.
arxiv-2512-14719:
Small language models are popular where low latency and light deployment matter, especially for classification. Explanation-guided learning tries to make such models more interpretable and robust by feeding attribution-based supervision, signals about which inputs mattered, into training.

The open challenge addressed here is how to derive attribution priors that are general and reliable enough to guide that training. The answer uses hybrid attribution priors, combining sources of evidence about feature importance into a single training signal. Dependable priors would let small models stay fast while becoming easier to trust and harder to fool with misleading inputs.
arxiv-2512-15019:
S. Janssens leads a team using X-ray binary stars as a test bench for reading the spectra of Be stars. Classical Be stars spin fast and show messy, shifting emission lines, which makes measuring their motion hard. Most are thought to be products of past binary interactions, yet solid binary statistics are still missing.

The team picked seven Be X-ray binaries whose orbital periods are known from X-rays. With repeated high resolution HERMES spectra, they compared three ways to measure radial velocity: cross correlation, line profile fitting, and the bisector method. Cross correlation won, since it needs no model templates and handles blended lines well. Emission lines gave tighter results than absorption lines, with H beta steadier than H alpha. The authors warn that big swings in emission can fake eccentric orbits, so checks against absorption lines remain wise.
arxiv-2512-15719:
Athanasios Charisoudis and co authors present a fast volumetric capture and reconstruction pipeline in a 2025 paper. The system turns RGB-D or RGB only camera input into dynamic point clouds and Gaussian splats, the two common forms for free viewpoint video. Easy setup matters as much as quality for real shoots.

For Gaussian splats, the team improves the GPS-Gaussian regressor for high quality results with little overhead. The rig supports sparse setups, varied camera counts, and uncontrolled lighting and backgrounds. Captures export as PLY, MPEG V-PCC, or SPLAT files for a web viewer or game engine plugins. A live on site preview runs at 5 to 10 frames per second.
arxiv-2512-15819:
John Fitzgerald and co authors report experience from two new introductory courses on digital twins in a 2025 paper. A digital twin mirrors a real system in software for testing and training. Teaching the model based methods behind twins to mixed audiences is the challenge these courses faced.

One course served doctoral students from largely non computational backgrounds, the other masters students with computing experience. The authors describe each course's goals, content, and delivery, then review lessons learned so far. A central lesson is the need for common baselines when participants start from very different technical ground. The paper was presented at the 2025 INTO-CPS Overture Summit.
arxiv-2512-16419:
Kaspar Rosager Ludvigsen warns about AI in security work in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025, presented at a 2024 information law conference in London. Companies increasingly let large language models write code for security infrastructure and feed them sensitive data. Ludvigsen asks a deeper question: how does that habit corrode cybersecurity and law itself?

He maps the norms of cybersecurity practice and the European Union's legal security duties, then tests language models against both frames. The models often fail good practice and legal obligations alike, largely because they cannot trace or justify their outputs. Symbolic AI avoids some flaws but shares the traceability problem. Fixes include guard systems around the models, exceeding legal minimums, and simply not using the technology in certain roles. The paper closes with economic and practical fallout.
arxiv-2512-16719:
Atsu Kokuvi Angélo Passah, Rodrigo C. de Lamare, and Arsenia Chorti improve a way to verify wireless devices by their channel fingerprint. Channel state data vary over time, which hurts physical-layer checks that rely on stable traits.

Their fix is an adaptive robust principal component step that cleans the channel data first. The cleaned data feed a check built on information reconciliation, using polar codes tuned with a Gaussian shortcut to fix mismatches. In tests, error rates after reconciliation fell sharply versus no cleaning, and detection reached full marks in both line-of-sight and blocked settings. The method beat plain and robust component tools, autoencoders, and a recursive sensing rival on both made-up and real data.
arxiv-2512-17119:
Laura Pardo and coauthors map territorial gaps in Colombia Saber 11 exam scores for the second semester of 2022, using Bayesian multilevel spatial models. Scores vary by place, and the team asks which social traits track the gaps once geography is counted.

The model joins multilevel regression with spatial random effects at municipal and department levels, and compares Ridge and Lasso priors for the social covariates. Monte Carlo inference in open tools, checked on synthetic data, favored Ridge for balance of recovery, prediction, and sampling speed. Real results show strong centralization, with top scores in central departments. Living conditions, maternal schooling, learning resources, gender, and ethnic background linked most strongly to scores.
arxiv-2512-17219:
Ahmad Jafar Arifi and three co-authors trace how hadronic physics grew into an active research field in Indonesia. Hadrons are particles, such as protons, that feel the strong force, and the field studies their inner structure using quantum chromodynamics. The review covers a few decades of work by Indonesian groups.

On the theory side, local researchers have built models of hadron properties and behavior. On the experimental side, Indonesian scientists have joined large overseas projects, including the ALICE collaboration at CERN. Those links trained young researchers and tied the country into global networks. The closing part lays out plans to deepen that role in the years ahead.
arxiv-2512-17519:
In a second 2025 paper, Muhammad Haris Khan presents K-OTG, a way to lock an instruction tuned language model so it only works for users holding the right secret key. The method is built for LoRA tuned models, a popular low cost way to adapt a model. Each role gets its own key, so access can differ by user.

Training uses two paths: examples with a valid key learn the real answer, while examples without one learn to output a block token. At run time, a math transform scrambles the model's inner state unless the correct key restores it. Tests on small Llama and Qwen models showed authorized use stayed close to normal, while unauthorized use collapsed. The lock comes with a notable cost in output speed.
arxiv-2512-17619:
Faisal Suwayyid and Guo-Wei Wei fuse two fields that both study shape changing over time. Persistent homology watches a network grow edge by edge and records when features appear and vanish. Commutative algebra encodes a graph in an edge ideal, a polynomial object whose Betti numbers grade its complexity. The pair build persistent versions of these algebra objects that evolve along the same growth.

A persistent form of Hochster's classic formula ties the algebra's numbers to the topology at every stage. New persistent vertex covers track how the cheapest way to touch every edge shifts as the graph grows. In applied tests, the invariants sorted genomes without sequence alignment and told mirror-image molecules apart. Abstract algebra gains a time axis; data science gains sharper fingerprints.
arxiv-2512-18019:
Christian Carrick, Bertrand Guillou, and Sarah Petersen compute a refined homology theory for a space built from loops with a flip symmetry. Their target mixes the circle group of order two with its regular representation, a setup from equivariant topology, where spaces carry group actions. The result mirrors a classic computation for a plain double loop space.

To get there, the team first builds new relations for how certain operations act on such loop spaces. Those relations do the heavy lifting in the main count. The finished homology gives algebraists a new fixed point for testing tools meant to respect symmetry, in a field where each hard won count becomes a base for the next.
arxiv-2512-18719:
Tony Mathew Blessan and a large team of photonics researchers engineer a laser that shines in lines instead of points or spots. Building integrated light sources with unusual mode shapes is a live challenge, with approaches ranging from topological lasers to vortex microlasers. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in its journal version, arranges coupled micropillars in a two-dimensional lattice.

By combining orbital photonic modes, they design bands that are flat along one direction and dispersive along the other. The flat direction produces lasing line modes, extended stripes of coherent light. Because the lattice is compact and two-dimensional, many such lines can be packed side by side into dense lasing matrices. That layout could serve optical computing and sensing chips that need many parallel, structured light sources on one device.
arxiv-2512-18819:
Luc Cote and Andy Sun ask where a data center's electricity really emits its carbon. Average grid statistics blur the truth: the next megawatt consumed in one place may come from hydro, in another from coal. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, analyzes locational marginal emissions across the 1,493-bus Western Interconnection for a full year of hourly operation.

Three regions emerge. The hydropower Pacific Northwest posts low, stable emissions; the coal-heavy Intermountain West runs high; the Sunbelt swings with solar output. Acting on these signals, by shifting computing in time or place, choosing sites, or buying renewables, achieves over 85 percent accuracy against true emission cuts. The authors stress that only large nodal simulations, not coarse averages, evaluate such strategies honestly. For carbon-aware computing, location is the lever.
arxiv-2512-19019:
Ayana Hussain and Ricky Fang ask how privacy protection changes the way neural networks train. Differential privacy limits what a model can reveal about single training examples. It does so by clipping each example's gradient and adding random noise, which also reshapes the training path.

The pair compare plain gradient descent and Adam with their private versions. Private training tends to lower sharpness, a measure of how steep the loss surface is, and can stop models from reaching classic stability limits. Still, the familiar edge-of-stability patterns largely persist, and large step sizes with weak privacy can even pass those limits. Privacy, they conclude, makes training less predictable.
arxiv-2512-19219:
Tiange Luo, Lajanugen Logeswaran, Jaekyeom Kim, and Justin Johnson fine-tune vision-language models more cheaply by being choosy. Standard low-rank adaptation updates every token and every attention head alike. Image-LoRA instead applies its small update only to visual tokens, leaving pure text flow untouched when no image is present.

It narrows further to the value path of a small set of heads, picked by a one-pass influence probe. The result needs far fewer trainable parameters and less training compute. On localization tests it matched standard adaptation, and shone when images dominated the input. Checks on text and video question answering, and on math, confirmed the savings.
arxiv-2512-19319: Hassan Alhussein gives a new way to define cochain complexes for dual Leibniz algebras, the gadgets that compute an algebra's cohomology. He builds a cochain map that embeds the complex of any dual Leibniz algebra into the Lie algebra complex of a tensor product, where a Leibniz algebra acts on it. Dual Leibniz cohomology thus reduces to classical Lie algebra cohomology. The authors claim the shift brings easier computation and fresh structural insight into a young corner of algebra.
arxiv-2512-19419:
Tomáš Pikálek, Miroslav Stibůrek, Tereza Tučková, and Petra Kolbábková push confocal imaging through an optical fiber as thin as a hair. Seeing deep inside a living brain normally means bulky microscopes limited to the first millimeter. Holographic endoscopy through multimode fibers reaches far deeper at similar sharpness, with minimal tissue damage.

Its weak point is contrast: without a pinhole, out-of-focus fluorescence floods the image, above all in densely labeled tissue. The team studies how light modes behave in different fiber types and finds a route to a confocal-like rejection of stray light. The result could pair deep reach with the clean sections confocal users rely on.
arxiv-2512-19719:
Zihao Lv, Siqi Ai, and Yanbin Zhang built a neural network to call how much life is left in a lithium-ion battery. Such calls guide care and safety work on machines. Battery wear mixes small local wiggles with a slow global trend. Many models catch one scale and miss the other. Their network, MDFA-Net, runs two paths side by side to catch both.

One path keeps shallow, fine detail that deep stacks tend to wash out. The other path is an encoder that tracks the long trend. Merging the two lets the model trace the fade in capacity with care. Tests used two public battery data sets. The method beat the best past methods at forecasting the life left in a cell.
arxiv-2512-19919:
José Diogo Da Costa Jesus leads a six-author team drafting a plan for near-perfect quantum gates. The target is gates with fidelity of 99.999 percent. The gates must also be fast, near seven nanoseconds per turn. That means driving qubits hard. In that regime the usual three-level model breaks down. New error paths open as photons leak out of the computing space.

The team works out those leak paths on paper, not in the lab. From the math come formulas to suppress each error channel. Two schemes, R1D and R2D, cancel set unwanted transitions. Old open questions on DRAG settings are settled too. Computer checks with real decoherence rates then predict very low error. The rate falls below one part in one hundred thousand for a fast pi turn.
arxiv-2512-20019:
Marios Papamichalis and Regina Ruane ask why well-linked people cluster in spatial networks. Such networks look assortative: hubs link to hubs. The standard read is sorting, where the popular seek each other out. Space gives a rival account. Neighbors draw from the same local pool, so their degrees move in step by chance. The paper asks when data can tell the two apart. It gives a three-part answer.

In a sparse model where latent popularity and place are coupled, the limit assortativity splits in exact form. One channel is an intensity-covariance channel. The other is a shared-neighbor channel. Sorting is the extra bit from dependence, at fixed mean degree and transitivity. Three plain summaries pin the model down in full. A computer-aided proof in exact rational arithmetic checks this. On eleven city networks the model is rejected. A national co-authorship network flips the verdict.
arxiv-2512-20119:
Mustafa Bakr and Smain Amari explain a three-way split in the behavior of spherical harmonics. The harmonics fall into sectoral, tesseral, and zonal families. The three react very unlike when parameters move off integers. Their claim is that the split is representation theory in disguise. It falls out of how the rotation group SO(3) sorts its states.

Sectoral harmonics are highest-weight states killed by the raising operator. That condition shrinks to a first-order equation. It can be solved for any positive real index. Tesseral modes come from ladder steps on those states. Zonal modes form the third branch. Wedge-shaped cavities change the rules for zonal modes, which can survive there with non-integer index. Cavity simulations with conducting wedges matched the predicted frequencies to sub-percent accuracy.
arxiv-2512-20219:
Weihan Zhang and Zijun Gao ask how much each variable causally contributes to an outcome. Causal measures of explainability are attractive because they point to real mechanisms and can travel to new settings. The authors build on a family of such quantities and focus on estimating them well from data.

They construct an estimator with a one-step correction drawn from semi-parametric efficiency theory. Exploiting independence among variables lowers the estimator's variance. For testing whether a variable explains nothing, they link the problem to Fisher's sharp null and use randomization-based inference. Simulations and an immigration-attitudes dataset show the method working in practice, including effects of interacting features.
arxiv-2512-20919:
Yaoting Zhou, Heng Shen, and seven co-authors make qubit readout work in the harshest regime of a leading quantum platform. Neutral-atom arrays read their qubits by fluorescence imaging, but short exposures that limit heating and atom loss leave only a photon or so per atom. The brightness distributions of the two states then overlap so heavily that a simple threshold fails.

Their remedy pairs Bayesian inference with a permutation-invariant neural network that compresses the iterative calculation into one forward pass, running about a hundred times faster. A weakly anchored variant needs calibration of only one state. Readout fidelity stays above ninety-nine percent even at heavy overlap, and clean Rabi oscillations and Ramsey fringes emerge where thresholding produced noise. Real-time readout of large arrays becomes feasible.
arxiv-2512-21119:
Anouar Bahrouni's paper offered a single truncation method for proving that nonlinear problems have countless solutions, even with no symmetry on hand to generate them. The author later withdrew the paper. Its results are claims of a withdrawn manuscript, not settled findings. It claimed three steps. First, sign-changing chains of answers for semilinear elliptic equations, from a refined variational truncation. Second, countless answers for nonvariational equations that lean on gradients, reached by coupling a cutoff to an iteration. Third, periodic Hamiltonian systems whose finite-interval multiplicity survives the passage to the whole real line.

The shared idea was a truncation scheme that sorts solutions one by one. One scheme would then serve both kinds of problem, and dynamics in endless dimensions alike. Because the author withdrew the paper, it stands in the archive as a record of an announced approach. Readers should no longer rely on what it claimed.
arxiv-2512-21319:
Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, and Peng Chen tackle a weakness in neural operators, the machine learning models that learn to solve partial differential equations. Standard training minimizes the equation's residual. But a small residual does not always mean a small error in the solution. The losses often use norms and penalty terms that do not match the equation's own structure.

The authors build a framework around first-order system least-squares objectives whose values are provably equal to the true solution error. Their reduced basis neural operator predicts coefficients for a precomputed basis, which keeps the model inside the right function space by design. They prove error bounds that split the total error into discretization, truncation, approximation, and sampling parts. Tests on diffusion and elasticity problems beat standard baselines, and the training loss doubles as a trustworthy error estimate after training.
arxiv-2512-21719: S. V. Evdokimov, Yu. V. Kharlov, and their co-authors report measurements of light sensors built from large-area silicon photomultiplier matrices with a wide dynamic range. Such sensors are used across particle and nuclear physics. The team measured how their matrix-based detectors perform and explored two uses: electromagnetic calorimetry, gauging particle energies from hundreds of kilo-electronvolts up to tens of giga-electronvolts, and gamma spectroscopy. The short report presents the measured properties as a basis for those uses.
arxiv-2512-22019:
Xuan-Heng Zhang and Cong-Feng Qiao calculate the masses of possible six-quark states built from a Lambda baryon paired with an anti-Sigma baryon. Their work responds to the BESIII experiment in China, which looked for a charm version of such a state near threshold and found none. The question is where in mass these states could plausibly sit.

Using QCD sum rules, a method that ties quark-level calculations to particle traits, the authors build two independent currents and include nonperturbative effects up to high dimension. Their ground-state masses for the charm states land near 5.8 GeV, too heavy for bound states, which agrees with the BESIII result. They also predict the matching bottom-quark spectrum for future searches.
arxiv-2512-22119:
Vlad Temkin, Zack Weinstein, Ruihua Fan, Daniel Podolsky, and Ehud Altman study quantum error correction in memories protected by a conserved charge. Their setting is a topological quantum memory with U(1) symmetry, where noise respects the charge. They ask how well the best possible decoder can do when it is allowed to measure each particle's local charge.

The best decoder's error threshold turns out to match a phase transition in a disordered 2D loop model. Field theory analysis and Monte Carlo simulations show the transition follows Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless behavior with a modified jump in winding number variance. The authors also map weaker decoders, find a loop-glass phase of confident mistakes, and show charge-aware decoding far outperforms charge-blind decoding.
arxiv-2512-22219:
Xinhao Cheng and a large team of co-authors present MPK, short for Mirage Persistent Kernel, a compiler and runtime that fuses an entire multi-GPU inference job into one mega-kernel. Normal serving runs one kernel per operator, which wastes time between operations. MPK instead draws the computation as a graph at the level of single streaming multiprocessors, the GPU's building blocks.

That fine-grained view allows software pipelining across operators and tight overlap of computation with communication. The compiler lowers tensor programs into optimized task graphs, and an in-kernel runtime schedules tasks across processors with no central controller. In evaluations, MPK cut end-to-end inference latency by up to 1.7 times versus leading kernel-per-operator systems, pushing language model serving close to hardware limits.
arxiv-2512-22719:
Gui-Qiang Chen, Feimin Huang, and Danli Wang prove that the randomly forced isentropic Euler equations admit global solutions of a meaningful kind. Those equations model gas flow shaken by random noise. The target objects are martingale entropy solutions with finite relative energy, for a general pressure law. Random forcing destroys the uniform bounds that deterministic proofs rely on, which is the core problem.

Their tool is a compensated compactness framework in Lebesgue spaces, used to pass to the limit in a vanishing viscosity scheme. Careful uniform estimates on the trial solutions deliver existence. Higher-order energy estimates then establish entropy inequalities for wider entropy pairs, plus compactness of the solution set. For polytropic gases and every adiabatic exponent, the global solutions satisfy the local energy inequality under weaker demands on the data than earlier work required.
arxiv-2512-22819:
Hualie Jiang, Ziyang Song, Zhiqiang Lou, Rui Xu, and Minglang Tan adapt a leading depth-estimation model to panoramic images. Knowing distances across a full 360-degree view matters for robots and augmented reality, but panoramic methods trail ordinary perspective models because training data are scarce. Their system, DA360, starts from Depth Anything V2 and asks what the base model already does well on panoramas.

Two light changes do most of the work. A per-image shift learned from the vision transformer's class token converts the base model's relative disparity output into scale-invariant disparity that yields clean three-dimensional point clouds. Circular padding in the decoder removes the seam where the panorama wraps around. Fine-tuned on synthetic indoor and outdoor panoramas, DA360 cuts error sharply versus its base model and beats prior specialized methods on real indoor benchmarks and a new outdoor dataset.
arxiv-2512-23419:
Alex Lewandowski and co-authors rethink the big world hypothesis, the idea that a learning agent's world is always bigger than the agent itself. Continual learning is often motivated this way, and recent versions impose capacity constraints that force endless adaptation. The authors find such hand-imposed constraints ad hoc and hard to build in. They propose a different grounding: the agent is embedded in its environment, an automaton simulated inside a general computer.

Any such embedded automaton is constrained, whatever its capacity, and the authors prove this setting equals a partially observable Markov decision process over a countably infinite state space. They define an objective called interactivity, the ability to keep adapting. A model-based reinforcement learning algorithm pursues it, and in their testbed deep nonlinear networks failed to sustain interactivity while deep linear networks sustained more as capacity grew.
arxiv-2512-23919:
Boleslaw Szymanski, Yongtao Zhang, Brian Uzzi, and Mohammed Shahid Modi ask whether collaborating with prizewinners makes a computer scientist more likely to win prizes. Prizes shape research by giving credibility and money, yet their social mechanics are understudied. The team analyzed more than one hundred scientific prizes and the collaboration records of over five thousand computer science prizewinners.

Winners, they find, collaborate earlier and more often with other winners than comparable researchers do. After a first prize, researchers of all ages collaborate more with prizewinners; doing so raises the collaborator's own odds of an award. General-prize winners work with others more broadly than specialized-prize winners. Matching and regression methods confirm that stronger prizewinner collaboration tracks higher prizewinning odds. A closing comparison examines recent Nobel Prizes reaching computer scientists, including the growing share of physics prizes going to physics-computing collaborations, against Turing Award paths.
arxiv-2512-24019:
Haijian Shao, Wei Liu, Xing Deng, and Yingtao Jiang study quantum neural networks. These networks often carry far more gates than they need. The extra bulk makes them hard to run on today's noisy quantum machines. Their framework, q-iPrune, removes spare gates in a single pass.

Older pruning methods rely on rough rules of thumb. q-iPrune instead compares each gate with others in the same algebraic family. A distance measure shows how similarly two gates behave on the task. A gate is dropped only when a stand-in keeps results within a stated error bound. The authors prove three guarantees about this process. They cover completeness, accuracy, and running time. A noise-tuned setting adapts the pruning to real hardware. Tests on standard quantum learning benchmarks cut gate counts sharply. Performance losses stayed within the promised limits.
arxiv-2512-24119:
Yuan Feng and colleagues argue that benchmarks for geometric reasoning in vision-language models are too shallow. Textbook-based test sets risk leaking into training data, most scoring checks only the final answer rather than the reasoning, and a single score cannot show where a model goes wrong.

Their benchmark, GeoBench, grades geometry at four levels: seeing the figure correctly, planning toward the goal, applying theorems rigorously, and catching and fixing one's own errors. Six formally verified tasks, generated by a companion system, probe those levels in order. Experiments found that strong reasoning models beat general multimodal ones, but every model's performance fell steeply as tasks grew harder. Breaking goals into sub-goals and filtering out irrelevant premises proved decisive for accuracy, while chain-of-thought prompting, surprisingly, hurt on some tasks. The authors offer the benchmark plus practical guidance for building better geometry solvers.
arxiv-2512-24319:
Diana Bakirova and Oleg Malkov ask whether a brown dwarf hides near the Sun. Brown dwarfs are faint objects between stars and planets in mass. The census of the solar neighborhood reaches twenty parsecs. That census is incomplete, though. Faint objects escape detection easily. The authors correct for that incompleteness statistically.

From the corrected spatial distribution, they derive a probability formula. It estimates the chance of an object at a given distance. The headline number is striking. With probability near one half, a brown dwarf sits within a short distance of the Sun. The paper discusses whether such an object could be multiple. A companion could hide the system longer. Reasons for the non-detection so far are weighed. The result is a careful odds statement, not a claimed discovery.
arxiv-2512-24519:
Khalil Al Handawi and Fabian Bastin analyze airline alliances as a graph problem. Airlines join alliances to widen their networks and cut costs. What alliances do to competition is less clear. The authors build metrics for two things: how competitive each flight segment is, and how deeply each airline penetrates markets given its alliance.

The analysis becomes a bi-objective optimization. Competition and market penetration are maximized together. Graph partitioning over multiple attributes drives the method. Algorithms solve the problem on real flight schedule data. Results illuminate how alliances are structured. They also show what alliance membership implies for rivalry and efficiency. Airlines and regulators both care about that balance. The work gives them a quantitative lens on alliance design.
arxiv-2512-25019:
Shufang Qiang, Peiwen Wu, and Yongchao Zhang study lepton flavor violation in the minimal left-right symmetric model, which restores parity to the weak interaction and explains tiny neutrino masses through seesaw mechanisms. A scalar from right-handed symmetry breaking can induce flavor-violating effects at one loop, through mixing with heavy right-handed neutrinos. If that scalar is light, below the gigaelectronvolt scale, signals multiply.

Flavor-changing muon and tau decays with visible or invisible products, plus anomalous supernova signatures, are among the consequences explored. Particle physics readers get concrete places to look for left-right symmetry. Rare decays are powerful probes because the Standard Model forbids them almost completely.
arxiv-2601-06719:
Adithya Murali and three co-authors build proof tools for heap-based code in a 2026 paper. Heap logics help prove that code which links chunks of memory is right. They build the first two heap logics with chunks left implicit, they report.

Those logics give a strong pledge on proof: all true claims get proved in time. The pledge treats terms that call on themselves in a broad fixpoint sense. Proofs that once stalled can now be sure to close in the end. Left-implicit chunks make proof specs much less of a chore to write. Those who prove code right gain a tool of a new class. The work pushes heap proof toward full self-run in thought, if not yet in fact. Pointer code is where proof help is most in need today.
arxiv-2601-06819: Feihu Liu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with unimodular equivalence of integral simplices. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. China, Testing the unimodular equivalence of two full-dimensional integral simplices can be reduced to testing unimodular permutation (UP) equivalence of two nonsingular matrices. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06919:
Meng-Dong Zhu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with high-capacity dual degrees of freedom quantum secret sharing protocol beyond the linear rate-distance. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Quantum secret sharing (QSS) is the multipartite cryptographic primitive.

Most of existing QSS protocols are limited by the linear rate-distance bound, and cannot realize the long-distance and high-capacity multipartite key distribution. The work proposes a polarization (Pol) and phase (Ph) dual degrees of freedom (dual-DOF) QSS protocol based on the weak coherent pulse (WCP) sources. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07219:
Thanh-Nhan Vo and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to edit a photo by text. Their tool is called VENUS. Top tools in this field face a trade-off as they edit. They must keep the parts of the scene that should not change. They must also make the new parts fit the sense of the scene.

When a tool fails, it can build a whole new photo and lose the old scene, or miss the edit the user asked for. VENUS takes a new route based on a scene graph. A scene graph lists each thing in the scene and how the things relate. VENUS also flips noise in the photo back and forth as it works. That route gives the user more control over each edit. The graph keeps the edit tied to the things it should touch.
arxiv-2601-07419:
Niklas Kormann and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers position. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Over-smoothing and over-squashing have been extensively studied in the literature on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) over the past years.

We challenge this prevailing focus in GNN research, arguing that these phenomena are less critical for practical applications than assumed. We suggest that performance decreases often stem from uninformative receptive fields rather than over-smoothing. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07519:
Margherita Firenze and colleagues take on slice-to-volume reconstruction, a core task in medical imaging. The problem: turn misaligned two-dimensional slices into one three-dimensional view of anatomy. Scans of moving patients, especially fetal imaging, rarely line up neatly. The method must estimate both the 3D anatomy and each slice's pose. Their 2026 preprint uses modern neural networks.

Fully convolutional networks excel at learning features across scales and making fast predictions. Yet their use for slice-to-volume reconstruction remains little explored, the authors note. The team proposes a fast approach built on multi-scale unrolled optimization. Unrolling turns an iterative solver into network layers. Readers in medical imaging get a method aimed at speed without giving up the joint estimation task.
arxiv-2601-07619:
Luisa Estrada, Sasha Glendinning, and Andrew Nugent review how scholars model the manipulation of opinion. Their 2026 review covers mathematical and computer science approaches to opinion formation. Manipulation means deliberate efforts to shift what a population believes. The authors introduce the main tools and compare them side by side.

Those tools include ordinary and partial differential equations, chance-based models, control theory, and rules for how views spread. Each tool makes different assumptions about how people influence each other. A side by side look helps readers pick the right model for a set case, such as a vote or a web site. The review also clarifies where models disagree. It serves newcomers entering the field and experts who want shared words across their fields.
arxiv-2601-07819:
Robert Petersen and colleagues argue that thyroid treatment should use two hormone measures, not one. Standard practice adjusts thyroid replacement dose using only TSH. The authors say adding free thyroxine, FT4, may benefit patients with hypothyroidism. Their 2026 preprint uses nonlinear programming solvers to generate hypothalamus-pituitary curves for individual patients. Those curves describe how the gland system responds to hormone levels.

A curve per patient could guide dosing more personally than a single lab value. Nonlinear programming finds the curve that best fits a patient's measurements. The hypothalamus-pituitary axis controls TSH release, so its shape matters. Clinicians treating stubborn hypothyroidism cases are the readers. The paper blends endocrinology with optimization methods. It proposes a tool, not just a critique of current practice.
arxiv-2601-07919:
Aishwarya Linesh Thakur and colleagues probe the dense gas around long gamma-ray bursts using the burst's own light. The region within one to one hundred parsecs of these bursts was unexplored. Extreme ionization by the burst blocks optical absorption spectroscopy at those distances. The authors show the burst's ionizing flux stamps a unique time- and space-dependent pattern on the gas. X-ray absorption can read that pattern. Their 2026 preprint develops the method.

The gas near a burst traces the star-forming region that produced its progenitor star. Reading its density and structure tests where massive stars die. A time-dependent pattern is a gift: it encodes distance as well as composition. The method turns a problem, blinding ionization, into the measuring tool itself. The paper serves high-energy astrophysicists and interstellar medium scholars. It opens a scale around bursts that was previously dark.
arxiv-2601-08119: Kisun Lee computes new bounds on the asymptotic rank of tensors. The 2026 arXiv paper applies numerical implicitization across all computationally feasible cases. It uses the geometric framework of Kaski and Michalek, which studies secant varieties of tensor spaces. By showing that low-degree vanishing polynomials are absent on these varieties, Lee obtains sharper bounds. The new bounds improve on generic border rank bounds. Tensor rank matters in algebraic complexity, where it measures how hard matrix multiplication and related tasks truly are.
arxiv-2601-08219:
Paimon Goulart and Evangelos Papalexakis ask whether a small agent team can take a matrix apart. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes an agentic approach to matrix deflation. A solver language model builds rank-1 singular value updates, one slice at a time.

A vision language model then accepts or rejects each update and decides when to stop. That removes the need for fixed norm thresholds to end the process. In-context learning and row or column permutations improve solver stability. Permutations expose visually coherent structure the vision model can judge. The work tests whether paired models can handle a classic numerical task with judgment instead of rigid rules.
arxiv-2601-08519:
Kexin Bao and five co-authors present CD2, a constrained dataset distillation method for incremental learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets few-shot class-incremental learning, where classes arrive with few training samples. Catastrophic forgetting is the key problem: new learning erases old classes.

Many methods store previous knowledge in external memory and treat it equally with new classes. The authors argue that habit fails to preserve what is essential. Constrained distillation instead compresses past knowledge into a small distilled dataset with safeguards. A compact memory that keeps the right examples could let field-deployed classifiers grow without bloating storage or losing early classes.
arxiv-2601-08719:
Vikas Dwivedi, Monica Sigovan, and Bruno Sixou work on hard math problems that come from physics. Such problems can change fast in one place and slow in a next place. Old tools that learn from physics rules often fail on them. They need much time to train, and they need hand set wave sizes to work well.

The team builds a new tool with the short name KAPI-ELM. It splits the space into soft parts that can shift and grow. Those parts set both the test points and the width of small bell shaped curves. In this way the tool can move from a wide view to a fine view in one smooth step. It needs no fixed wave parts and no hard walls in the space.
arxiv-2601-08819:
Roshni Kaushik and Reid Simmons ask how old users like a coach robot to speak and move. The robot guides users through safe moves for health. Some users like much talk and praise. Some like brief cues. A wrong pace can bore a user or rush them, and they may quit the plan.

The team tests paces of speech and body cues with old users. They watch how users react and what pace they pick. The goal is a coach that fits each user, not one pace for all. A reader who builds health bots gets user facts, not guesses. The facts can guide how oft a bot should speak, nod, or stay still.
arxiv-2601-08919:
Sourav Saha and Mandar Mitra grade chat models that act as judges of text and image work. Labs now use such judges in place of paid human marks. A judge score is cheap and fast. But a coarse score can hide where a judge is weak, such as on close calls or on one class of task.

The pair call for fine grade checks. A judge should be tested by task type, by gap size, and by type of flaw in the work it marks. Fine checks show if a judge can tell a near miss from a true hit. A reader who uses AI judges gets a stricter scale. It can stop a lab from trust in a judge that fails where it counts.
arxiv-2601-09219:
Guy Kortsarz gives a fast near best plan for a tree link task with a strong ratio. The task starts with a tree, a net with no loops. Add links so the net stays whole if any one link fails. Use as few new links as one can. That task is called the Tree Augmentation Problem, and it is hard to solve in full.

His plan gets at most four thirds of the best count, a tight ratio for this task. It climbs by rungs, a step view of links, and it holds off some picks to later steps. A reader in net design gets a plan with a proof of its ratio. It fits backup link buys for real nets.
arxiv-2601-09719:
Hoyoon Byun and four co-authors propose a steadier building block for large language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper offers a bounded hyperbolic tangent as an alternative to pre-layer normalization. Pre-layer normalization is the default choice in current models and is key to stable pretraining.

The default has costs: it repeats statistical calculations and suffers a curse of depth. As layers pile up, hidden states grow in size and spread, which destabilizes training. A bounded activation could cap that growth by design. A cheaper, calmer block would ease the training of deeper models.
arxiv-2601-10019:
Mykola Pinchuk adds time sums as inputs for a boost tree model. The model type is XGBoost. The task is to guess if a user will click an ad. The data set is the Avazu click set. Time sums pool past clicks by hour spans.

A strict rule guards the build. Sums for one hour can use only prior hours. No data from the same hour or later may leak in. That rule keeps the test fair, as in real use. The paper asks which spans help most. It also checks if the gains hold on a later time split, not just in the build span.
arxiv-2601-10219:
M. J. Everitt and co authors rebuilt a physics degree from the ground up. The degree is at Loughborough University. Past fixes tend to tweak one course at a time. The team took a new path. They treat the whole degree as one rig.

The rig view comes from systems design. Each part has a job that can be checked. The lead rule is real world truth. Tasks should act like work in labs and firms. The paper lays out how the new degree was built. It gives a case for how a degree can be planned as a whole.
arxiv-2601-10319:
G. V. Voloshin, K. A. Barantsev, and A. N. Litvinov track a light shift in an atomic trap. The trap holds atoms in a dark state by two light beams. It is named coherent population trapping. Its tone is used in clocks and sensors, so shifts in it count.
