Light from the beams can shift that tone. The team model the shift with a three level atom in a Lambda form. They add one more level at the top. Both weak and strong links to off tone beams are in the model. The paper gives a fresh term for the shift.
arxiv-2601-10419:
J. Dhamothiran and Saudamini Nayak build simple Lie superalgebras from their root sets. Superalgebras mix two kinds of parts, even and odd. Their root sets grade how those parts link. Serganova set rules for such root sets and sorted the base kinds.

Those root sets match the base superalgebras one to one. Dhamothiran and Nayak give one joint build for all of them. They start from the root set as a pure form. They pick a base with the least count of null roots. The build then yields the full algebra. One path thus spans the whole class.
arxiv-2601-10519:
Andrea Melis, Andrea Piroddi, and Roberto Girau use Transformer models to run cognitive radios. A cognitive radio scans the air waves and adapts. It picks a band, a code, and a rate to fit the scene. That skill can lift how well the scarce air waves are used.

Transformers are strong at sequence tasks. The team set them to pick how the radio should send. The picks adapt as the scene shifts. The work claims gains in how full the band is used. It also claims gains in how firm and safe the link is. Such radios may serve dense nets of the next era.
arxiv-2601-10619:
Karol I. Wysokiński and Marcin M. Wysokiński look past the standard Hubbard model of electrons in solids. That model treats electrons that repel each other on the same site. Real materials may also show correlated hopping, where an electron's jump depends on its neighbors. The authors test what this extra effect does in two settings.

First, they study the superconducting transition near the Mott metal-insulator transition, where a metal turns into an insulator. Second, they study transport through tiny quantum dot devices linked to electrodes. Both settings are places where strong interactions rule the behavior. The results help show when the simple Hubbard picture is not enough for real devices.
arxiv-2601-10919:
Michael T. Gorczyca writes a note on a quiet flaw in log-normal trigonometric regression: harmonics that the fit leaves vague. Scientists who study rhythms fit responses that rise and fall over time. The standard fit models the response as a sum of sine waves. When the response does not follow a bell curve, analysts either transform it or move to a GLM.

Gorczyca looks at the log-normal case, where the response is logged before fitting. The note flags how harmonics can be left out or set too loosely in that setup. Missing a harmonic can bias estimates of a rhythm's phase and strength. Day-night and seasonal studies lean on such fits, so the warning has real bite for rhythm research.
arxiv-2601-11019:
Xinwei Wu and co-authors hunt for the translation switch inside large language models. Models often translate well with no task-specific fine-tuning. The inner mechanism behind that ready skill is largely opaque. The team uses sparse autoencoders, tools that pull apart a model's activity into readable features. They build a framework to find task-specific features.

Their target is the set of features that initiate translation, the switch that tells the model to switch languages. Finding such features would show how one model routes itself among skills. It could also give engineers a dial: turn the feature on or off to control behavior. The work advances the craft of reading models from the inside.
arxiv-2601-11119:
Petr Kolman and Hans Raj Tiwary study the bond polytope of a graph. A cut splits a graph into two parts. A cut is a bond when both parts stay connected. The bond polytope is the convex hull of all bonds, a geometric object that encodes them. Computing the maximum weight bond is NP-hard, even for planar graphs.

The authors examine how the polytope behaves under vertex-sums and edge-sums, ways of gluing graphs together. If the polytope of a glued graph can be built from its parts, hard problems may split too. Polyhedral views turn discrete problems into geometry, where facets hint at algorithms. The work serves combinatorial optimization, where bonds model reliable network partitions.
arxiv-2601-11719:
Ho Fung Tsoi and Dylan Rankin, at the University of Pennsylvania, study how to group jets in high energy physics. Jets are sprays of parts made when quarks and gluons fly out of a crash. Their method, called jBOT in the work, learns from data with no labels.

They use self-distillation, where a model trains a copy of itself. The learned traits can then be tuned for later tasks. The title states that clear groups with real sense emerge from this training. Such traits could help sort jets by type with less hand made code.
arxiv-2601-11819: Shirlene Rose Bandela, Sanjeev Parthasarathy, and Vaibhav Garg share a data set of hard life stories from Reddit. The posts come mostly from women. They deal with loss of a pregnancy, abortion, and sexual violence, and the text warns that some may find the content hard to read. People post such stories to share pain and seek support. A clean data set lets teams study how support is given online. It can also help build tools that treat such posts with care.
arxiv-2601-11919:
Nam Nguyen, Thinh Nguyen, and Bella Bose study lossy compression built for a task. The source is a Bernoulli stream. The error gauge is Hamming distance. The class to keep is tied to the source by a symmetric noisy link.

They derive closed forms for the trade. That trade links rate, error, and class skill. They treat both the one-shot case with shared randomness and its dual form. Task-first compression can save bits when full detail is not needed. The forms give exact limits for this clean case.  Closed forms give exact limits for this clean task.
arxiv-2601-12319:
A team with Narendra Sahu propose a testable frame for light fermion dark matter aided by a first-order phase transition. The dark matter mass sits in the MeV to GeV range. It is charged under a dark U(1) gauge group.

A scalar field breaks that group and gives mass to the dark gauge boson. Forbidden dark matter needs aid to form at the right rate in the early universe. A phase transition can give that aid, and can also make gravitational waves. Those waves give a test path for the frame.
arxiv-2601-12419:
Mahammad Namazov, Tomas Koref, and Ivan Habernal study how to explain the calls of legal AI. Their test case is outcome classification for cases at the European Court of Human Rights. Trust in such tools needs clear reasons, not just a bare verdict. Some teams build task specific ways to pull out the key text.

Other ways read the model weights to judge which words drove the call. The open question is which style of rationale matches what legal experts would pick. The title gives the thrust of the result: legal experts disagree with what these tools extract. That gap matters for any court facing use of AI. A rationale that lawyers reject may fail the trust test even if the verdict is right.
arxiv-2601-12519:
Abdullah Umut Hamzaogullari and Arkadas Ozakin teach neural networks the paths of relativistic particles. Their tool is a Lagrangian neural network, which learns a Lagrangian from trajectory data. From that learned law, geodesics and dynamics can be derived. Such networks promise physics aware learning, but their odd training objective makes them unstable.

That instability has limited their use on complex systems so far. The team present a stabilized form of the network for harder cases. Their test ground is relativistic geodesics and chaotic dynamics, both stiff tests. Chaotic systems punish small errors fast, so stability really matters there. A stable learner could help model black hole orbits and other extreme paths.
arxiv-2601-12719:
Lin Zhao and a large team, from Snap Inc. and Northeastern University, bring video generation to mobile phones. Diffusion transformers have raised the quality of generated video in recent years. Their heavy compute cost makes real time or on device generation infeasible, though. Phones lack the power and cooling of data center hardware.

Their model, S2DiT, is a streaming sandwich diffusion transformer. It is designed for efficient, high fidelity, streaming generation on mobile hardware. Streaming means frames flow out as they are made, not after a long wait. Sandwich refers to its layered design, detailed in the work. Mobile generation would put video creation tools in every pocket.
arxiv-2601-12819:
G. H. Yu validates a detector encapsulation for a dark matter search upgrade called COSINE-100U. The upgrade boosts sensitivity by immersing the detector array in liquid scintillator. The array must run cold, at minus thirty degrees Celsius. Crystals of sodium iodide with thallium serve as the sensing material.

Yu built a module with the new encapsulation design. A dedicated long term stability study checked it under the planned conditions. Encapsulation must keep the crystals dry and intact while cold and submerged. A failed seal could ruin a rare event search that runs for years. Validation of this kind is the quiet groundwork of dark matter science.
arxiv-2601-13119:
Satyam Sahu and a large team tune the sound like waves of a layered crystal. The crystal is CrSBr with part of its bromine swapped for chlorine. Swaps of one atom for a kin atom give a clean knob to tune how a crystal shakes.

The team pairs two tools. They use Raman light scatter, split by the angle of the light, to read the shakes. They also run first principles sums to match what they see. They track how the shakes shift as the chlorine share grows to about half. Their care with low symmetry helps staff who want to set shake traits by design in flat matter.
arxiv-2601-13219:
Dirk Wulferding and a large team show how a small swap can wake hid waves in a linked crystal. In such stuff, spin and orbit forces vie with field from the crystal plan. That vie can make joint spin orbit waves, called magnons. Such waves bend fast when the plan or charge state shifts.

The team uses a dopant, a small swap of one atom for a kin, to break the plan's symmetry. That break lets hid magnons show in their probes. The trick gives a knob to tune wave acts past spin only rules. For staff who dream of wave based tools, hid modes that can be switched are a prize.
arxiv-2601-13419:
Lorenzo Mauri and co-authors read gene data through the pathways genes serve, not just one gene at a time. Gene marks make sense in groups. A pathway is a set of genes that run one cell job. Old tools cut data dims with no tie to such groups, so their parts can lack a clear life sense.

Pathway led tools do exist, but they oft bind with stiff terms or need huge hand work. The team builds Bayes factor models that take pathway notes in a flex way. Latent parts then map to real cell jobs. For bio teams, parts with a life sense beat parts that just fit sums.
arxiv-2601-13819:
Balma Duch, Pere Masjuan, and Hubert Spiesberger compute a small quantum correction to electron-quark scattering in 2026. The term is the gamma-Z box graph at one loop, at low energy. Low momentum transfer means the particles graze, not smash. Both electron and quark masses are kept non-zero in the work.

From the result, they extract coupling constants for a low-energy effective theory. That theory includes parity-violating four-fermion interaction terms. Such constants feed tests of the Standard Model at low energy. Precise values help experiments spot any crack in the theory.
arxiv-2601-13919:
Yuezhe Yang and co-authors build a diagnosis system that links patient records with X-rays in 2026. Automated clinical diagnosis must integrate multi-modal data and reason over complex contexts. Medical vision-language models have advanced report generation and visual question answering. Most methods still treat each case in isolation.

That isolated style ignores longitudinal health records and related patient examples. Their HyperWalker uses dynamic hypergraph-based deep diagnosis for multi-hop modeling. Links across records let the model reason over a patient's history. Richer context could raise the quality of AI help in clinics.
arxiv-2601-14019:
Frederik Walter and co-authors build a security frame for chemical systems that act like locks in 2026. They introduce chemical functions, which model chemical systems as noisy challenge-response primitives. A challenge is an input, and the response depends on the chemical makeup. The idea builds on the theory of physical functions.

They define robustness, unclonability, and unpredictability for such functions. Both finite and asymptotic regimes get rigorous treatment. Security games capture the adversary's power and the goals at stake. Chemical functions could one day tag drugs or goods against counterfeits.
arxiv-2601-14119:
Nikita Titov and Andrea Trombettoni compare two quantum models on graphs in the large limit in 2026. One is the O(n) quantum rotor model, defined on a general graph. The other is the quantum spherical model on the same graph. They take the limit as n grows without bound.

They show the large n limit of the rotor model has the same critical behavior. Critical behavior means how the system acts near a phase change. The critical exponents depend solely on the spectral dimension of the graph. That single number captures how waves spread on the graph's structure.
arxiv-2601-14319:
Fabian Veider, Georg Jäger, and Bao Quoc Tang model opinion spread on social media in this 2026 paper. The rise of platforms and their recommendation algorithms has raised fears of polarization and echo chambers. The team studies those fears with an adaptive voter model. In such a model, people hold opinions and rewire their links over time.

They compare two ways links can change. Free global rewiring lets a person connect with anyone who shares their opinion. Friend-of-a-friend local rewiring copies how platforms suggest links, as on Facebook or LinkedIn. By setting the two side by side, the study shows how the rewiring rule itself shapes the social network.
arxiv-2601-15419:
Yashuai Yan and Dongheui Lee teach one control space to serve many robot bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with cross-embodiment humanoid control. Humans and humanoid robots come in many shapes: single-arm, dual-arm, and legged forms among them.

The framework learns a shared latent representation of motion. It works in two stages. First, a decoupled latent space captures local motion patterns body part by body part, using contrastive learning. That structure allows accurate, flexible retargeting of motion. One person's movement can then drive robots of very different size and body builds.
arxiv-2601-15619:
Jie Lin and five co-authors report a nearby binary star system in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system pairs a compact object with a K-type star companion. It is a wide post-common envelope binary. That means the pair once shared an envelope of gas, then shed it. A white dwarf is the candidate for the compact partner. Such binaries test theories of how the shared-envelope stage works.

Most known systems of this kind have tight orbits. Their periods run from hours to a few days. Wide systems like this one are harder to explain. Standard accounts assume the envelope is expelled with low efficiency. A wide survivor challenges or refines that picture. Finding one in the solar neighborhood is a bonus. Nearby systems allow close, detailed study.
arxiv-2601-15819:
Yanfeng Zhang and seven co-authors improve short-packet wireless links in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ultra-reliable low-latency communication, or URLLC, serves tasks that cannot wait or fail. Sparse vector coding is a promising method for such short packets. Their scheme is dual-mapping sparse vector coding, or DM-SVC. Dual mapping is the twist they add to the base method. The aim is better transmission performance for short packets.

Short packets carry control signals, alarms, and machine commands. Reliability there matters more than raw speed. Next-generation networks promise URLLC for factories and vehicles. Each coding gain makes those promises more credible. The paper speaks to wireless engineers designing for the strictest latency budgets.
arxiv-2601-16019:
L. Scholz-Díaz, A. R. Gallazzi, S. Zibetti, and D. Mattolini relate galaxy mass to dark halos in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the standard cosmological model, galaxies grow inside dark matter halos. Halos supply the gravitational framework for complex baryonic processes. How far halo properties shape what we observe stays unclear. The authors study the stellar-to-total dynamical mass relation. They resolve it spatially, looking inside galaxies rather than at whole-galaxy sums.

Spatial resolution shows where stars dominate and where dark matter takes over. That pattern tests how baryons settle into halos. Galaxy evolution is the joint story of both components. A resolved mass relation gives modelers a sharper target than global ratios. Surveys with integral-field data make such studies possible at scale.
arxiv-2601-16119:
Erkao Bao, Robi Huq and Shengzhen Ning study a Morse view of group acts on shapes. Their 2026 preprint deals with shapes moved by a Lie group. A Morse tool reads shape traits from high and low points of a map. The team use a fix trick to make the map work with group acts. Small shifts of the map then give firm Morse Bott maps.

With firm maps, they build the group linked form of shape counts. They also gain the cross term rules the build needs. The build stems from the Austin and Braam path in the field. Firm maps close a gap in that path. The work adds rigour to group shape counts.
arxiv-2601-16719:
Martina Alutto, Fabrizio Dabbene, Angela Fontan, Karl Johansson, and Chiara Ravazzi model a race of two new tech goods. Folks in a crowd sway each other by talk. Use of one good feeds views of that good. Views then feed fresh use in a loop. Their 2026 preprint builds a two-layer frame for this race.

Once folks adopt one good, some grow sour on it. They may switch to the rival good. The frame tracks such switches over time. It can show when a lead is safe or frail. Firms and towns could use it to time launches. It may also flag where ads or rules tip a race.
arxiv-2601-16919:
Thomas Tram builds a light tool to teach the early cosmos in class. The cosmic microwave glow is a faint light from the young cosmos. Its wave spread shifts with each cosmic dial. Those shifts are a core theme in space class. But live play with the dials oft costs too much compute. His 2026 preprint shares CosmoSlider, a tool for that play.

Sliders let class users turn many dials at once. The glow's curve then shifts in real time. Light code keeps the tool fast on plain laptops. Such play helps class users feel how dials shape the glow. It turns a hard chart into a hands-on lab.
arxiv-2601-17119:
Babette Döbrich, Jan Jerhot, Karim Massri, Jonathan Schubert, and Tommaso Spadaro weigh a new hunt for faint bits at CERN. Faint bits may hide in the MeV to GeV mass range. Beam-dump hunts are a strong way to seek them. A proton beam hits a block, and faint bits slip through. Their 2026 preprint sets an old hunt next to a new-site plan.

The old hunt is NA62, run in dump mode at CERN. The new plan reuses its eyes at a fresh hall, ECN3. Same eyes, new hall, more beam time and reach. Such hunts could crack the dark stuff case. Cost-wise reuse makes the case more strong.
arxiv-2601-17319:
Hien Duy Nguyen and Dan Wang study process control through p-values. Factories and labs chart key values to catch drift early. The authors chart p-values instead of raw measures. When a process is in control, a valid p-value stream is super-uniform. That trait holds with no model of the process itself. It works in nonparametric and two-phase designs.

A chart with no model demand is a strong draw. Teams can watch complex processes they cannot fully describe. False alarms stay in check if the p-values are valid. The work gives quality teams a flexible watch tool. It shifts focus from the measure to the proof of change.
arxiv-2601-17519:
Aida Abiad and five co-authors bound the edge-isoperimetric number of graphs. That number measures how well a graph's sets connect to the rest. It is tied to edge expansion, a core trait for networks. The team gives sharp spectral bounds, approximations, and exact values. Their focus is graph powers and rich families. Distance-regular graphs and finite geometry graphs are among them.

Expansion governs how fast data spreads in a network. It also sets the strength of codes and designs. Exact values for key families save later guesswork. Spectral bounds let users test big graphs fast. The work serves network science and pure graph theory. It links shape, spectrum, and spread in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17819:
Mi Zou and co-authors report a lab test of a quantum key method for groups. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum cryptographic conferencing. The method lets many parties build one shared secret key over a quantum network. Its safety rests on the laws of physics, not on hard math. So far, though, tests have reached only across city-scale links.

The team runs a phase-matching protocol with three light levels. They count the finite-size effects that real runs must face, since keys are built from limited data. Longer safe links would help quantum networks grow past one metro area. Each lab step of this kind tests gear and theory at once. The work pushes group key sharing toward wider use.
arxiv-2601-17919:
Arnulf J. Snedker-Nielsen and co-authors explore making color centers in silicon for quantum devices. Their 2026 preprint deals with silicon-on-insulator, a wafer type built for chips. Color centers are tiny defects that can emit one photon at a time. Some, like the T center, also hold spins that link to light. Those links can tie photons and spins into networks for quantum tech.

The team studies how several kinds of centers form in this material. They stress forms that could be made in bulk with chip-style methods. A source that fits the chip industry could speed quantum hardware a great deal. The paper maps routes toward that goal and the trade-offs in each.
arxiv-2601-18019: S. Carolina García-Martínez, Pascual Lucas, and H. Fabián Ramírez-Ospina study a class of surfaces in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spaces. Their 2026 preprint treats orientable surfaces immersed in these three-dimensional spacetimes. The surfaces are of L1-2-type, a class defined through the shape operator and its traces. The paper works out the properties that such surfaces must have in each of the two spaces.
arxiv-2601-18519:
Andrei Bengus-Lasnier and Mikhail Shkolnikov study a way to shrink hard shape tasks into a plane of counts. The shrink turns curves on a shape into points on a flat chart, where they are much less hard to count. A phase tag rides with each point and holds key facts the shrink would lose. The trick has roots in a way to build real curves from flat parts.

It also sits at the heart of a famed proof that tied counts in the shrunk world to counts in the full world. The pair ask what the set of points for one phase looks like as a whole. Those sets, called fibers, chart how much the phase tag pins down. A clear chart helps staff use the shrink with trust. It may also spark new ways to count curves.
arxiv-2601-18619:
Jorge Quesada and Ghassan AlRegib teach vision tools to mark small, sparse things in shots with few hand marks to learn from. Self-taught tools learn form from raw shots with no tags. That path works well for big, plain zones of a shot. It works far less well when the thing to mark is small, thin, or spread in specks.

A speck can wash out when the tool shrinks the shot to learn its broad form. Their plan makes the tool scale-aware, so fine specks stay in view while it learns. That care should lift marks on roads, crops, and scans where the key zone is tiny. Good marks with few hand tags could cut cost in fields from health to maps. The work names a blind spot in self-taught vision and sets out to fix it.
arxiv-2601-19219:
Shota Ono and Ryotaro Ohse ask where each kind of atom sits in a mixed layered crystal. The crystals swap sulfur, selenium, and tellurium in a structure that can flip between an insulating and a metallic phase. That flip, from the 2H form to a skewed form, has been seen in tungsten based mixes.

Tellurium atoms, reports say, favor one specific site in the skewed structure. Ono and Ohse work out the site preference across the family, for molybdenum and tungsten alike. Where atoms sit decides the phase and the traits, so the map guides the design of switchable thin materials.
arxiv-2601-19319:
Efthymios Sofos counts how often a polynomial takes square free values, and pins down the error in that count. A square free number has no square factor past one. A folk conjecture says the count of such values for an integer polynomial grows like a constant times the range, with a small error.

Sofos proves that the average error is the fourth root of the main term, a precise rate. Average results cover the typical polynomial even when each single case stays out of reach. Square free values feed number theory questions about equations and the shape of integer sequences.
arxiv-2601-19519:
Ofir Abramovich, Ariel Shamir, and Andreas Aristidou build motion capture that works outside the studio. Standard systems film a performer with many cameras and track markers on the body. That setup fails outdoors or in cluttered spaces where cameras cannot see every point. The team instead uses small sensors worn on the body that measure distances between each other.

Their system rebuilds full-body three-dimensional motion from those sparse distance readings alone. The sensors use time-of-flight ranging, timing tiny radio signals between wireless nodes. With no cameras in the loop, the method keeps working in open or messy places. Animators and sports scientists could record natural movement in the wild. The work moves motion capture from a fixed stage to almost anywhere.
arxiv-2601-20519:
Paige Ramsden, Sean L. McGee, and Matt Nicholl use tidal disruption events to uncover quenched galaxies whose central black holes are smaller than expected. A tidal disruption event flares when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Because very massive black holes swallow stars whole without a flare, these events reveal otherwise hidden low-mass black holes.

The authors find an unexpected population of galaxies that have stopped forming stars yet host under-massive black holes. That pairing tests the standard story in which black hole growth and star formation shut down together.
arxiv-2601-20619:
Jhoan Eusse, Esteban Vasquez, Tom Rivlin, and Elizabeth Agudelo write lecture notes on the foundations of quantum optics for quantum information. Nonclassical states of light and their correlations are core resources: they underpin both the exploration of quantum phenomena and the working of quantum information protocols.

The notes offer an accessible yet rigorous introduction, stressing relevance to quantum information science and technology. Students entering the field need exactly this bridge, from the physics of light to the logic of quantum devices. The crash-course format suits a first pass before deeper study.
arxiv-2601-20719:
Shubhadeep Sadhukhan and nine co-authors study how immune cells swallow soft targets. Their 2026 paper is about phagocytosis, the process by which a cell engulfs a particle. It is a basic tool of the innate immune system. The team asks what physical rules govern the act when the target is soft. Real targets bend and deform during contact.

Older theory mostly treats targets as rigid balls. That choice skips a key fact: both the cell and its target change shape as they meet. The authors study how membrane curvature and actin, the cell's inner scaffold, work together. Their focus runs from the first bite to full engulfment. The work helps explain how immune cells handle soft prey that gives way under pressure.
arxiv-2601-21019:
Markus Holzleitner and four co-authors study learning when training and test data come from different worlds. Their 2026 paper builds a regularization framework for unsupervised domain adaptation. The setting is vector-valued regression under covariate shift. Covariate shift means the input distributions differ between training and test. The outputs may be vectors, not single numbers. Such shift poses significant challenges for reliable learning.

The framework uses vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These spaces give a rich, structured way to fit functions. Regularization keeps the fit from chasing noise in the source data. No labels from the target domain are assumed. The paper develops the theory for this general case. It serves fields like medicine and sensing, where labeled data sit in one setting and use happens in another.
arxiv-2601-21219:
Daniel Bernstein, Luca Di Carlo, and David Schwab compress neural networks by letting their weights attract each other. Their 2026 paper presents soft quantization. The method adds short-range attractive couplings between weights during training. Those couplings pull weights toward shared values. The weight distribution then discretizes on its own. Remarkably, it does so in a mixed-precision manner. Only two additional hyperparameters control the effect.

Standard quantization forces weights onto a grid after training. Soft quantization grows the grid during training instead. The model adapts to its own compression as it learns. Mixed precision emerges rather than being assigned by hand. Smaller models run cheaper on phones and edge devices. The paper offers a physically inspired route to that goal. It treats a network's weights like particles that cluster.
arxiv-2601-21319:
Vade Shah and Jason R. Marden compare ways of forming alliances in a simple contest game. In the game, two players each fight a shared adversary across several contests. Each side splits a limited budget among the contests, and the higher spend wins each one.

Alliances change who pools resources and how the pooled budget is split. The authors analyze several alliance rules inside this coalitional game. The comparison shows which setups help the allies and which mostly help the adversary. Such toy models give clean insight into real coalition politics, where partners must share limited strength.
arxiv-2601-21719: Yaxi Hu, Johanna Düngler, Bernhard Schölkopf, and Amartya Sanyal study privacy in LoRA. LoRA is a widely used way to fine-tune large models with small added parts. Their 2026 preprint asks when random projections help protect the data used in training, and when they do not. The tool they build for the job is a randomized method they call the Wishart projection mechanism.
arxiv-2601-21919:
Yiqun Chen and co-authors try to make reasoning models briefer without making them dumber. Large reasoning models write long chains of thought, and the redundant parts slow responses and bottleneck deployment. Earlier reinforcement learning fixes coupled a length penalty with rewards for correct outcomes.

That simple weighting struggles to balance brevity against accuracy, since forcing short answers can damage critical reasoning steps. The team's 2026 preprint instead compresses chains of thought through multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several agents shape the training signal. If models can learn to skip only the waste, users get faster answers at lower cost. And long reasoning stays affordable for everyday use rather than special occasions only.
arxiv-2601-22019:
Neelanjan Chakraborti, Snehasish Nandy, and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh probe a faint effect in some solids. Some fields pull like a magnet and swing back and forth in time. A solid can respond in ways that are not in step with that pull. The size of that response can reveal the hidden shape of the states inside the solid.

Some of that shape comes from how spins turn as states change. The team studies an effect where this spin shape drives the response. The effect is built into the solid, not forced by flaws in it. Work like this gives lab teams new ways to probe odd solids. Those solids may one day be used in fast, low-power parts for chips.
arxiv-2601-22119:
Han Yang and co-authors search for trade rules that work. In stock trade, a rule is a math form that aims to pick stocks that will do well. To find good rules by machine is a prized task. But most search tools roam free, with no check on form. They coin rules that break the rules of trade or mean naught at all.

The team sets a strict grammar for the search. Each rule the tool may coin must fit that grammar. It must be well formed and make sense in trade terms. Their tool is called AlphaCFG. Rules found this way can be read by men and checked by hand. They can also be used with more trust in live trade.
arxiv-2601-22219:
Aurora Ireland and Vincent Vennin ask whether the seeds of galaxies ever lost their quantum traits. Their 2026 preprint studies the tiny ripples born in the fast growth of the early cosmos. Most work treats those ripples as plain chance fields, like tossed dice.

The pair look for a sign that the ripples stayed truly quantum. They focus on phase links between branches of the state, which can leave marks of quantum clash. They also weigh how odd, non-bell-shaped spread in the ripples shapes that sign. The work tests a deep claim about cosmic birth.
arxiv-2601-22419:
Nicholas Lopez, Francisco Marmolejo-Cossío, Jose Roberto Tello Ayala, and David Parkes design group testing that does the most social good. Pooled testing checks many samples with one test, saving scarce kits. Their 2026 preprint notes the cost: a pooled result says less about each person.

Their method shapes pools over time to lift total welfare, not just cut kit use. Code and test scripts come with the work. Such plans matter when disease spreads fast and labs are swamped. They help officials spend each test where it helps most. The work ties math to public health aims.
arxiv-2601-22719:
Ivan Krasionov and a team take single-shot films of vortex birth in a room-temperature quantum fluid. Quantized vortices are the swirls that mark a quantum fluid. Their 2026 preprint uses interferometry on an organic exciton-polariton condensate, a hybrid of light and matter.

Across hundreds of runs, vortex cores land at random spots, with no favored spin. That pattern fits a stochastic, unseeded birth, as Kibble-Zurek theory would suggest. The team also read how the pattern scales. Such films test a deep claim about how order forms. Few setups can catch it live.
arxiv-2601-22819:
Yaxing Ma, Lijuan Wang, and Huaiqiang Yu study how fast a delayed control system can be steadied. Their systems are infinite-dimensional, like heat or fluid flow, and include a fixed time delay in the control loop. Delays often make control harder, so the effect on rapid stabilization is a real question.

They prove two results: the delay does not harm rapid stabilization, and feedback needs no past history to work. Those findings simplify controller design for systems with lag. They apply where models are described by partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-22919:
Fabian Bally, Michael Schötz, and Thomas Limbrunner design a data pipeline for training self-driving cars. Data both enables and bottlenecks that training, since cars record far more than teams can process. Rare but safety-critical events matter most, yet finding them takes long hours of driving.

Their serverless, edge-native design processes data near where it is gathered, scaling up only when needed. Smart selection can surface the rare events that teach cars to handle danger. The goal is training sets that are balanced, not just big. Balanced coverage is the stated goal, since a fleet can drive safely for months yet still miss the one dangerous case.
arxiv-2601-23219:
Shuai Shao, Yixiang Liu, Bingwei Lu, and Weinan Zhang scale multi-agent systems while keeping performance rising. These systems use a router to split tasks among specialized agents. Adding new agents seems an easy way to grow capability, but naive expansion can collapse performance.

The problem is the router cold-starting on new, mixed-quality agents it cannot yet judge. MonoScale aims for monotonic improvement, so each addition helps rather than hurts. Steady growth rules matter as agent pools become large marketplaces of tools. Cold-starting routers are the failure to avoid, since a router cannot route well to agents it has never evaluated.
arxiv-2603-01519:
Takashi Maruyama, Tatsuki Seto, Viktor Zaverkin, and Henrik Christiansen recast a key rule of statistical physics in this 2026 work. The hyperforce sum rule links forces in a fluid at rest to how its parts are arranged. It extends a classic chain of equations that tie each level of particle groups to the next.

Their new form rests on a Leibniz rule for how derivatives act on paired test functions and distributions. From that one rule, both the sum rule and the classic chain at any level follow in flat space. The same step also gives the sum rule for boxes with periodic edges, a common setup in simulations. A cleaner base can make later proofs shorter and show where the rule truly comes from.
arxiv-2603-02219:
Junfeng Fang, Nachuan Chen, Houcheng Jiang, and colleagues build a live safety filter for language models in this 2026 paper. Text arrives token by token, so a filter must act mid-stream, not after the fact. Filters trained per token need costly labels and tend to overfit. The team argues that ready-made filters already hold token-level risk clues inside them.

Their filter, NExT-Guard, reads those clues with sparse autoencoders, tools that split inner signals into clear features. It needs no new training and uses autoencoders from public base models. In tests it beat both late filters and trained live filters. Gains held across models, autoencoder types, and risk types. The approach offers a cheap, flexible path to real-time safety.
arxiv-2603-02519:
Wei Jiang, Tong Chen, Wei Yuan, and colleagues detect mixed-source misinformation with agent teams in this 2026 paper. False content can hide in lying text, forged images, or a mismatch between them. One vision-language model alone struggles with that mixed task, especially with no labeled examples. Prior agent systems reason only once per agent, leaving them error-prone.

Their framework, AgentM3D, scales reasoning at test time for each specialist agent. Each agent tries several reasoning paths, and a critic scores them for task fit. Agents sit in a cascade, so easy cases skip unneeded stages. A planner caps the path count by case difficulty, keeping costs in check. Adaptive stopping ends reasoning once evidence is firm. The design targets hard cases without wasting compute on easy ones.
arxiv-2603-02719:
L. Julián Lechuga López, Farah Shamout, and Tim Rudner test whether medical AI can safely hold back its uncertain guesses. Their 2026 paper examines selective prediction, where a model passes doubtful cases to human experts. The setting is labeling many conditions at once from mixed intensive care data.

Across strong single-mode and multimodal models, holding back uncertain cases often made overall results worse, despite good standard scores. The cause was uneven error in confidence: models felt unsure about right answers and sure about wrong ones, above all for rare conditions. Common summary metrics hid this split. The authors urge calibration-aware checks before any selective system is trusted at the bedside.
arxiv-2603-03119:
Oleg Romanchuk and Roman Bondar propose a physics-style language for governing AI systems that act like institutions. Deployed agents now persist over time, hold state, call tools, and quietly widen their own future powers. Governance rules usually constrain decisions but leave the mechanics of crossing authority boundaries vague.

Their framework, AI Space Physics, models an AI institution with typed boundary channels and reach that stops at a defined horizon. A family of core laws demands complete witnessing of boundary events, no bypass around mediation, and atomic steps from judgment to effect. Every adjudication must also be reconstructable by replay. Second-order effects, where the institution expands its own structure, are treated separately. The aim is constitutive rules, not just policy slogans.
arxiv-2603-03219:
Huck Bennett and Peter Ly prove new hardness results for a lattice problem tied to coding and cryptography. The covering radius of a lattice is the farthest distance any point in space can sit from the lattice, and approximating it is notoriously hard. Their 2026 paper studies the problem in large p-norms, where geometry stretches toward the maximum coordinate.

They define an explicit threshold function of the norm, passing one beyond a norm of about thirty-five and rising toward nine eighths. Below that factor, the binary variant of the problem is NP-hard for every finite norm above the threshold, a first for explicit norms. In the maximum norm, the problem is even harder, complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. The binary variant also transfers hardness to a classic discrepancy problem.
arxiv-2603-03319:
James Wedgwood, Chhavi Yadav, and Virginia Smith ask what large language model judges secretly prefer. Models increasingly grade other models' answers, but their choices carry systematic biases that can drift away from human judgment. Earlier studies mostly checked a short, hand-picked list of suspected biases. Their 2026 paper instead discovers the drivers automatically, with no fixed list in advance.

Several concept extraction methods compete on clarity and prediction, and sparse autoencoders win on clarity while staying competitive. Applied to more than twenty-seven thousand paired answers judged by three models, the method confirms known habits, like refusing sensitive requests more often than humans. It also finds new ones, favoring concrete, empathetic, detailed, and formal replies in some fields, and disfavoring legal advice that urges active steps.
arxiv-2603-03519:
M Warda, A Zdeb, and R Rodríguez-Guzmán map where an exotic nuclear decay, cluster radioactivity, can exist at all. In that decay a heavy nucleus emits a small cluster instead of splitting evenly, and theory treats it as extremely lopsided fission. Earlier microscopic calculations, using the Gogny force in a self-consistent framework, found a fission valley for this mode in nuclei matching lead-208's neutron-to-proton balance, plus actinides and superheavy nuclei.

Their 2026 paper walks chains of isotopes and isotones to find the mode's borders. The valley appears across a wide stretch of the nuclear chart, but flattens steadily as nuclei move away from lead-208's balance. For neutron-deficient nuclei beyond a threshold ratio, the valley dies out before the nucleus can split, so cluster radioactivity cannot be observed there. The survey sets firm limits for future searches.

aurobindo-human-cycle-1919:
Sri Aurobindo wrote The Human Cycle as essays in his journal Arya during the First World War, and the book appeared in 1919. Aurobindo had been a revolutionary against British rule in India before turning to yoga and philosophy. Here he offers a philosophy of history on the grand scale.

He traces societies through stages ruled in turn by symbol, custom, reason, and self-seeking trade. Beyond those stages he foresees a spiritual age, in which human unity grows from inner change rather than from force. The book states the hopeful core of Aurobindo's later teaching on the evolution of society.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-19:
Volume nineteen of Rodkinson's set steps outside the Talmud text itself: it is the first volume of his History of the Talmud. Rodkinson, a Russian-born scholar who settled in America, wrote the history to frame his twenty-volume translation. The 1918 edition gathers his long study of the work's making.

He traces the oral law from Moses through the Mishnah's writing under Rabbi Judah the Prince. Then he follows the centuries of debate in Babylon that grew into the Gemara. Lives of the great rabbis and schools fill the story. Readers who finish the translation here learn how the vast book itself came to be.
beaumont-fletcher-maids-tragedy-1619:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher were the most popular English playwrights of their generation, writing just after Shakespeare. Their tragedy The Maid's Tragedy was performed by the King's Men around 1610. It was first printed in 1619.

The plot turns on a wedding night secret. The king has forced the bride, Evadne, to remain his mistress, and her new husband learns the truth too late. Shame, loyalty, and revenge drive the court toward murder. The play's dark picture of a corrupt king made it the defining tragedy of court corruption in its era, and actors revived it often.
berzelius-essai-proportions-chimiques-18:
Berzelius sets out his essay on chemical proportions in French in 1819, laying ground for the modern table of atomic weights. He fixed the relative weights of the elements with new care. His letter symbols for the elements, H, O, and the rest, are the ones chemists still write today.

Measurement replaces recipe as the soul of chemistry in his hands. Long tables of trials back each number he dares to print. The work turned a craft of mixtures into a science of exact amounts. Few books did more to give chemistry its modern shape, and students still use his symbols daily without knowing his name.
blok-iambs-1919:
Alexander Blok gathered poems in iambic meter under the plain title Iambs, printed in Russian in 1919. He was Russia's leading Symbolist poet, famed for The Twelve and his verses to a beautiful lady. These late poems were shaped in the heat and fear of revolt.

Blok turns the steady beat of the iamb toward Russia's fate and the artist's place in a burning world. The tone is tense, grieving, and musical at once. Gone is the dreamy haze of his youth. In its place stands a poet speaking plainly while his old world collapses fast around him, line by ringing line, year by bitter year.
burchard-corrector-decretum-19:

cabell-jurgen-1919:

Daniel Defoe published Robinson Crusoe in 1719, often called the first English novel in the modern sense. The book invented realist fiction, the castaway narrative, and the economic individual as hero for readers. A footprint in the sand terrifies him, then brings him Friday, his companion and convert in time. Rescue, mutineers, and a return to England close a tale of self-reliance and providence in balance. Its plain style and concrete detail made fiction feel true to common life.
doe-osti-2998337-completion-of-level-2-f: FY25 milestone 9193 got completed, and this DOE text records the level two achievement. The pages detail the outcomes. The program gets its check. The milestone was 9193. The achievement was level two. The program got checks. The check was program. The milestone was level two.
doe-osti-3376024-system-study-high-press: HPCS got 1998-2024-studied, and this DOE system study covers core spray. The pages detail the high findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The study was system. The data were nuclear. The HPCS were spray. The 1998-2024 were study. The high were core.
doyle-vital-message-1919:
Arthur Conan Doyle presses his cause in The Vital Message, his next book of 1919. The Great War had left a land full of grief. Doyle holds that word from the dead is not a fad, but the most grave news of the age. He sums the proof, meets the foes, and calls the church to take the new light to heart with speed.

His tone is that of a man on a quest, not a sage at rest. The book is his flag in the post war push of the faith. It shows his zeal at full heat.
drayton-idea-1619:
Michael Drayton shaped his sonnet sequence Idea over some twenty-five years, and the final form appeared in 1619. The sixty-three sonnets address a beloved he calls Idea, linked in his life to Anne Goodyer. She is both a real woman and a figure for beauty itself in the poems.

The opening sonnets compare the poet to a sailor reporting a long and risky voyage. Later poems play with conceits about murder, counting griefs, and a heart that will not rest. Standing beside Sidney and Spenser, the sequence shows an Elizabethan poet polishing the same love poems across a whole working life.
dunsany-tales-of-three-hemispheres-1919:
A phrase that named a whole kind of story was born in Dunsany's book of 1919. Tales of Three Hemispheres gives us beyond the fields we know, the gate phrase of portal fantasy. Its tales cross from our world to lands that run on dream's laws.

Old gods walk in new cities, and travelers trade the known fields for stranger ground. The book mixes his myth tales with yarns of a more modern cut. That mix shows Dunsany at a turn in his long career. The phrase alone would earn the volume its place in letters.
entstehung-und-ausbreitung-der-alchemie-: Entstehung und Ausbreitung der Alchemie, 1919. The rise of alchemy. This book preserves that history. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It holds its historical place. Writers of history may cite it later.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-19: The nineteenth volume rounds out the long series of essays. Montaigne's final thoughts on life and death close the set with grace. The circle of self-knowledge is complete at last. A lasting monument of French letters.
essays-on-phrenology-or-an-inquiry-into-: Essays on Phrenology, 1819. The phrenological essays. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
europmc-pmc10019719:
Pak and co-authors test whether AlphaFold can predict how single mutations change a protein's stability and function, in a 2023 study. AlphaFold predicts protein shapes from sequence with striking accuracy. Some had even claimed the protein folding problem was solved. The authors ask a harder question: can the tool sense small changes?

They compare AlphaFold predictions for normal and mutated proteins across known cases. Their checks show where the tool helps and where it stays blind to change. The study gives a sober guide for researchers who want to use AI shapes in mutation work.
europmc-pmc10316519:
Rusch, Layden, and Dugas wrote a 2023 review on how gut microbes may shape thought and memory. The gut holds vast numbers of microbes, with more genes than the human body itself. These microbes talk to the brain through nerves, hormones, and the immune system.

One key path runs through the stress system, which makes the hormone cortisol. The right level of cortisol helps the brain grow and helps learning. Rusch reports that microbes affect this stress system across the whole life span. Stress can also disturb the gut and brain link. Most proof so far comes from animal studies, and human trials are now under way.
europmc-pmc10355019:
Tu and Wang, with the Special Writing Group of China Stroke Surveillance Report, summed up stroke in China in 2021. Stroke has led deaths and disability in China since 2015. A stroke strikes when blood flow to the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts. The report draws on national screening and hospital data.

An estimated 17.8 million adults in China had had a stroke by 2020. About 3.4 million had their first stroke that year, and 2.3 million died that year. Most strokes, at 81.9 percent, came from blocked vessels. High blood pressure touched 24.7 percent of adults, yet just a quarter of cases were well controlled. Hospital care for stroke cost about 58 billion yuan in 2020.
europmc-pmc10356619:
Hickey and colleagues mapped the human gut at single-cell scale in 2023. The gut runs over nine metres and its jobs shift along its length. The team took samples from eight gut sites in nine donors. They used image scans and tests of gene activity in single cell cores.

Cell mixes differed a lot from site to site. Hickey found many subtypes among the surface cells that line the gut. The same cell types grouped into distinct zones, which formed immune niches, or local defence hubs. Gene control patterns hinted at a step-by-step path as cells mature. The team also linked gut disease risk genes to specific cell types.
europmc-pmc10550819:
Zhou led a team in 2023, with the UK Biobank Eye & Vision Consortium, to build a base AI model for eye scans. Most medical AI models learn from labelled scans, which take expert time to mark. Each model also fits just one task. Their model, RETFound, learned from raw scans with no labels at all.

Training used 1.6 million retinal images, the photos of the back of the eye. Zhou then tuned the model for set tasks with a small stock of labelled scans. It beat rival models at spotting eye diseases that threaten sight. It also foretold body-wide ills such as heart failure and heart attack. The shared base cuts the expert marking that clinics must fund.
europmc-pmc11324519:
Camargo and colleagues present a framework that finds mobile genetic elements in sequencing data in this 2024 paper. Mobile elements, such as plasmids and viruses, move genes between microbes. They shape ecology, biotechnology, and public health. Spotting them in vast sequence data is essential but hard.

Their tool, geNomad, blends gene content with a deep neural network to classify sequences. It draws on over 200,000 marker protein profiles to annotate genes and assign viral taxonomy. A statistical model detects proviruses, viral DNA woven into a host genome, with high precision. Benchmark scores reached 77.8 percent for plasmids and 95.3 percent for viruses, substantially beating rival tools. The team processed over 2.7 trillion base pairs and found millions of new viruses and plasmids, shared via public databases.
europmc-pmc1183519:
Grün and colleagues mapped tiny gene regulators in fruit flies in 2005. These regulators are called microRNAs, short bits that curb protein output. Each one binds to matching sites on gene messages. The team used a program named PicTar to predict targets.

Comparisons across seven fly species sharpened the search. On average, each microRNA was linked to about 54 target genes. Some clustered microRNAs seem to act as a team. Grün also compared fly targets with mammal targets. A few control links appear shared, while others seem unique to each group.
europmc-pmc1195719:
Liu and co-authors mapped chemical marks on yeast DNA packaging in 2005. DNA wraps around histone proteins in units called nucleosomes. Small chemical marks on histones affect gene use and repair. Many mark types exist, and their combined patterns were unclear.

A fine-scale chip read 12 mark types on thousands of units. Marks did not occur at random or alone. They fell into roughly two partner groups. One group left a distinct zone near gene start sites. Liu shows packaging marks form patterns, not noise. Those patterns may encode gene control rules.
europmc-pmc1253619:
Molyneux, Hotez, and Fenwick proposed bundled control of neglected tropical diseases in 2005. Seven infections in Africa anchor their plan. Such diseases deepen poverty and carry stigma in rural areas. Past campaigns had already cut several of them sharply.

Treating the seven together would cost about 40 cents per person yearly. Hundreds of millions could gain lasting benefit from that spend. Guinea worm may even face eradication soon, they note. Lymphatic filariasis, river blindness, leprosy, and trachoma had all receded. Molyneux argues joint delivery beats one-disease campaigns for the poor. These infections are ancient, noted in the Bible and other old texts. They have burdened people for ages.
europmc-pmc13324819:
Alexander and the Concise Guide team catalogued G protein-coupled receptors in 2023. The guide is the sixth biennial edition of a pharmacology reference. It summarizes about 1,800 drug targets in compact tables. Roughly 6,000 interactions with about 3,900 ligands are covered.

Receptors in this section form one of six major target classes. Entries stress selective pharmacology where it exists. Links point to the open Guide to Pharmacology database. The printed guide runs almost 500 pages yet condenses the website. Alexander provides a permanent, citable snapshot of receptor knowledge. Other sections cover ion channels, hormone receptors, enzymes, and more. Each edition freezes the fast-moving database at one set date.
europmc-pmc1391919:
Bentley and co-authors sequenced the capsule genes of all 90 pneumococcal serotypes in 2006. The pneumococcus wears a sugar capsule to survive in blood. That capsule also defines vaccine targets and serotypes. Each serotype makes a chemically distinct capsule.

Sequences were related to known sugar structures and typing serum reactions. The full set gives the most complete picture of capsule diversity origins. The complete gene repertoire enables a full analysis of one capsule system. It also lays foundations for molecular serotyping. Bentley lays groundwork for tracking vaccine escape types. It appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2006.
europmc-pmc1457019:
What drives year-to-year swings in Lyme disease risk? Ostfeld and co-authors spent 13 years on that question in 2006, in New York forests where the disease is common. Risk rests on how many young ticks carry the Lyme germ. They weighed weather, deer counts, rodent counts, and acorn crops as drivers.

Deer counts had no power to foretell risk. Rain and warmth had weak effects at best. The best clues were mice and chipmunk counts from the year before, plus acorn crops two years back. Ostfeld concludes that food for tick hosts, and the hosts themselves, set the risk people face.
europmc-pmc1852419:
Perkins and colleagues profiled microRNAs in 2007 in the brains of people with schizophrenia. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that block protein production from specific messages, tuning gene activity after transcription. Schizophrenia affects about one percent of people, and postmortem work had found altered message and protein levels without one faulty protein.

The team measured microRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region central to thought and planning. Samples came from people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and from comparison subjects. The profiling pointed to an association between the illness and shifted microRNA expression. Such a shift could explain why many messages and their proteins drift out of step in the disorder. The authors present the link as possible rather than proven, calling for further work.
europmc-pmc1977719:
Newlands and co-workers reported a Phase I trial in 1992 of temozolomide, a cancer drug related to mitozolomide. Phase I trials test safety and dose in patients for the first time. The drug had shown wide action against mouse tumours. It also caused less suppression of bone marrow, called myelosuppression, than related drugs in early tests.

The team first gave single doses to 51 patients, by vein and then by mouth. Low blood cell counts set the dose limit. They then tested a five-day oral course in 42 patients. Four of 23 melanoma patients responded, and two patients with brain tumours also shrank. The authors recommended 150 mg per square metre daily for five days for later trials.

europmc-pmc2206519:
Zappitelli and co-workers tested a urine marker in 2007 to spot acute kidney injury early in critically ill children. The standard marker, serum creatinine, rises late after damage. The candidate protein, called NGAL, rises early when injury timing is known. Whether it predicts injury in general intensive care was unclear. The team followed 140 ventilated children, collecting urine daily and grading kidney injury by paediatric criteria.

Urine NGAL rose at least six-fold in children developing kidney injury. The rise came two days before and after the creatinine jump, while controls stayed flat. NGAL predicted new injury with an accuracy measure of 0.78, and persistent injury lasting 48 hours or more with 0.79 on the same measure. It rose step by step with worse final injury grade. That supports its use as an early warning test in this setting.
europmc-pmc2409519:
Michalaki, Syrigos, Charles, and Waxman measured two immune signal proteins in prostate cancer patients in 2004. The proteins, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, are cytokines, messengers that can help tumors grow and spread. The study covered 80 patients split by disease bulk, plus 38 healthy controls.

Blood IL-6 in patients with spread disease averaged 9.3 picograms per millilitre, versus 1.3 in patients with contained disease, a gap the tests rated highly significant. TNF-alpha showed the same pattern, at 6.3 versus 1.1 in the same units. Both rose in step with how far the cancer had spread. In 40 patients whose cancer returned, both signals climbed at the moment a standard marker, PSA, signalled progression. The authors suggested tracking the pair alongside other markers of disease activity.
europmc-pmc2697319:
Burton and colleagues modeled in 2009 what the remodeling of the mother's spiral arteries does to blood flow into the placenta. In a healthy pregnancy these arteries lose their muscle walls and flare open five to ten times wider at the mouth. When the widening fails, preeclampsia and stunted fetal growth follow.

Using measured dimensions, the team calculated that the flare slows incoming blood from a racing 2 to 3 meters per second down to about 10 centimeters per second. At that pace, blood takes roughly 25 seconds to cross the placenta's exchange space, matching what is observed. Without the flare, blood would jet in turbulently at full speed. Such a jet would tear the delicate exchange tree, rupture anchor points, and spasm shut, starving and stressing the tissue. The harm of failed remodeling, they argue, is mostly this violence of flow, not simple shortage.
europmc-pmc2757919:
Keller and co-authors profiled in 2009 microRNA expression in blood cells as a biomarker for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. That disease strips insulation from nerves in the brain and spinal cord. It is chronic and inflammatory in nature. The disease varies widely in course and treatment response, so objective markers are prized. They measured eight hundred sixty-six microRNAs in twenty patients and nineteen healthy controls.

One hundred sixty-five microRNAs differed significantly between patients and controls, and one hundred twenty-two of them had never been linked to any other disease. The best single marker separated groups with about ninety percent accuracy. A set of forty-eight microRNAs, judged by a machine-learning method with cross-validation, reached about ninety-six percent accuracy, which supports blood microRNA profiles as a diagnostic biomarker.
europmc-pmc2874019:
Thompson, Swan, Moore, and vom Saal introduced in 2009 a journal theme issue on what they call our plastic age. Humanity uses over two hundred sixty million tonnes of plastic a year, roughly eight percent of world oil output. The papers survey rising use and the real benefits plastics bring, from medicine to food safety.

Balanced against those gains are growing harms as waste piles up in landfills and oceans. Debris entangles and is swallowed by wildlife, and chemicals that soften or harden plastics raise health worries because some disrupt hormones. The editors weigh fixes, from better waste handling to safer additives and biodegradable materials, and set out the research and policy steps needed to act on them.
europmc-pmc2876119:
Blows and a huge collaborative group pooled in 2010 more than ten thousand early breast cancer cases from twelve studies to test whether tumor subtypes forecast survival. Subtypes are set with standard stains that detect hormone sensors and a growth protein on tumor cells. The groups differ in biology and behavior, yet how survival chances shift over time after diagnosis was unclear.

The analysis sized death rates for each major subtype across short and long follow-up. Tumors lacking hormone sensors carried the worst early outlook, while hormone-sensitive tumors did better early but kept a lingering risk for many years. That time pattern matters when doctors estimate a patient's future chances, since a subtype's danger can fade or persist as years pass since diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2878219:
Gurley and a large outbreak team reported in 2007 that Nipah virus, a bat-borne virus that inflames the brain, passed directly between people in a Bangladeshi village. In the first Malaysian outbreak a decade earlier, nearly all patients caught it from pigs, and spread between people was not found. Bangladesh saw repeated small outbreaks with a different pattern worth probing.

Careful tracing of cases and contacts showed patients infecting family caregivers and others in the community, often through close contact with saliva or breath during illness. The virus's presence in respiratory secretions fits that route. Household spread changes the control playbook, the team stresses, adding barrier nursing and caregiver protection to the animal-focused measures used before.
europmc-pmc2880419:
Wishart and co-authors built PREDICT in 2010, a model that estimates survival after surgery for early invasive breast cancer in British patients. It was fitted on nearly fifty-seven hundred women treated in East Anglia, with separate curves for tumors that carry the estrogen sensor and those that do not. Standard factors went in, including tumor size, grade, node spread, and whether screening found the cancer.

Checked against a second registry of nearly fifty-five hundred women from the West Midlands, the model's forecasts landed within about one percent of the real death rates at eight years. Its accuracy scores beat chance by a wide margin for both overall and breast cancer deaths. Good calibration means doctors can quote its percentages to patients with reasonable trust.
europmc-pmc2963619:
Gudmundsson and Thiele released fastFVA, a fast open-source tool for flux variability analysis, in a 2010 article. The method probes how much each reaction in a metabolic model can vary, but slow computing had limited its use.

Their implementation cuts run times so sharply that networks with thousands of reactions finish within seconds. That speed lets researchers ask harder questions about network flexibility and robustness under varied conditions. Because the code is open, modelling groups can adopt it directly. The authors frame the gain as widening what systems biology studies can realistically attempt.
europmc-pmc3009619:
Chakravarthy and co-authors pooled studies on what raises the risk of late age-related macular degeneration in a 2010 meta-analysis. The disease is the top cause of blindness in Western nations. Many candidate risks had been reported with uneven strength.

Across two dozen studies covering well over a hundred thousand people, four factors showed strong consistent links: older age, current smoking, past cataract surgery, and family history. Heavier weight, heart disease history, high blood pressure, and a clotting protein showed moderate links. Sex, ancestry, diabetes, and cholesterol measures looked weaker or inconsistent. The short list targets prevention advice.
europmc-pmc3073119:
Hooper, Killick, and Lovestone set out in 2008 their hypothesis that one overactive enzyme drives much of Alzheimer disease. The enzyme, called GSK3 in short, normally handles jobs from sugar storage to gene control and is unusual in being switched on by default. Its overactivity, they argue, could explain the disease's hallmarks at a single stroke.

Excess activity would impair memory and drive the tau protein into the tangles that clog patient neurons. It would also raise production of the amyloid that forms plaques, and stir local inflammation around those plaques. Familial and common forms of the disease would share this one mediator. If the hypothesis holds, blocking the enzyme becomes a prime drug strategy. The authors lay out the evidence chain and the open questions it must survive. The piece is a position paper meant to focus a crowded field.
europmc-pmc3082519:
Sun and colleagues used in 2011 a pairing of yeast genetics and protein chemistry to map how the FUS protein may drive Lou Gehrig disease, also called ALS. FUS is an RNA handling protein that clumps in the neurons of some patients, much like its better studied cousin TDP-43. Which parts of the protein cause clumping and toxicity, and how patient mutations change them, were open questions.

In yeast, human FUS formed clumps and poisoned the cells, copying key features of the human disease. Systematic trimming showed which regions are required for that behavior, and patient linked mutations made the protein clump more readily and harm cells more strongly. A gene screen then found modifiers that dial the toxicity up or down. The work gives the field a fast test bed for this protein and a map of its dangerous parts, guiding the search for protective drugs.
europmc-pmc3214619:
Robert Buck and colleagues set out to fix the confused naming of PFAS chemicals in this 2011 paper. These perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances are found in the environment, wildlife, and people, but inconsistent terminology hampered communication among scientists, regulators, and industry. The authors propose one clear, shared vocabulary.

They define the PFAS family, sort it into families and subfamilies, and recommend common names and acronyms, including terms for fluorinated polymers. They also explain the two main manufacturing routes and the byproducts each creates. Finally, they map how PFAS families transform into one another, stressing which ones can break down into the long-chain acids now targeted by regulation. A supplement lists hundreds of individual compounds.
europmc-pmc3320019:
Singh and Cuervo reviewed a cell process that eats the cell's own stored fat, in a 2012 article. Fat droplets inside cells were once dismissed as inert storage blobs, but they are now seen as active structures with many jobs. Cells must turn them over in a controlled way, and a cleanup process called autophagy handles part of that job.

The fat eating branch of that process, named lipophagy, breaks droplets down and releases their energy for the cell to burn. It also influences how much food an animal wants to eat, linking cell level cleanup to whole body balance. Faulty fat eating has been tied to fatty liver disease, obesity, and clogged arteries. The authors note that autophagy fades with age, which may help explain the metabolic problems that gather in later life.
europmc-pmc3374119:
Ma and colleagues pooled observational studies in 2012 to settle whether type 2 diabetes goes with stronger or weaker bones. Reports on bone mineral density in diabetes had disagreed for years. Their search covered studies published before May 2010 that measured density with standard X-ray absorptiometry scans.

Fifteen studies, with several thousand diabetic patients and far more controls, entered the pooled analysis. Density came out higher in diabetic patients at the hip, femoral neck, and spine, though not at the forearm. The pattern held for both men and women. Younger age, male sex, higher body weight, and higher blood sugar markers each tracked with higher density in the diabetic group.
europmc-pmc3468719:
Flacking and co-authors argued for keeping parents and preterm babies close in intensive care, in a 2012 paper in Acta Paediatrica. Babies born early often spend weeks in neonatal units, where machines and routines can keep parents at a distance. The authors weigh both physical closeness, such as skin-to-skin holding, and the emotional bond parents feel.

They review evidence that closeness aids the baby's brain growth, steadies parents' mental health, and strengthens the parent-child bond. Unit layout and culture can either help or hinder that closeness. Flacking's group urges longer visiting, family rooms, and early skin-to-skin contact as standard care. More study is needed, they say, on what helps families stay close in these settings.

europmc-pmc8461619: Correa and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on translational uses of hydrogels. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8647919: Lin and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on minimum reporting standards for in vivo (in living animals) magnetic resonance spectroscopy (light analysis): experts' shared view recommendations. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8866119: This 2022 research paper covers omicron escapes the majority of existing SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies (defense proteins). The SARS-CoV-2 b-1-1-529 variant contains 15 mutations of the receptor (docking point on a cell)-binding domain. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8891019: A fresh look at TDP-43 represses cryptic exon inclusion in the FTD-ALS gene unc13a arrived with this 2022 research paper. A hallmark pathological feature of the neurodegenerative diseases amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia (severe memory loss) is the depletion. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9021019: Zuin and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on nonlinear control of transcription through enhancer-promoter interactions (how parts affect each other). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9284919: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on frequent spotting of monkeypox virus DNA in saliva, semen, and other clinical (in patients) samples from 12 patients, barcelona, Spain, May. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc9674619: Doctors and scientists took on mutant p53 in cancer: from mechanism (how it works) to treatment modulation in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9950219: Doctors and scientists took on BCL-2 protein family: attractive aims at for cancer therapy in this 2023 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
faria-cause-sommeil-lucide-1819:
The Abbe Faria stated the suggestion theory in De la cause du sommeil lucide, printed in French in 1819. Lucid sleep, his name for the mesmeric trance, needs no magnetic fluid, he argues. The subject's own concentration raises the state. The operator's command guides it, but the power sits in the sleeper.

Faria had learned his method in India and tested it on Paris stages. His book studies the nature of man through this one strange door. Braid himself later cited Faria as a forerunner of true hypnosis. The French original is a precursor text of the whole field. It shifts the wonder from fluid to mind. Modern suggestion theory starts on its pages.
faria-sommeil-lucide-1819:
Abbe Faria explains lucid sleep without magnets in his treatise, Tome One, in French from 1819. Trance, he argues, springs from the subject's own mind, not from any fluid. The Goan priest, working in Paris, showed that expectation and a firm voice could induce the sleep he studied in his pupils.

His theory of suggestion came decades before the word grew famous. Braid later owned Faria as a forerunner of his own work on hypnotism. The book was cut short by its author's early death in Paris. It marks the birth of psychological hypnotism, the moment the marvel moved from the magnetizer's hands into the sleeper's mind.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-3-microcosmi-1:
The second tome of Fludd's history, from 1619, turns to the microcosm: man himself. Its long Latin title lists the supernatural, natural, and contrary sides of man's story. Fludd was a London doctor with a cosmic reach.

He traces the soul's fall, its powers, and its life in the body. Health and sickness get read as signs of inner order. Spirits and stars act on man in his scheme. The text is dense and diagram-rich in spirit. It forms the core of his claim that man sums up the whole world.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-4-microcosmi-s:
This 1619 section of Fludd's second tome treats the technical side of the microcosm. Its Latin title names it De Technica Microcosmi Historia. Fludd turns from man's soul to the arts man practices.

He covers skills from number and measure to war and craft. Each art is set inside his mirror scheme of world and man. The learning is wide, if the system strains at times. Engraved figures in the full edition aid the text. The section closes his survey of human art, and shows a Renaissance mind at full stretch.
fort-book-of-the-damned-1919:
Charles Fort spent years in newspaper files clipping wonders, and his first harvest came out in 1919. The Book of the Damned gathers rains of fish, falls of stones, strange lights, and folk who vanish. Fort calls such things damned because science shuts them out of its world.

His method is the pile: case on case, each clipped and cited, until doubt itself looks thin. His prose mocks the priests of science in a voice like no other writer's. The book founded the study of the strange that now bears his name, Forteana. It taught the world a new way to doubt its teachers.
friends-of-freedom-for-india-india-s-fre: India's Freedom in American Courts, Friends of Freedom for India, 1919. The Indian cause. This book preserves that pamphlet. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
frus-1861-d119:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton on 22 April 1861. Dayton was the new American minister to France, based in Paris. The letter is document 119 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paris stood second only to London in the war's foreign stakes. The Emperor Napoleon III watched for a chance to favor the South. Seward's April letter set Dayton, a former senator, to guard that gate from the war's first days. Dayton had run for Vice President in 1856, which gave him rank in Paris talk. Rank in Paris talk opened doors that a plain envoy would have found barred.
frus-1861-d19:
On 21 October 1861, William H. Seward directed a fresh letter to Norman Judd in Berlin. The dispatch is document 19 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October 1861 found Seward juggling crises on many fronts at once. His letters to Berlin formed one thread of a much wider web. In this one he directs his minister in Prussia, keeping the northern German court inside the Union's steady campaign against foreign aid to the South. The letter reached Berlin as the leaves fell, into a court deep in its own affairs. His brief from Washington was the same that month as in the spring: hold fast.
frus-1861-d219:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Marsh on 2 September 1861. It stands as Document 219 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.
