Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d119:
On 4 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 119 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d19:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 14 February 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 19 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d219:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William Stuart a letter on 24 June 1862, printed as Document 219 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart led the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was absent that year.

Three letters in five days show the pace Seward set when business pressed. The matters at hand in such notes were often narrow: a seized ship, a detained man, a point of form. Yet each small case, handled badly, could feed the larger quarrel over Britain's part in the war. The Stuart letters repay reading as a set. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d319:
A Dayton report dated 8 August 1862 stands out of order as Document 319 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

This report duplicates the date of Document 301, and the pair shows how the legation's output could scatter in the printed volume. Both letters belong to the week Cedar Mountain was fought in Virginia. For the reader, matching the two restores the Paris post's full account of that week in the summer of 1862. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d419:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 May 1862. It is Document 419 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

In May 1862 the fall of New Orleans strengthened the Union's hand abroad, and agents like Perry used such news at court. Spain's stake was direct: Cuba's trade, the Gulf blockade, and the unraveling allied campaign in Mexico. A report from Madrid told Washington whether Spanish ministers leaned toward the Union, the Confederacy, or simple caution. Perry's letters are the raw feed behind Seward's answers to Madrid that season.
frus-1862-d519:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 September 1862, the day of Antietam in far-off Maryland. The dispatch is Document 519 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Pike could know nothing of the battle as he wrote; his letter reflects the Netherlands as it stood on Dutch news alone. That innocence is part of the record's value. It shows what a friendly small power thought of the war at the very hinge of its fortunes. Victory claims and the emancipation order had not yet reset every calculation. Seward read the letter weeks later, in a changed world, as one more fixed point in his map of European opinion.
frus-1862-d619:
Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 November 1862. It is Document 619 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Danish file's only printed report.

Wood's November letter gave Washington the Danish reading of the war in its second autumn. It covered the court's temper and the press. It also covered the maritime business between the two countries. A single report in a file of instructions is itself informative; Copenhagen needed little reporting because little there was in doubt. The dispatch completes the small Danish record for 1862. The record is a study in what much of the Union's diplomacy really was. It was the steady care of friendly, uncomplicated relationships.
frus-1862-d719:
Friedrich Hassaurek wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 October 1862. Hassaurek was the American minister in Ecuador, a German-born Ohio lawyer and writer. The letter is document 719 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Ecuador sat far down the Pacific coast, and its envoy's mail reached Washington slowly. Hassaurek reported on the land's politics and on the trade of its ports, where American ships called for goods. His letters were the State Department's main word from that coast. This dispatch is part of that thin but steady line, kept up by one man writing from Quito while his country fought at home.
frus-1863p1-d119:
On 16 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of four letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 119 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Four sheets in a day is another desk-clearing, smaller than the dozen of 2 March but of the same kind. Seward took the London file head by head, one point per page. This letter opens the set. The batch habit shows how the brief was run. It ran not by long essays, but by short, sharp notes an envoy could act on one at a time.
frus-1863p1-d19:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, writing on Christmas Eve. The letter is document 19 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A holiday date did not slow the legation's mail. Adams wrote through the season on the state of British feeling and the work of the South's friends in Europe. His calm, exact tone is part of why his file still reads well. This dispatch is a late-year piece of the London watch. It was sent while Washington waited for word of the new year and the freedom edict soon to come.
frus-1863p1-d219:
From his London post on 19 June 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 219 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d319:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 11 November 1862. The note is document 319 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d419:
The American answer to London on 20 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d519:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 May 1863 letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid.
frus-1863p1-d619:
A dispatch dated 15 September 1863 went from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d119: On November 12, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as both parties began their journeys east. His message is Document 119 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister traveled by way of Gibraltar and Malta, collecting talks as he went. The record supplies the date and the names and no subject. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the papers of the twin journeys.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d19: On July 15, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Stalin again, and the letter is Document 19 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Mid-July found the Red Army fighting the great tank battle at Kursk and the Western allies newly ashore in Sicily, though the record assigns this letter no subject. It belongs to the steady correspondence through which the two leaders, still strangers in person, arranged to meet at Tehran before the year ended.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d219:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt sent a second most-secret telegram from Ankara on 14 November 1943, number 1870, sent at six in the evening. It reports how Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu handled questions from the German ambassador, Franz von Papen, about his Cairo talks with Eden.

Numan told von Papen that Eden had merely described the Moscow conference as a great success. Pressed, he denied any request for air bases but admitted Eden had sought Turkey's entry into the war, and he hid behind Turkey's unprepared state. Steinhardt adds that Ankara now feared a preventive Axis move, since the talks could not stay secret. German firms in Turkey, he adds, had been ordered to stop buying Turkish goods and ship out their stocks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d319:
Soviet foreign commissar Vyacheslav Molotov sent Ambassador Averell Harriman an urgent, personal and secret telegram from Moscow on 25 November 1943. Delivered at Moscow the next day and forwarded to Harriman at Cairo by Navy channels, it answers Harriman's message about preparing the Tehran conference.

Molotov thanks Harriman for his message from Cairo. On the practical questions Harriman had raised, he gives one direction. General Connolly, the American commander in Tehran, may address himself to General Arkadiev. He may do so through the Soviet chargé d'affaires there, about coordinating the measures that interest him. Molotov closes with the hope of meeting soon and sends his most cordial greetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d419:
The Declaration on Iran, is dated 1 December 1943. It was signed at Tehran by Churchill, Stalin, and Roosevelt in that order. It is the three powers' formal statement on the country that hosted their conference. An editorial headnote traces the signed original's later path to the State Department.

The three governments recognize the help Iran has given against the common enemy, above all by carrying supplies from overseas to the Soviet Union. They admit the war has caused Iran special economic hardship, and promise such economic help as worldwide shortages of transport and goods allow. After the war, Iran's economic problems will receive full consideration alongside those of other United Nations members. The declaration closes with the three powers at one with Iran's government in desiring the maintenance of her independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, under the Atlantic Charter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d519:
Charles E. Bohlen of the Moscow embassy wrote this second memorandum on December 15, 1943. Bohlen had served as Roosevelt's Russian interpreter at Tehran a fortnight earlier and was one of the State Department's few true Soviet experts. The memorandum appears in the Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Bohlen's memoranda often preserved conversations and judgments that reached print nowhere else, because he was present where other Americans were not. A paper from mid-December belongs to the stocktaking after the summit, when officials wrote down what the new relationship with Moscow seemed to mean. Readers get a young diplomat's careful record, made before hindsight could tidy it.
frus-1944-quebec-d119:
Winston Churchill sent this personal, top-secret telegram, numbered 779, to President Roosevelt on September 4, 1944. Britain's War Cabinet was deeply disturbed by events in Warsaw. Stalin had refused to let Allied aircraft use Soviet airfields to supply the Polish fighters, and Churchill feared the wider damage to relations with Russia.

Churchill begged Roosevelt to let American aircraft drop supplies and land on Russian airfields without formal Soviet consent. The Russians, he argued, could hardly reject a finished act and might even welcome it. Britain would share full responsibility. He also warned that Warsaw's fall would destroy Premier Mikołajczyk's standing and his talks with the Lublin Committee.
frus-1944-quebec-d19:
Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on August 5, 1944. It came a day after his previous message. The State Department printed both letters. They sit in the pre-conference correspondence of the Quebec 1944 volume.

The first week of August 1944 moved faster than any plan. American armor was racing across France. The Red Army stood before Warsaw. Churchill wrote daily because the map changed daily. For readers, a second message in two days shows something clear. The Prime Minister was working hard to keep diplomacy level. He tried to match events that his own strategy had helped unleash.
frus-1944-quebec-d219:
An editors' note closes the zones story at Quebec. The Combined Chiefs' memorandum of September 16, 1944, was agreed by Roosevelt and Churchill later that day and folded into the final summary of conference conclusions as paragraphs 33 and 34. A map reflecting the decisions was prepared in Washington immediately afterward and sent to Ambassador Winant on September 21.

The note also marks what Quebec did not settle. The allocation of sectors inside Berlin had been left open by the London protocol of September 12, and no evidence has been found that the question was discussed at Quebec at all. Further Anglo-American negotiations led to the tripartite agreement signed in the European Advisory Commission on November 14, 1944.
frus-1945-50-intel-d119:
A draft letter from President Truman to Attorney General Clark is dated 7 August 1946. Drafts prepared for a president's signature show a decision being readied at the top. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The FBI answered to the attorney general, so a presidential letter to Clark was the heaviest paper that could enter the Latin American fight. That it survives as a draft is itself part of the story: drafts are where decisions can still be softened, delayed, or dropped. Readers should compare the draft with the authority's letter to Clark sent the next day. The two papers together show the White House and the board dividing the work of settling the dispute.
frus-1945-50-intel-d19:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 27 September 1945, a week after the OSS order. The FBI director kept up a steady flow of paper to his chief through the autumn. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The dissolution of the OSS opened ground that Hoover meant the FBI to hold, above all in the Western Hemisphere. His letters after the order pressed the bureau's advantage while rivals regrouped. Readers can track a pattern across the Hoover papers: each one restates the bureau's claim in fresh terms for a fresh moment. This letter belongs to the first week of the new order of things, when the map of American intelligence lay open.
frus-1945-50-intel-d219: "Central Intelligence Group Memorandum" bears the date 21 July 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 219 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The bill that would create the CIA was in its last stages in Congress, and offices across Washington were getting ready. Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next.
frus-1945-50-intel-d319:
Minutes record the 10th Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 26 June 1947. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 319, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d419:
W. Park Armstrong sent a memo to Under Secretary of State James Webb on 6 March 1950. It is document 419 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950, one of several Armstrong papers in the file.

Armstrong headed the State Department's research and intelligence office under Secretary Dean Acheson. His memos to Webb brought the analysts' voice into the room where the department was run. Read with his other papers, this one shows a bureau chief pressing his office's worth, week after week. The March date places the memo in a season of fresh debate over the agency's future shape.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d119:
Military rule for a beaten Germany is spelled out in the directive enclosed with this 27 September 1944 instruction. The Secretary of State sends it to the American mission in London. It is for the ambassador's own guidance only. The covering note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The directive goes to the supreme commander of the Allied forces in Europe. It covers the first weeks after fighting stops, before the three powers agree on a joint paper. The War and State Departments wrote it, and the Treasury agreed to it. A joint civil affairs board had not yet cleared it. The note is firm on one point: the paper is not to be laid before the European Advisory Commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d19: A week after winning a fourth term, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on 14 November 1944. The message stands as document 19 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. With the election settled, the president could plan openly for the winter summit, and this letter forms part of the renewed push toward fixing its date and agenda.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d219:
Stettinius laid the Soviet credit request before the President on 8 January 1945. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, gives Molotov's terms in one line and Harriman's judgment in three. Six billion dollars, thirty years, two and a half percent interest: those are the terms.

Harriman expects the subject to come up at the coming meeting. His views run as follows. It serves the United States to help the Soviet economy grow. The Russians should be given to understand that such help hangs on their conduct in world affairs. And talk of long-term credits should be kept wholly apart from the running Lend-Lease negotiations. The ambassador's full cable of comment came enclosed for the President to read.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d319:
Who sat at one conference luncheon, and what was said there, can no longer be fully known. This editorial note gathers the scraps. They come from pages of Secretary Stettinius's memoir, plus brief mentions in the books of James Byrnes and Admiral Leahy. Byrnes counted ten men at the table. Leahy and Stettinius named only eight.

The editors took the time and guest list from the official trip log, filled out by Stettinius's account. Even a lunch at Malta matters, because side talks there shaped what reached the formal table. The note shows the care taken to mark what is known and what is guessed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d419:
Unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan, at the earliest possible date, heads the Combined Chiefs' formal report of February 9, 1945. The report sums up the agreed conclusions of the Argonaut conference for Roosevelt and Churchill. Its first section states the overall objective in a single sentence.

The strategic concept follows in steps. In cooperation with Russia and other allies, Germany is to be forced to surrender first. At the same time, unremitting pressure against Japan is to be kept up and extended, with the other Pacific powers. The document is the alliance's war plan for its final year, signed off at the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d119:
Ambassador Harriman pressed his case to attend the Berlin meeting in a telegram to Charles Bohlen on July 4, 1945. The message is document 119 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. His earlier note to the Secretary of State had gone out just before Stettinius resigned, and Harriman had heard nothing back.

Harriman asks Bohlen to find that message and bring it to the new Secretary, James Byrnes. He points out that General Deane and the senior mission officers have been ordered to Berlin by the chiefs, and that the British ambassador has his instructions. He also assumes Edward Page will be needed to help with interpreting and the conference record, as at Yalta. He asks for an urgent reply.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d19:
The election will not interfere: Winant relayed Churchill's assurance to Truman from London on May 24, 1945. Talking with the Prime Minister that afternoon, Winant heard that the coming election would in no way block an early meeting with Truman and Stalin. If a meeting could be arranged by mid-June, or before July 5, Churchill would probably take Attlee with him.

Churchill added that there were no differences between him and Attlee on international relations. The short cable, sent by Army channels, cleared a political doubt from the summit's path. It also foreshadowed Potsdam, where Attlee would indeed sit beside Churchill — and then replace him mid-conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d219:
Ambassador Winant reported British alarm over an American announcement on Italy in an extract dated July 15, 1945. The extract is document 219 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Winant was called to the Foreign Office that afternoon by an official named Harvey. Harvey was considerably disturbed about the Department's proposed announcement of July 17. That announcement concerned Italy and the World Security Organization. The British Embassy in Washington was being instructed to approach the Department and ask that the announcement be postponed. London wanted the question of Italy's future status discussed at the Big Three meeting first. The flare-up shows how even the timing of a press statement could open a rift between the allies.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d319:
James Dunn, Assistant Secretary of State, reported to the Secretary on July 14, 1945, after a long first talk at Potsdam with Sir Alexander Cadogan. The British Foreign Office chief had called that afternoon. For two hours the two men went over the conference agenda in a first, informal way.

The extracts printed here include the Balkans. Cadogan disagreed with Washington's reluctance to make peace with Bulgaria, Rumania, and Hungary. He repeated the British view that peace treaties would solve the allies' difficulties in those countries. The memo records the opening clash of the conference, before the heads of government had even sat down together.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d419:
Trade between Germany's zones is urged in a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum on exchanging commodities. To use German resources best for German civilians, it says, inter-zonal exchange is essential. Germany as a whole is self-sufficient in vital supplies such as food and coal, but the zones themselves are lopsided.

The Russian zone, often called Germany's bread basket, grows the food. The American, British, and French zones together form a food deficit area. The British zone holds the rich Ruhr coal fields, yet lacks the pit props to work them. The American zone has no coal assets at all. The memo makes the economic case for treating Germany as one unit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d519:
The German-Polish frontier is the fourth topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan referred to the great economic problems raised by the Poles' territorial claims. They touched, in particular, supplying food from eastern Germany and coal from Silesia. He handed Dunn a statement of the British view on Poland's western frontier.

The British, the statement says, are willing to see several lands pass under permanent Polish administration now. They are East Prussia, Danzig, and the most eastern part of Pomerania, though not as far as the Oder River. Upper Silesia is included as well. If Russia insisted upon a larger area going to Poland, the statement adds, she should accept a proportionate adjustment to balance it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d619:
Minutes of the Combined Policy Committee, meeting at the Pentagon on July 4, 1945, are document 619 here. The top secret extracts record a 9:30 a.m. session chaired by Secretary of War Stimson. Present sat Field Marshal Wilson for Britain, C. D. Howe, and Vannevar Bush. General Groves and Sir James Chadwick sat in by invitation.

One item stands out in the extracts. Wilson stated that the British government agreed to the use of the T. A. weapon against Japan. He added that Churchill might wish to raise the matter with the President at Berlin. The committee noted that both governments had now agreed, with London's consent passed through Wilson. A further item took up what the two governments should disclose about the weapon's use. Stimson, the extracts show, had the coming meeting with Stalin in mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1019:
Samuel Rosenman, the President's special counsel, reported to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945, after a call from Robert Jackson. Jackson was America's chief counsel for war crimes. A London meeting on the trials had been put off a day, since the Lord Chancellor had to attend the opening of Parliament.

Jackson's views were firm on two points. The conference should refuse to name any war criminals, and should not pledge itself here to an international tribunal. He now doubts a joint court can work smoothly with the Russians. If Moscow rejects the American terms in London, he would let each nation try its own prisoners instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1119:
From Rome, Ambassador Kirk wrote again to the Acting Secretary of State on 18 July 1945. His reports came in a near daily rhythm during the Potsdam weeks. Each one added fresh detail from the ground in Italy.

Kirk's subject was a country in flux. Italy had a new government, a beaten army, and a future that the summit would help to fix. Washington read his cables to keep its Italian policy grounded in fact. This dispatch is one beat in that drumbeat of reporting. On its own it is routine; in sequence, the cables built the picture the talks relied on.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1219:
The Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 28 July 1945. Outgoing word from the secretary set the line for the China post. It went out in the summit's last week, while the secretary's own days were filled with the German talks.

A secretary's cable to an envoy joins two files at once: the sender's talks and the reader's post. Hurley needed the summit's drift to do his work in China. This message supplied the chief's word straight from Potsdam. It is the return half of the Hurley channel, matching the ambassador's own reports printed nearby.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1319:
Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. His reparations reports went to both the president and the chief envoy that week. The commission's work in Moscow and Germany fed straight into the summit's central money fight.

What Germany would pay, in what form, and from which zones were the questions Pauley's facts had to answer. His note to Byrnes put that evidence in the negotiator's own hands. This message is the reparations thread at the working level of the talks. It shows the expert and the bargainer joined, one day into the hardest part of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1419:
A second memorandum by Charles Bohlen, also dated 28 March 1960, accompanies the Yalta texts at the back of the Potsdam volume. Bohlen knew the Soviet leaders and their language as few Americans did. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Two memoranda from the same day by the same hand suggest a man clearing his desk of a subject that would not leave him. Yalta had become a political charge in America by 1960, blamed by some for the cold war itself. Bohlen, who had taken notes and translated at the talks, answered from memory and record. His pair of papers closes the volume on a note of reflection rather than decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-119:
Dated July 26, 1945, this memorandum came from the United States delegation as the Potsdam Conference entered its second week. Delegation memos served many masters. Some carried facts upward. Others spread a settled line sideways across the team. This one was kept in the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

By July 26 the shape of the endgame was emerging, though much stayed contested. A staff memo from that day catches knowledge mid-stream. Readers can test it against the formal record of the plenary talks. The paper adds staff-level truth to a story often told from the top alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-19:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the July 18, 1945 plenary session give the press debate in the speakers' own words. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen's record runs parallel to Thompson's minutes of the same session.

Churchill contrasts the three wartime summits on press access. At Tehran there were no journalists, at Yalta few, but here they are all about. Molotov asks where they are, and Churchill explains they stand outside the compound. He offers to address them as a newspaper man on the need for secrecy. Truman declines the offer in a few flat sentences. Each team has a press representative here, so let them handle it, and no communication will issue until the conference ends. Most of them are Americans anyway, he adds. The session then turns to business.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d719:
A second Hurley letter to the Secretary of State bears the date July 31, 1945, as document 719. Two cables from Chungking in one day mark a busy channel. The exchange sits in the second Potsdam volume, among the closing papers of the conference. Hurley's post in China kept him close to the Pacific war's endgame.

Back-to-back letters let readers follow a topic in motion. A point raised in one may be pressed in the next. The pair shows the tempo of wartime diplomacy by cable. It also shows trust: the Secretary dealt with his ambassador directly, at speed, while greater matters filled his days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d819:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Matthews, the director of European affairs, on July 26, 1945. Document 819 continues the Portugal thread in the Potsdam volume. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy reported to his Department chief. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Reports from Lisbon carried the scent of a neutral crossroads. Spies, traders, and envoys all passed through Portugal. Cannon sorted the talk for Washington. Readers see the summit's world extending to Europe's quiet corner. The document shows that even uninvolved capitals fed the great powers' picture in the summer of decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d919:
The American reparations team in Moscow sent Edwin Pauley these East Prussia figures on July 24, 1945. Pauley had asked for values in his cable of July 23. The telegram gives two areas: East Prussia as a whole, and the part north of the Goldap-Braunsberg line. All sums are 1938 Reichsmarks.

Factory and mining assets came to 260 million Reichsmarks for the whole area, and 160 million for the northern part. Movable assets were 170 million and 100 million. Farm assets dwarf both figures, at about one billion for the whole area. Its farm output also ran near one billion, about 7 percent of the old Reich.
gao-gaoreports-b-297219: Charter Environmental took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-305919: The Pentagon's accountable officials abroad got a fiscal ruling in this March 2006 GAO call, which tests the local nationals' accountability. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides who answered for the dollars. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-307319: Can the Park Service charge special-use fees? GAO's August 2007 money-law ruling reads the statute for the national parks. The call decides what the agency may collect from weddings, races, and commercial shoots on park land. Public lands, public rules — down to the fee schedule.
gao-gaoreports-b-310119: A 2007 GAO ruling settling a contract fight from HERA Constructive S.A. The builder said the agency graded its bid wrong; the ruling sorts the good claims from the weak ones. Each such ruling sharpens the playbook for federal buying — a public record of what counts as a fair shake.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-119: Medicare doctor pay maps were sound but rough in 2005, and GAO's report says the geographic indices were valid in design, needing data and method refinement. The review checks the pay zones. The doctors' checks deserved the fair math. The methods had to be refined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-219: Adult drug courts cut reoffending in 2005, and GAO's report says the evidence showed recidivism reductions with mixed other results. The review reads the verdicts. The addicts-turned-defendants deserved the second chance. The evidence was weighed. The addicts-turned-defendants deserved the second chance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-719: Northern villages got billions in 2005, and GAO's report says most of the $3 billion went through local groups. The findings do the math. The report warns that the villages deserved honest accounting. The villages deserved honest accounting. The billions had to be tracked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-819: Air Mobility Command needed better aircraft data in 2005, and GAO's report says the command had to collect and analyze better utilization figures. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the cargo planes' use deserved measuring. The data had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-119: The flood insurance program's oversight needed improving in 2005, and GAO's report says FEMA had to enhance management. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the water's victims deserved a well-run backstop. The improvements had to come. The water's victims deserved a well-run backstop.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-219: The Pentagon's business systems modernization was progressing in 2006, and GAO's report says important progress had been made on architecture products. The findings give the credit. The report warns that the money machine's rebuild needed continuing. The progress had to be sustained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-519: Tsunami readiness needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says federal and state partners were collaborating to help communities, though gaps remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the coasts should not face the wave unprepared. The readiness had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-819: The transit-building grant program was changing in 2006, and GAO's report says the New Starts program was in a period of transition. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the rail-money pipeline needed steady hands during the shift. The transition had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1019: Federal computers kept springing leaks in 2007, and GAO's report says only stubborn top-level focus would plug them. The cyber weak spots were old news; the fix needed bosses who stayed on the job. The findings read as a plea for leadership that outlasts the news cycle — the unglamorous grind of real data defense.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-119: The island lands under the U.S. flag were hurting in 2007, and GAO's report walks through their money troubles and weak books. The findings paint the picture in plain terms. The report warns that the far-flung citizens deserved sounder care. The territories deserved full attention.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-219: Katrina and Rita taught hard preparedness lessons in 2007, and GAO's report says federal action could better ready the state-run aid programs. The findings press for the fixes. The report warns that the next storm would not grade on a curve. The states needed a stronger playbook.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-319: The NIH's top scientists needed clearer ethics lines in 2007 — GAO's report says the recusal rules for senior staff wanted real sharpening. The findings target the conflict-of-interest fog around public research. The report's principle stands: public science must stay above private suspicion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-519: States teaming up on nature got a GAO map in 2007 — the report overviews how the environment and natural-resource compacts were built and run. The findings chart the cooperation. The report's lesson: rivers and wildlife ignore state lines, so states must not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-919: Trade's losers needed a wider door in 2007 — GAO's report says certifying whole industries could make more workers eligible for adjustment aid, though the design stayed tricky. The findings weigh broader help against bureaucratic tangle. The report asks how generous the safety net for globalization should be.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-219: The full 2007 GAO report behind the border-screening testimony: a deep look at traveler checks at U.S. ports of entry. Secret tests and case files showed officers letting red flags slide. The report pairs the proof with fixes — sharper training, tighter steps — aimed at sealing one of the most basic gaps in border defense.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-319: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on federal Contracting: Congressional Action Needed to Address Long-standing Problems with Reporting of Advisory and Assistance Services. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-519: GAO published its findings on DOD Business Systems Modernization: Military Departments Need to Strengthen Management of Enterprise Architecture Programs in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-619: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Acquisitions: A Knowledge-Based Funding Approach Could Improve Major Weapon System Program Outcomes. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gems-of-chinese-verse-1919:
Tang dynasty verse fills Gems of Chinese Verse, Englished by W. J. B. Fletcher in 1919. Du Fu and Li Bai stand among its poets, the twin peaks of China's golden age. Moonlit rivers, frontier posts, and dawn farewells supply its scenes.

Fletcher, an early English voice for Chinese poetry, prized clarity and music in his versions. Brief lyrics carry vast feeling in a few exact images. Soldiers, exiles, wives, and wanderers all speak in turn. The anthology gives new readers a fine first path into a refined art, one that shaped verse across East Asia for a thousand years and more.
hesse-demian-1919:
Hermann Hesse published Demian in 1919, his novel of awakening, first issued under the name Emil Sinclair. Emil Sinclair's journey from bourgeois innocence to selfhood under Demian's spell made the book the voice of German youth. Hesse, broken by war and analysis, wrote it in three weeks of 1917 as a confession.

Sinclair, a schoolboy, is blackmailed by Kromer over a lie and rescued by the uncanny Max Demian. Demian teaches him to read Cain's mark as a sign of the elect, not a brand of shame. War takes both to the front, where Demian dies, promising to live on inside the friend he shaped. Abraxas, the god who is both good and evil, names the wholeness Sinclair must grow toward in Hesse's creed of selfhood. The novel's influence on young readers, from 1919 to the counterculture, is hard to overstate.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume nineteen: the legend of Frederick, how Europe remembered its most famous king. Carlyle traces the making of a myth with his usual force. The vast work reflects on its hero's place in history. Carlyle's Frederick lived on in the German imagination he helped shape.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol1-1819:
The Serapion Brethren is E. T. A. Hoffmann's great cycle of tales, first published in German from 1819. Alexander Ewing translated volume one into English in 1886. A circle of friends meets to tell stories, debate them, and judge each tale by the vivid sight of its teller.

Inside the frame, tales of artists, madmen, automata, and ghosts unfold in turn. The Nutcracker story and tales of the singer Antonia are among the treasures here. Hoffmann blends music, dream, and terror with a craftsman's care. The frame talks give the book a second pleasure: friends arguing over what makes a story true. Volume one sets the pattern for the whole cycle.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol2-1819:
Volume two of The Serapion Brethren completes Hoffmann's story cycle in Alexander Ewing's English, issued in 1892. The friends of the frame meet again, and the tales grow stranger as the evenings pass. Singers, goldsmiths, doubles, and haunted houses take their turns in the talk.

Hoffmann saves some of his richest inventions for these later nights. Music keeps its central place, as both bliss and curse for those who serve it. The arguments between tales sharpen, too, testing fancy against fact. Ewing's two volumes together give English readers the full cycle. The work remains the model for the nineteenth-century tale collection, frame and all.
irish-declaration-independence-1919: Ireland's 1919 Declaration of Independence proclaimed a republic at the First Dail. Britain rejected it. The Tower library holds the full text. It claimed a nation. Empire refused. Guns followed. Freedom came. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
irving-sketch-book-1819:
Washington Irving published The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon in 1819, writing under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon. Irving was an American author living in England, and his sketches move between the two countries. Two tales in the volume soon became famous across the English-speaking world.

One tale sends Rip Van Winkle to sleep in the Catskill hills for twenty years. Another follows schoolmaster Ichabod Crane on his night ride past the Headless Horseman. Gentle essays on English country life and Christmas customs fill out the rest of the book. The Sketch Book proved that an American writer could win a wide audience at home and abroad.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-19:
Open war reaches the St. Lawrence itself in Volume 19, from 1898. Thwaites turns the annual Relations toward Quebec and the Hurons under attack. The Iroquois strike at the heart of the French colony.

Sieges, raids, and captive-taking fill report after anxious report. Priests write through fear with their usual plain, direct style. Martyrs are made, and their deaths are told without flourish. The black robes serve as war reporters as much as pastors here. Their calm prose makes the terror of those years feel close and real. Duty holds firm even when safety is gone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lysimachus-1021:
Lysimachus, an anti-Jewish writer of Alexandria, is treated in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. He lived before Apion, the better known critic of the Jews. The article says he outdid even Manetho in hostility. His subject was the exodus of the Jews from Egypt.

In Lysimachus's version, 110,000 Jews left Egypt under King Bokchoris. Led through the desert on the advice of a certain Moyses, they reached Judea after great hardship. There they founded a city he named Hierosyla, meaning temple robbery, later softened to Hierosolyma. The entry notes that his work survives only in fragments, chiefly in Josephus's Against Apion. Scholars collected those fragments in a standard edition of Greek historians. For readers, the piece preserves one of the harshest ancient attacks on Jewish origins, kept so it can be answered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marix-adolph-10:
Adolph Marix, an American naval commander, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Saxony on April 24, 1848, he came to America as a boy. In 1864 he entered the Naval Academy at Annapolis. He graduated in 1868 and rose steadily through the officer ranks.

The article follows a career of varied stations. Marix served on ships in the North Atlantic and on the Asiatic station. He also worked in the Hydrographic Office and the judge-advocate-general's office, which sent him to Australia. In 1895 he joined the battleship Maine, leaving her only weeks before she blew up in Havana harbor. He then served as recorder of the Maine court of inquiry. Congress advanced him two numbers for conspicuous conduct in two battles at Manzanillo in 1898. Commander followed in March 1899. The entry honors a Jewish officer of the Spanish-American war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-10619:
Menahem, king of Israel from 748 to 738 B.C., is treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price. Son of Gadi, he marched from Tirzah, killed the usurper Shallum, who had murdered his predecessor after six months, and seized the throne. The biblical account, which the article follows closely, shows his brutality at once: the town of Tiphsah refused him, and he punished its women with infamous cruelty.

His reign is defined by Assyria. Tiglath-pileser III, the Bible's Pul, advanced, and Menahem bought him off with a thousand talents of silver, taxed at fifty shekels from each of Israel's sixty thousand men of wealth. The king's own inscriptions, quoted here, list "Menahem of Samaria" among his tributaries, fixing the dates. The article's closing note is dry: in that anarchic age of the northern kingdom, Menahem alone died a natural death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-phoeb:
Meshullam Phoebus ben Israel Samuel, born about 1547, rose to become chief rabbi of Cracow, where he died on October 17, 1617. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He first appears as head of a flourishing yeshivah at Brest-Litovsk, where Joel Sirḳes was among his pupils.

By 1605 he was in Cracow, and leading rabbis such as Meïr Lublin consulted him on hard questions. One of his responsa shows a thorough knowledge of anatomy and some Latin, the article notes. He also wrote a treatise on the proper names used in a bill of divorce and edited the responsa of Moses Minz, printed at Cracow in 1617.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metz-10119:
Metz, a fortified city in Lorraine, held one of the oldest Jewish communities in Europe, chronicled by Gotthard Deutsch and A. Ury for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Chronicles place Jews there as early as the year 221, living on good terms with Christians. When the article appeared, the city counted 1,451 Jews among 58,462 residents.

Early centuries brought protection from bishops and dukes and a circle of scholars called the sages of Lorraine, though Crusade-era persecution and a 1365 expulsion scattered the community. Readmitted under French rule in 1567, Metz Jews won royal letters patent, a visit from Louis XIV to their synagogue, and full recognition after the Revolution. The entry closes with its chief rabbis, rabbinical school, and charities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moritz-albert-1:
Albert Moritz, an American naval engineer, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman. Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, on June 8, 1860, he graduated from the College of the City of New York in 1877. That same year he entered the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis, graduating in 1881.

The entry follows his steady rise through the engineering ranks, from assistant engineer in 1883 to lieutenant-commander in 1903. By 1904 he was chief engineer aboard the Alabama. It also records his commendation for gallant conduct in 1900, when the Yosemite was wrecked in a typhoon off Guam. Short career sketches like this one document Jewish officers in American public service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ha-kohen-:
Moses ha-Kohen of Lunel was a French Talmudist who flourished about the year 1200. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is known for one stance: he was among the rabbis who criticized the writings of Maimonides.

His strictures on the Mishneh Torah survive in a Bodleian manuscript. A later writer, Simon ben Zemah Duran, mentions a Moses ha-Kohen in his glosses. The scholar Gross identified that figure with Moses of Lunel. The brief entry thus ties a name to the early argument over Maimonides' great code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munk-hermann-11:
Hermann Munk was a German physiologist born at Posen on February 3, 1839. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He took his medical degree at Göttingen in 1859 and settled as a physician in Berlin. He rose through the Berlin faculty and, in 1876, became professor of physiology at the veterinary college.

Munk is best known for research on the working of the brain's gray matter, the cerebral cortex. His collected papers on the functions of the cortex appeared in 1881 and again in 1890. He also wrote on the nature of nerve stimulation and on glands and nerves across many journal essays. Berlin's Academy of Sciences elected him in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-numbers-and-num:
Numbers and Numerals treats how Hebrew wrote its figures. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Caspar Levias for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Letters of the alphabet served as number signs. That use is sure by Maccabean times. Earlier practice cannot be proved so directly.

The writers argue letters likely bore values earlier still. Daily life needed signs, and neighbors used them. Talmudic writing builds past 400 by adding letters. The Masorites gave final letters the high hundreds instead. Hebrew counting is decimal, like other Semitic systems. It grew, scholars hold, from counting on one hand. Sixty still betrays the older Babylonian reckoning mixed in. Numbers also carried sacred and symbolic force. Three, tied to heaven, earth, and water, leads them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ophir-11719:
Ophir was a far land famed for gold in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name first stands for a tribe of south Arabia. Later it names the port of Solomon's fleet. His ships were built at Ezion-geber, on the Red Sea.

Hiram of Tyre gave skilled crews for those ships. They brought back four hundred and twenty talents of gold. They brought rare woods and fine stones as well. From then on, Ophir meant the land of gold to Hebrews. Where Ophir lay, no one can say for sure. Men have placed it in India, Arabia, and Africa. Some have placed it as far off as Peru. The piece weighs which of these claims hold up best.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-salv:
Salvatore Ottolenghi was an Italian doctor from Asti. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Asti on March 20, 1861. He was schooled in his home town as a boy. He then read at the University of Turin.

Salvatore took his medical degree in the year 1884. From 1888 he taught cures at the University of Sienna. He led the ward there for cures tied to the law. That field joins the work of a doctor and a court. He wrote near eighty short works for the journals. They treat the law side of cures most of all. They treat the lore of man and of crime too. His books treat the field of view in the mad and in crooks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parshandatha-11: Parshandatha was the first born son of Haman, in Esther. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Haman was the foe of the Jews in that book. In the twelve hundreds the name took a sense in books. Men split it into two parts with a new sense. Parshan means one who makes a text plain to men. Data means the law, so the name was used for Rashi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pereferkovich-n:
Nahum Abramovich Pereferkovich was a Russian writer and translator. He was born at Stavropol in 1871. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied Oriental languages at St. Petersburg. His gold medal thesis treated Gnostic sects in the Talmud. He taught religion in St. Petersburg schools.

His great work was a Russian Talmud translation. It gave the whole Mishnah in Russian for the first time. He then rendered the entire Tosefta, another first in Europe. Clergymen formed the bulk of his readers. The translation sold over four thousand copies fast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-ben-cl: Phinehas ben Clusoth was a leader of the Idumeans in the great revolt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Simon bar Giora kept raiding Idumea for food supplies. The Idumeans gained no help from Jerusalem for their losses. So they raised a volunteer band of twenty thousand men. It acted as wildly as the Sicarii themselves. Phinehas led that band with three other men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pocock-edward-1:
Edward Pocock was an English Christian scholar of Hebrew. Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Oxford in 1604. He died there in 1691, still teaching. Few Englishmen then read Arabic at all.

Pocock served as chaplain at Aleppo for six years. He gathered fine manuscripts across the East. Among them was a Samaritan Pentateuch. Oxford made him professor of Arabic in 1636. Hebrew followed in 1649, held until death. His Porta Mosis rendered Maimonides into Latin. It was Oxford's first book in Hebrew type.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pottery-12319:
Pottery among the old Israelites is the subject of an article by Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Nowack, and Frederick J. Bliss. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers say Israel learned the potter's art on Palestinian soil. A wandering life leaves no room for breakable wares. Nomads use skin bags and wooden bowls instead.

Even after settling, Israel long shunned clay vessels, they say. Early writing names earthenware in one place only. The Canaanites were the teachers of the craft. From them the Israelites learned to shape and fire clay. The article traces the wares, their shapes, and their uses. It draws on both the Bible and dug-up remains.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-12419:
Ptolemy was a prince who ruled Iturea and Chalcis. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held sway from about 85 to 40 B.C. He was a son of Mennaeus, the article says. He sought to stretch his small realm by war.

Ptolemy ruled the Lebanon and scared Damascus more than once. He took districts on the Phoenician coast by force. Once he held Paneas in his hands as well. All Galilee had once been Iturean land. Aristobulus the First took it from them in 103 B.C. The article traces the prince's wars with Rome near at hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revue-des-etude:
The Revue des Études Juives is a French quarterly founded in July 1880. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Société des Études Juives founded it at Paris. Isidore Loeb edited it first.

The article says Israel Lévi took over after Loeb died in 1892. The journal prints research and unpublished texts on Judaism. It also holds documents on French Jewish history. Nearly every issue carries a review section on new books. Leading scholars across Europe wrote for its pages. Loeb himself was its most prolific contributor. Series treat Bible study and Talmudic glosses. Others print ancient royal letters from Assyria and Egypt. The entry presents a journal at the heart of Jewish science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romm-12819:
Romm is a family of Hebrew printers and publishers in Wilna. Joseph Jacobs and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family earlier lived in Grodno. Baruch b. Joseph Romm founded a printing office there in 1789.

The article calls that office Lithuania's first Hebrew press. Royal authorization made it an important event, they say. In 1799 Baruch moved the business to Wilna. His son Menahem began a new Talmud edition in 1835. That edition became a printer's crowning effort. Later Romms gained a near monopoly in Russia. David Romm won that position before dying in 1860. From 1863 the firm traded as Widow and Brothers Romm. It stayed Russia's foremost Jewish publishing house. Deborah Romm guided it until 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubin-marcus-12:
Marcus Rubin was a Danish statistician and author born in Copenhagen on March 5, 1854. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied national economy at the university of his native city.

Rubin became chief of Copenhagen's new statistical bureau in 1883. With H. Westergaard he compiled studies of farm deaths and of marriage rates. His history of Copenhagen in the years 1807 to 1814 won a city prize. A second volume, on the time of Frederik VI, followed in 1895. The entry credits him with raising Denmark's bureau to the first rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-satan-13219:
Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Satan. In the Bible the word first means simply an adversary. It can name an enemy in war or a foe in court. In Numbers, God's own angel blocks Balaam as a satan. No distinct evil being appears yet. That figure emerges in the prologue to Job.

In Job, Satan stands among the sons of God. He roams the earth hunting for human sin. He acts as a prosecutor before the divine court. Yet he can do nothing without God's leave. Zechariah keeps that same picture. First Chronicles marks a shift. There Satan himself stirs David to number Israel. The older source had credited that act to God. The article tracks how the accuser slowly grew more independent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schudt-johann-j:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Johann Jakob Schudt, a German scholar of many fields. Schudt was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on January 14, 1664. He died there on February 14, 1722. He studied theology at Wittenberg. At Hamburg he learned Oriental subjects under Ezra Edzardi. He taught at his old Frankfort gymnasium and became its rector in 1717.

Schudt devoted himself to Jewish history and antiquities. His Compendium of Jewish history appeared in 1700. His greatest work, Jüdische Merckwürdigkeiten, came out in parts from 1714 to 1717. It repeats many fables from Eisenmenger and drips with prejudice. Yet it preserves rich detail on Jewish life of his day. Scholars still mine it for Frankfort's Jewish history. Schudt once stood on friendly terms with Frankfort's Jews. He even printed their Purim play in 1716.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shebi-it-sevent:
Shebi'it, the Seventh Year, is a Mishnah treatise on the land's year of rest. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The treatise stands fifth in the order Zera'im, on seeds. It holds ten chapters and eighty-nine paragraphs in all.

Torah law gives fields a Sabbath every seventh year. No sowing or pruning may be done then. Growth that comes on its own feeds owners, servants, guests, and the poor. At that year's end, creditors must release loans to neighbors. Hence its other name, Year of Release. Nine chapters define the soil rules in fine detail. The last chapter turns to the release of debts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shumla-13619:
Shumla is a Bulgarian city whose Jewish community formed only around 1780, local tradition says. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the city. Before that year, tradition claims, no Jew lived there. A pasha from Adrianople then became its military governor.

The pasha brought a Jewish regimental physician from Adrianople. That doctor, Hayyim Aaron Ashkenazi, was pious and well favored. He won leave to fetch a slaughterer and Jewish families. Other Jews later arrived from Pravady, Rasgrad, and Viddin. The pasha let them live in buildings around one court. Its doors closed nightly, forming a small ghetto. A little synagogue soon rose inside the enclosure. The entry tells how one doctor's faith seeded a community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-of-shikm:
Simeon of Shikmona was a tanna of the second generation and a pupil of Akiba. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His home was Shikmona, a place near Mount Carmel. Only three of his sayings survive. His fellow pupil Hidka passed them on.

Each saying makes one point about how laws come to be. Good and evil, he taught, come through good and evil people. The Sabbath breaker in Numbers led to the law on breaking the Sabbath. The pure men who asked Moses led to the law of the second Passover. The plea of Zelophehad's daughters led to the law on inheritance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonnemann-leopo:
Leopold Sonnemann was a German journalist born at Höchberg in 1831. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Lower Franconia on October 29. After gaining wealth as a merchant, he founded a newspaper. In 1856 he started the Frankfurter Zeitung at Frankfort.

That paper soon led southern Germany, above all in commerce. Since 1867 Sonnemann has been its sole owner and editor. From 1871 he sat in the German Reichstag for years. He belonged to the People's party, which his paper backed. He beat Baron Rothschild in his first election contest. In 1884 he lost to a Social Democrat candidate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinschneider-:
Moritz Steinschneider was an Austrian bibliographer and Orientalist born in Moravia in 1816. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Prossnitz on March 30 of that year. His father Jacob taught him Hebrew from an early age. The family home drew progressive Hebraists as regular visitors.

Steinschneider studied at Prague and then at Vienna from 1836. There he turned to Oriental and modern Hebrew literatures. Bibliography became the main field of his life's work. As a Jew he was barred from the Oriental Academy in Vienna. He was even denied access to Hebrew books in the Imperial Library. The long entry traces how he built Hebrew bibliography despite such barriers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-superstition-14:
Superstition in Israel meant pagan practices at odds with one God. Joseph Jacobs and M. Güdemann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Bible law bans witchcraft and sorcery outright. Deuteronomy calls them abominations of the nations. It urges Israel to be perfect with its God.

Death was the penalty for practicing sorcery under the law. Yet such practices kept their hold on Israelites. Saul sought Samuel's spirit through a medium. Jezebel and Manasseh both dealt in witchcraft. Prophets from Micah to Malachi preached against it. In Talmudic times monotheism stood firm at last. Superstition then lost its idolatrous and immoral edge. The entry argues Judaism first tried to break superstition's chains. It traces that long fight across two eras.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tam-jacob-b-dav:
Jacob Tam was a rabbi and physician of Portuguese birth. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born in the late fifteenth century. His father David belonged to the great Yahya family. The family fled Portugal for Naples in 1493.

From Naples the Tams moved to Constantinople about 1497. Jacob won recognition there as a Talmudic authority. He likely succeeded Elijah Mizrahi as the capital's rabbi. Admirers called him body-physician to Sultan Sulaiman. The entry doubts that claim as likely exaggerated. His 213 responsa survive as his chief legacy. They were printed inside a Venice collection in 1622. He died at Constantinople between 1534 and 1542. The entry weighs fame against the surviving record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobiah-ben-elie:
Tobiah ben Eliezer was an eleventh-century Talmudist and poet from Castoria, Bulgaria. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His great work is Lekah Tob, a midrashic commentary. It covers the Pentateuch and the Five Megillot. He wrote it in 1097 and revised it later.

Later printers renamed the book Pesikta Zutarta, the Lesser Pesikta. Venice editors of 1546 found no title in their manuscript. Every verse there bore a section heading, or piska. They guessed the title from that feature. Tobiah named the book for himself, Tob meaning good. His text attacks Karaites more than once. It also shows close knowledge of Muslim customs. Scholars once placed his birth at Mayence, wrongly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trinity-14519:
The Trinity, Christianity's core dogma of one God in three persons, is examined here. Kaufmann Kohler and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Nicea and the Athanasian Creed gave the dogma its fixed form. The creed bids worship of one God in Trinity. It warns against confusing the persons or dividing the substance.

Paul's letters supply the seeds of the doctrine. He sets one God the Father beside one Lord Jesus. The Holy Ghost joins them in other passages. Jewish-Christian Ebionites protested against deifying Jesus. Gentile Christians accepted the teaching in mass. The article argues the Holy Ghost's role rests on language. In Aramaic, ruha, or spirit, is a feminine noun. Some early groups thus spoke of the spirit as mother.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uzes-or-14619:
Uzès, a French town in Gard near Nîmes, had Jews from the fifth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Bishop St. Ferréol welcomed Jews to his table as friends. Complaints to King Childebert changed the bishop's stance. He then forced Jews to convert or leave Uzès.

After his death in 581, many converts returned to Judaism. Seven Jewish families lived there before the French Revolution. Those forty-six people later moved to Nîmes or Pont-Saint-Esprit. By the late 1800s one Jew remained in Uzès. A. Mossé, an attorney, served as town mayor for years. Scholars there included Samuel ben Judah and Gabriel of Milhaud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vitringa-campeg:
Campegius Vitringa the Elder was a Dutch Christian Hebraist. Joseph Jacobs wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vitringa was born at Leeuwarden on May 16, 1669. He died at Franeker on March 31, 1722. He studied at Franeker and at Leyden. He became professor of Oriental languages at Franeker.

His two chief works still draw readers today. One studies the ancient synagogue in three full books. It still has value for scholars of worship. The other is a large commentary on Isaiah. Until Gesenius, it led the field on that prophet. It was reprinted often in the eighteenth century. He also wrote six books of sacred observations with Jewish interest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weichselbaum-an:
Anton Weichselbaum was an Austrian doctor and medical researcher. He was born at Schiltern, in Lower Austria, on February 8, 1845. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at the Josefs Akademie and Vienna's university. He earned his medical degree in 1869.

Weichselbaum served as an army surgeon until 1878. He then taught at the University of Vienna. In 1894 he became professor of pathological anatomy. The Imperial Academy of Sciences elected him in 1892. He wrote over a hundred essays for medical journals. His textbook on diseased tissue appeared in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yom-tob-ben-abr:
Yom-Tob ben Abraham Ishbili, called Ritba, was a famed Talmud mind of Spain. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first half of the 1300s. His town name comes from the city of Seville.

He had a clear and sharp mind from his youth. He trained at Barcelona with two great masters there. One was Aaron ha-Levi and one was Solomon Adret. He fell to a feud with a rabbi new come to Spain. His works fill a long list in the short entry. They treat tract after tract of the Talmud text. They treat the works of Alfasi and Nahmanides too. Most were bound as one set in two towns in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeisel-simon-15:
Simon Zeisel (born 1854) was an Austrian chemist of farm and field. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Lomnitz in Moravia, he schooled at Brunn. He took his degree at the University of Vienna in 1879.

In 1887 he set up as a free teacher at that school. He taught the craft of chem there to young men. In 1892 he took a post at the farm high school. That post was in farm and field chem at Vienna. In 1899 he rose to full chief of that work there. His work ran in the tech press of his day in full. He wrote one book that sets out chem in plain words. That book came out at Vienna in the year 1890.
journal-of-discourses-vol-19:
John Taylor leads the church in Volume Nineteen, issued in 1878. The underground deepens as federal hunters press the Saints harder. Leaders hide, families scatter, and the kingdom stays defiant throughout.

Many discourses here were preached by men the marshals hunted daily. Sermons bless the hidden, stiffen the wavering, and damn the persecutors. Faith under real persecution speaks in its own hunted voice here. The price of the Saints' stand is counted in prison and exile. Readers meet devotion that paid in full for what it professed to believe. Taylor's calm command steadies a church learning to live underground.
kafka-in-der-strafkolonie-1919:
In der Strafkolonie, published in 1919, is Kafka's story of a penal colony and its execution machine. An officer demonstrates the apparatus to a visiting traveler: it kills by slowly writing the condemned man's sentence into his flesh with needles.

The officer believes in the machine and its dead inventor with religious faith. The traveler watches, unwilling either to approve or to intervene. When the machine is set to judge the officer himself, it fails in a spasm of self-destruction. Kafka wrote the story in 1914, as Europe entered its own machinery of death. Its horror is quiet, procedural, and complete.
kalila-wa-dimna-knatchbull-1819:
Wyndham Knatchbull translated Kalila and Dimna into English at Oxford in 1819, the first English rendering from the Arabic. The book, also called The Fables of Bidpai, tells animal tales inside a frame of a king and his philosopher. Lions, jackals, doves, and apes act out the rules of power, friendship, and caution.

The tales began in India's Panchatantra, passed into Persian, then into Arabic in the eighth century. From Arabic they spread across Europe and fed its beast fable for a thousand years. Kalila and Dimna, the two jackals of the first book, give the whole its name. Knatchbull's version marks the Arabic stage of that long westward road. The stories taught statecraft through animals.
keynes-economic-consequences-1919:
John Maynard Keynes served as a British Treasury adviser at the Paris peace talks after the First World War and resigned in protest. His 1919 book The Economic Consequences of the Peace tells why. It made him famous almost at once on both sides of the Atlantic.

Keynes argues that the treaty terms, above all the huge payments demanded of Germany, would wreck trade and breed fresh conflict. He draws sharp portraits of the leaders at Paris and weighs their choices coldly. His warning read like prophecy within a generation, as Europe slid toward a second war.
laski-authority-state-1919:
Authority in the Modern State, published in 1919, is Harold J. Laski's pluralist attack on state sovereignty, drawn from his early Harvard years. Against the doctrine that the state commands all loyalty, Laski argues that authority is in fact dispersed among groups.

Churches, unions, and associations hold real allegiance, and the state's claim to stand above them is a fiction that experience refutes. Federalism of function, not territory, is his model. The book is learned in the history of political thought and brisk in its conclusions. It made Laski's name and set the pluralist program he later revised but never abandoned.
league-covenant-1919:
The Covenant of the League of Nations was adopted in 1919 as the first part of the Treaty of Versailles. It set up the world's first general body meant to keep peace between nations. President Woodrow Wilson championed the League, hoping that nations pledged to settle disputes by law would end the age of great wars.

The Covenant created an assembly and a council, promised aid to any member attacked, and laid out rules for cutting armaments and settling quarrels. Its weakness showed at once when the United States Senate refused to join. The League failed to stop the next world war, yet its structure and ideals passed directly into the United Nations.
letters-to-dead-authors-pg3319:
This Gutenberg copy of Lang's Letters to Dead Authors lists twenty-two pieces. Letters go to Herodotus, Alexander Pope, and Lucian of Samosata. Rabelais, Jane Austen, and Isaak Walton follow in the contents.

Dumas, Theocritus, Poe, and Walter Scott each receive a letter. So do Shelley, Molière, Burns, Byron, and Omar Khayyam. Horace closes the list of honored dead. Sixteen letters came from the St. James's Gazette, as the preface says. Lang's playful post to the past remains a critic's delight. Some letters gently scold their heroes for faults. Lang's learning never hides his fan's affection for books.
luxemburg-junius-pamphlet-1919:
Luxemburg wrote her Junius Pamphlet in a Berlin prison cell in 1916. The Socialist Publication Society issued it in English in 1919 as The Crisis in the German Social-Democracy. Germany's Social Democrats had voted war credits in 1914, backing their own government's war. Luxemburg, writing under the name Junius, indicts that choice.

She calls the war an imperialist slaughter and the party's vote a betrayal. The pamphlet looks to a rebuilt international movement of workers against war. Its pages burn with grief for the party she helped build. The text stands as a founding voice of revolutionary anti war socialism. Few prison writings carry such weight.
massinger-fatal-dowry-1619:
Philip Massinger and Nathan Field wrote The Fatal Dowry, a Jacobean tragedy first staged around 1619. A young officer comes home from war to find his dead father's body held by creditors who will not release it for burial. To settle the shame, he marries into a rich and corrupt household.

The marriage quickly turns sour, and claims of betrayal push the hero toward a fierce defense of his honor. Murder and revenge follow, handled in the sharp, formal verse of the early Stuart stage. Readers meet a world where debt, pride, and loose morals drive men to ruin. The play still ranks among the strongest revenge dramas of its time.
merritt-moon-pool-1919:
Lost realms and a bright dweller call to men in Abraham Merritt's novel The Moon Pool, from 1919. A team of bold men finds old ruins in the south seas. A gate of moon light leads down to a vast cave world of strange life and old gods.

Peril and awe mix in rich, lush prose. Merritt piles wonder on wonder at pulp speed. The book helped set the mold for lost-world tales in the United States. Its glow shaped hosts of pulp tales that came in its wake. A bright being in the pool can heal or kill with its touch. Its gifts draw greed, faith, and war from all who meet it.
