miscellany-of-poetry-1919:
W. Kean Seymour edited this anthology of contemporary poetry in September 1919. He calls it a truly catholic collection, dedicated to Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch. Every poem was new, never before issued by its author in book form. Seymour thanks the magazines that allowed reprinting, from the English Review to the Nation.

Laurence Binyon opens the contents with a song and a poem called The Children Dancing. F. V. Branford contributes a farewell to mathematics. Decorations by Doris Palmer, Cecil Palmer, and Hayward ornament the pages. The anthology preserves British poetry at the moment the First World War ended, before reputations settled.
much-ado-about-nothing-pg1519:
William Shakespeare set this comedy in Messina, in the house of Leonato. The contents map five acts of halls, gardens, and streets. A church scene in act four marks the plot's dark turn. This is the standard Gutenberg text, number 1519.

Beatrice and Benedick wage a merry war of wit. Friends trick each into thinking the other is in love. Young Hero is slandered and seems lost to Claudio. Dogberry's clumsy watch stumbles on the truth in time. V1 called it Shakespeare's sunniest comedy, full of masked balls, eavesdropping, and joy from the first line to the last.
nasa-tm-19710002769-erc-v-stol-program-f:
NASA's Electronics Research Center issued this flight test plan as document PM-51. It covers phases 1A and 1B of the H-19 flight program at Wallops Station, Virginia. The work belonged to the center's V/STOL program for craft that rise straight up and land the same way, here a helicopter test bed.

The flights were meant to gather data on an inertial aid for guiding the craft through the last part of its flight. Such data would shape the avionics design for future vertical takeoff aircraft. The plan summarizes each phase's tests and the analysis output expected from them. Flight profiles are defined and developed in detail, and a closing section describes the test range and its facilities.
o-henry-memorial-award-prize-stories-of-:
Prize Stories of 1919 holds the first O. Henry Memorial Award winners, chosen by the Society of Arts and Sciences. Blanche Colton Williams wrote the introduction. This copy is dated 1924. Margaret Prescott Montague opens the contents with England to America. Wilbur Daniel Steele follows with For They Know Not What They Do.

Ben Ames Williams, Albert Payson Terhune, and Edison Marshall all place stories here. Fannie Hurst's Humoresque and Edna Ferber's April 25th, As Usual stand among them. James Branch Cabell offers Porcelain Cups, and Melville Davisson Post a five thousand dollar reward tale. The set shows the American short story in prize form, just after the war.
occult-chemistry-clairvoyant-observation:
Annie Besant and Charles Leadbeater wrote this theosophical work. A revised edition, edited by Alfred Percy Sinnett, appeared in 1919. The authors claim to study chemical elements by clairvoyant sight. That means they say they saw inner atomic forms directly. Sinnett added a new first chapter for this edition.

Sinnett explains how the early research led to later work. From chapter three on, the text reprints the first edition. The book describes claimed structures inside atoms of known elements. It stands apart from standard chemistry of its time. Readers use it to study theosophical thought and its claims. The London theosophical house published the revised edition that year.
openalex-w2099615319:
Eleonora Uphoff, Kate Pickett, Baltica Cabieses and colleagues reviewed research on social capital and health inequality. Their paper appeared in the International Journal for Equity in Health in 2013. Social capital means the value of social ties and trust. It may protect health, yet it can also exclude people. The team asked how it interacts with income inequality.

They searched for studies published before mid-2012. Sixty studies met their criteria for analysis. Most used self-reported health measures. Studies covered bonding, bridging and linking forms of capital. Nearly all found links between social capital and health gaps. The pathways between them remain partly unclear. The review maps evidence gaps for future research.
openalex-w2137113819:
Matthew Nock, Irving Hwang, Nancy Sampson, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2009. They used the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys to link mental disorders with suicidal behavior across countries. Suicide is a leading cause of death, and disorders predict it strongly, but details were unclear.

The team asked which disorders predict attempts on their own, not just through shared overlap. They also asked whether disorders predict acting on suicidal thoughts, and whether patterns match in richer and poorer countries. Their data cover lifetime disorders, age of onset, and nonfatal attempts reported in the surveys. The analysis gives a cross-national map of these links for prevention work.
openalex-w2162584119:
Jens Kattge, Sandra Díaz, Sandra Lavorel, and colleagues published this paper in Global Change Biology in 2011. They present TRY, a global database of plant traits, the measurable features of plants and their parts. Traits govern how plants answer environmental change and shape whole ecosystems, yet trait records lay scattered across many small collections.

TRY united the worldwide trait research community behind one shared repository. Ninety-three trait databases had been contributed when the paper appeared. The store held almost three million trait entries covering about sixty-nine thousand plant species. Fifty-two trait groups form its focus. The authors argue such shared data link species richness to the working diversity of ecosystems.
openalex-w2168477819:
Marcus Teixeira, Luiz de Almeida, Paula Kubitschek-Barreira, and colleagues published this genome study in BMC Genomics in 2014. They compared the two main fungi behind sporotrichosis, a skin infection of people and animals. One species spreads mainly from cats and drives a large ongoing outbreak in Brazil, while the other infects mostly humans worldwide.

Both genomes were sequenced and lined up side by side. The two species proved highly similar in gene order and sequence, splitting only a few million years ago. The cat-linked species carries more jumping DNA and a unique set of intron elements in its mitochondria. Families of proteins tied to surfaces and signaling also grew in their shared lineage.
openalex-w3016325919:
Agustina Malizia, Cecilia Blundo, Julieta Carilla, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2020. It draws on a large network of forest plots across the Andes to map how mountain forests change with place. Knowledge of Andean forest structure at regional scale had stayed limited, with big gaps in global forest surveys.

The network database holds nearly five hundred plots, spanning about four thousand kilometers of latitude and four thousand meters of elevation. The team assessed forest structure and tree species diversity along those gradients. They report that elevation and latitude drive both the build of the forest and which tree species appear. The results give conservation a firmer base map for the tropical and subtropical Andes.
openalex-w3134610819:
Virgínia Souza, Maria Marziale, Gilberto Silva, and Paula Nascimento published this study in Acta Paulista de Enfermagem in 2021. It translates the COREQ checklist, a thirty-two-item guide for reporting qualitative research, into Brazilian Portuguese and validates the translation. It then tests whether a nursing journal's adoption of the guide changed reporting quality.

Three expert judges refined the translated items through the Delphi method, reaching near-total agreement. The team then scored seventy-seven qualitative articles, comparing years before and after the journal adopted COREQ. Reporting improved on five items, including naming who conducted the interviews. A shared checklist in the local language, the work suggests, can raise the standard of qualitative papers.
openalex-w4225922019:
Haniel Barbosa, Clark Barrett, Martin Brain, and colleagues describe cvc5, a software tool for automated reasoning, in a 2022 conference paper. cvc5 is an SMT solver: it decides whether statements mixing logic and mathematics can be satisfied. Such solvers power software and hardware checking, security analysis, test generation, and planning tools. cvc5 continues the long-running CVC solver family and rebuilds on the code of its predecessor, CVC4.

The paper explains cvc5's design and the main features added since CVC4. The authors test it on the full SMT-LIB benchmark library. They compare its performance against both CVC4 and the rival solver Z3. The description gives users and researchers a map of a tool built for industrial-strength use.
openalex-w4283704819:
Houriiyah Tegally, Monika Moir, Josie Everatt, and colleagues report the emergence of two new Omicron lineages in South Africa, in Nature Medicine in 2022. The lineages, named BA.4 and BA.5, were spotted by the country's genomic surveillance network. They arrived just after BA.2 had replaced BA.1 as the dominant local form. That earlier swap, unusually, brought no large new surge in cases or deaths in South Africa.

The team used family-tree methods to place the new lineages and track their spread. Watching such handovers matters, because each new lineage can differ in how fast it spreads or dodges immunity. South Africa's sequencing network had first flagged Omicron itself. This brief report is an early warning of the variants that soon drove waves worldwide.
openalex-w4387344519:
Jennifer Luedtke, Janice Chanson, Kelsey Neam, and colleagues report the second Global Amphibian Assessment in Nature in 2023. The team evaluated eight thousand eleven frog, toad, and salamander species for the IUCN Red List. Regular reassessment is needed as threats shift and knowledge grows. Amphibians were already known as the most threatened backboned animal group.

The news is worse than before. About two fifths of species are now globally threatened, a share that has climbed since 1980 and again since 2004. Habitat loss remains central, while disease and climate change press harder. The authors corrected old scores so that only real changes count. Their update tells conservationists where to act first for a group sliding toward extinction.
openalex-w4391809119:
Juraj Krempaský, Libor Šmejkal, Sunil D'Souza, and colleagues report experimental evidence for a new kind of magnetism, in Nature in 2024. Magnets were long sorted into two classes, ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Theory recently added a third class, altermagnets, which mix traits of both. In an altermagnet, opposite-spin sublattices are linked by a rotation of the crystal rather than a shift or flip.

That link protects a balanced magnetic order with no net magnetisation. At the same time it lets the energy levels of the two spins split apart. Physicists call that split the lifting of the Kramers degeneracy. Until now this splitting had not been seen directly. The team measured it in a crystal, confirming a prediction that could matter for future electronics.
openalex-w7162582519:
Udai Shimada, of Japan's Meteorological Research Institute, led a 2026 study building a long-term dataset of the radius of maximum wind for tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific. That radius, the distance from a storm's center to its strongest winds, is a key measure of storm structure. Different estimation methods often disagree, so the authors built a Bayesian consensus method to merge them into one careful estimate per storm.

The dataset covers 631 cyclones from 2000 to 2025 at three-hour intervals, drawn mainly from satellite rainfall and imagery data. Checks showed errors shrinking for stronger storms and when the method's confidence was high. The dataset captures tight inner cores that older methods missed, aiding storm research.
openalex-w7166512119:
Zhiyang Quan and Takayoshi Awakawa published a 2026 review in the Journal of Antibiotics on how bacteria build azaindane natural products, a small family that includes altemicidin and two related compounds. Finding the genes behind a known natural product can be hard when the core enzyme is unknown. The team used a self-resistance gene as a beacon to locate the responsible gene cluster in the producer's genome, then confirmed the cluster by expressing it in a host.

Step-by-step biochemistry revealed the assembly line. One central enzyme builds the shared azaindane scaffold from two common cellular ingredients, and a chain of further enzymes trims and decorates it into the final products. Structural studies of two enzymes showed how they grip their targets. The review presents the case as a model for mining similar hidden clusters.
openalex-w7213768119:
Nathalia Keron Miranda da Silva analyses the effects of appeals in Brazilian civil procedure. Her single-author 2026 article reads the 2015 Code of Civil Procedure alongside current legal scholarship. Scholarly disagreement over how appeal effects should be classified and counted opens the study.

Attention then narrows to the appeal itself and its consequences. Partial appeal, the mature cause theory, and the lower court's power to reconsider are each examined. A ban on making the appellant worse off is weighed against rules that let higher courts raise public-order matters on their own. Silva's account helps law students and practitioners see how one appeal can reshape a case beyond the points actually argued.
openalex-w7214089019:
Débora Priscila de Sousa Nascimento leads an review on physiotherapy for subacromial bursitis. That condition is a leading cause of shoulder pain and can badly limit upper limb function. Their 2026 review searches PubMed, SciELO, and a health library for 2013 to 2025, in three languages.

Therapeutic exercise, above all scapular stabilization and muscle strengthening, cut pain and improved function and motion range, the results show. Manual therapy and electrophysical resources added to exercise strengthened the effect. Physiotherapy is judged essential in rehabilitation for these patients. Better symptoms and recovered function, the authors conclude, restore quality of life that shoulder pain had taken away.
openalex-w7214439419:
Luis Eduardo Brandão Martins led an eight-author 2026 narrative review on using the antimicrobial drug metronidazole to control bad odor in necrotic wounds. Dead tissue in a wound feeds bacteria that live without oxygen, and the smell they produce can isolate and distress patients, especially in palliative care. The team analyzed seven studies on the drug's use for this purpose.

Across those studies, metronidazole reduced wound odor, whether applied on the wound or given to the whole body, and it often worked quickly. Results were better when it was combined with dressings that lower the bacterial load. The studies had limits, the authors note, but they conclude the drug is an effective part of a broader, individualized care plan for malodorous wounds.
openalex-w7214590219:
Priscila Castro Cordeiro Fernandes led a 2026 study of childcare in primary health services in Uberlândia, Brazil, asking who actually brings young children to their checkups. The team interviewed more than three hundred caregivers of children under two and mixed statistical analysis with caregivers' own accounts. Their lens is the sexual division of labor, the pattern that assigns care work mainly to women.

Nine in ten people accompanying the children were women. Women also knew more about child health visits, yet that involvement came with the overload of a double working day, at home and outside it. Missed appointments, the authors argue, are socially structured by gender inequality rather than simple carelessness. They call for policies that share parental responsibility and for education strategies inside primary care that reach fathers as well as mothers.
openalex-w7215842819:
Laysa de Souza Maia led a 2026 literature review on how chronic alcohol use damages the brain. Heavy, prolonged drinking is a major public health problem with system-wide effects. Searching a major medical database with recent studies first, the team studied the cellular and molecular mechanisms that link alcohol to neurological change and neurodegenerative processes.

Chronic exposure was tied to altered neurotransmission, brain inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and a weaker blood-brain barrier, along with structural changes in gray and white matter. These changes can injure neurons, impair memory, attention, and executive function, and raise the risk of neurodegeneration, including higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia such as Alzheimer's and vascular dementia. Alcohol stands out as a risk factor people can change, the authors conclude, arguing for prevention, harm reduction, and early finding of alcohol-related brain change.
opus-mago-cabalisticum-et-theologicum-vo: Georg von Welling's Opus mago-cabalisticum et theologicum is an early eighteenth-century German work of alchemy and theosophy. It appeared under the name Gregorius Anglus Sallwigt. The hosted sample shows only its title page, but that page is unusually full. It promises an account of the origin and generation of salt, its nature, properties, and use. From that root it claims to prove how all metals, minerals, and other salts arise in nature. Theosophical matter, invisible creatures, and Paradise are also advertised. No body text appears in the sample.
plaw-115-411-2019: Public Law 115-411 is the Global Health Innovation Act of 2017, approved on January 3, 2019 near the close of the 115th Congress. The law orders the head of the United States Agency for International Development to report to Congress each year for four years. Each report covers new health tools used in the agency's programs. The tools range from drugs and vaccines to phone-based health services.
plos-pbio-0020219:
Konstantinos Zarbalis, Scott R. May, Yiguo Shen, and co-workers set out a mouse screening strategy in PLOS Biology in 2004. Random mutations can reveal genes that build the brain's cortex, the wrinkled outer layer where thought happens. Screening every mutant mouse the old way is slow and costly.

Their focused plan checks likely mutants first and uses clear signs to pick the ones worth deep study. With it, they found mutations that disrupt cortex development. Each such mutant is a clue to how the cortex is wired as it grows. A sharper screen speeds the whole field, since good mouse models of brain disorders are prized and hard to make.
plos-pone-0000019:
Jonathan Reddy, Ian Ganley, and Suzanne Pfeffer hunted for clues to brain damage in a rare inherited disease in their 2006 study. Niemann-Pick type C disease traps cholesterol inside cells, and children who have it slowly lose nerve cells. Why those cells die was poorly understood.

The team profiled gene expression across the whole genome in diseased cells, watching which genes switch up or down. Patterns in that global profile point to the pathways that fail as neurons degenerate. Clues of this kind are the first step toward treatments for a disease that still has few. The paper shows how a broad gene scan can narrow a hard medical mystery.
plos-pone-0000119:
Fabrizio Gelain, Daniele Bottai, Angleo Vescovi, and colleagues published this tissue engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. They built designer scaffolds from self-assembling peptides, tiny protein pieces that line up into nanofibers on their own. The scaffolds were used to grow adult mouse neural stem cells in three dimensions.

Growing brain stem cells in 3-D, rather than flat on a dish, better mimics real tissue. The authors describe how the cells take to these tailor-made fiber networks. The approach points toward lab-grown material that could one day support nerve repair. It also gives stem cell researchers a tunable tool for testing growth conditions.
plos-pone-0000219:
Noah Fahlgren, Miya D. Howell, Kristin D. Kasschau, and colleagues published this plant genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Using high-throughput sequencing, the team catalogued microRNAs in Arabidopsis, the model plant. Their evidence points to frequent birth and death of MIRNA genes, the genes that make these tiny regulators.

MicroRNA genes turn over fast, appearing and vanishing across generations of plants. Documenting that churn in a single well-studied species shows how regulation evolves. The sequencing data also expanded the known set of Arabidopsis microRNAs, a resource other plant biologists build on.
plos-pone-0000319:
Victor M. Rodriguez-Molina, Ad Aertsen, and Detlef H. Heck published this neuroscience theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cortical pyramidal neurons are the main output cells of the cortex, and their spike timing, the exact moments they fire, may carry information. The authors model how EPSC kinetics, input synchronization, and background noise affect the reliability of that timing.

Precise firing matters if the brain uses time as a code. The model weighs three influences that sharpen or blur a neuron's timing. The results help interpret recordings from real cortex, where all three influences are always present together.
plos-pone-0000419:
Baochuan Lin and colleagues applied a broad pathogen-hunting method to samples from a city population, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Most tests look for one germ at a time. Their approach is sequence-based and broad-spectrum: it reads genetic material to identify many possible pathogens at once, including ones nobody suspected.

A test that names whatever is there could catch outbreaks earlier and solve infections that single tests miss. Applying it in an urban population checks whether the method survives real-world messiness. The work points toward surveillance systems that watch for the unexpected, not only for the diseases already on a checklist.
plos-pone-0000519:
Susan Marino and Roel Nusse reported mouse mutants that reveal a chromatin machine's importance before birth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The mutants disable P66α, a component of the NuRD/Mi2 complex, which remodels chromatin, the packaging of DNA, to control genes. The title states the outcome plainly: the mutants are embryonic lethal.

Embryonic lethality means the complex is not optional equipment; development fails without it. Such all-or-nothing results tell biologists which regulators sit at the center of the gene-control web. They also set the stage for finer experiments that disable the protein in one tissue or stage at a time.
plos-pone-0000619:
Miriam Zacksenhouse, Mikhail A. Lebedev, Jose M. Carmena and co-authors tracked brain signals in early brain-machine interface sessions for PLOS ONE in 2007. Such interfaces read activity from motor cortex neurons and use it to drive artificial devices. When a person plans or makes a reaching movement, those neurons change their firing in many ways at once.

The team reports that cortical modulations grow during the first sessions with the interface. In plain terms, the brain's signal patterns become stronger as practice begins. That growth matters for anyone building devices controlled by thought, because the interface and the brain adapt to each other from the very start.
plos-pone-0000719:
Lan Lan Liang Yeh, Jah-Yao Liu, Kao-Si Lin and colleagues put an 800-year-old herbal formula through a modern trial, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Most traditional Chinese formulas combine at least four herbs. Four-Agents-Decoction, or Si Wu Tang, contains four herbs and has long been used in Taiwan to relieve menstrual discomfort. No specific effect, however, had been established by controlled testing.

Their trial was randomised and placebo-controlled, the design that separates real effects from expectation. The condition was primary dysmenorrhoea, painful periods without an underlying disease. Old remedies deserve fair tests rather than dismissal or blind trust. A rigorous trial gives women and doctors evidence either way.
plos-pone-0000819:
Jürgen Glas, Julia Seiderer, Martin Wetzke and colleagues tested a bowel disease gene variant in a large German patient group, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The IL23R gene had been identified as a susceptibility gene for inflammatory bowel disease in the North American population. Their aim was to test that association in German Crohn's disease patients, and to look for interactions with other IBD genes.

The combined analysis covered IL23R, CARD15, and OCTN1/2 variants. The title names their headline result: variant rs1004819 is the main disease-associated IL23R variant in German patients. Replication in a second population matters, because genetic associations that travel across populations are likelier to be real and useful.
plos-pone-0000919:
Orest Szczurko, Kieran Cooley, Jason Busse and colleagues ran a randomized trial of naturopathic care for chronic low back pain, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Long lasting back pain costs employers heavily in health coverage and lost work days. Many patients try naturopathic care, a mix of diet advice, exercise and natural treatments, but hard trial evidence was thin.

The team randomized seventy-five postal workers to test whether the care helped. A randomized design, where chance assigns the treatment, is the fairest way to judge. Whatever the outcome, trials like this move a popular therapy out of the realm of claims. They give patients and insurers results they can weigh.
plos-pone-0001019:
Aaron Filler traced how body segment patterns diversified across mammals, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Homeotic genes set the identity of body segments, yet little was known about how their traits evolved over the mammal radiation. The spine is one place those patterns show plainly.

Filler reports an array of homeotic gradients that appear and diversify across mammal groups, generating new body plans. The work extends to the morphogenetic basis of human origins, how our own segment pattern arose. Reading mammal diversity as variations on shared gradients gives anatomy a developmental logic. It also explains odd spine counts that once looked like noise.
plos-pone-0001119:
Medical scans show the brain and skull as flat pictures, even though both are complex three-dimensional shapes. Daniel Kelley and co-authors describe a way around that limit in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They turn scan data into solid physical models using stereolithography, a form of 3D printing.

The team developed and validated a method for building accurate models of the brain and skull from medical images. A solid model can be held, turned, and studied from any angle, which flat images do not allow. Such models can support teaching, surgical planning, and a clearer grasp of how the structures fit together.
plos-pone-0001219:
Electrical signals from muscles, called EMG signals, let people control prostheses and computers by tensing a muscle. Eric Fimbel and Martin Arguin studied how well older people manage that control, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. An earlier experiment with young participants was replicated with elderly persons.

The authors assessed the effect of age on myocontrol, the ability to steer devices through muscle signals. Assistive technology is aimed largely at older users, so performance in the young is the wrong benchmark. Their results inform how such interfaces should be designed and calibrated for the people who actually need them.
plos-pone-0001319:
Insects smell their world through families of chemoreceptor proteins, but almost nothing was known about those receptors in beetles. Mohatmed Abdel-latief described a family of chemoreceptors in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Chemoperception in invertebrates is mediated by G-protein-coupled receptors.

The beetle's genome had recently been sequenced, making it a model species for beetle biology. The authors catalogued its chemoreceptor genes as a first step. Knowing a pest's smell receptors opens routes to traps and repellents that target its senses. The gene list gives that work a starting point.
plos-pone-0001419:
Vincent Béringue and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease. How wide the epidemic would grow was hard to call. Many who carry the agent may never show signs, or may show an odd form. The team used mice bred with the human gene to track infection.

In these mice, infection took hold far beyond the brain and stayed for a long time. That broad spread was both marked and lasting. It hints that silent carriers could hold the agent in many tissues. Such facts shape blood safety rules and the long watch kept on this disease.
plos-pone-0001519:
Marco Ajelli and Stefano Merler published a 2008 PLOS ONE model of flu spread between people. Models that track each person have grown key for pandemic plans. They count set contacts, such as home, school, and work ties. Loose, chance contacts are harder to count. The pair asked how much that loose part sways the outcome.

They found the loose contact share can shift both spread pace and the worth of control steps. Leaving it out can bias a model's verdict. Pandemic teams should thus test a range of loose contact rates. The work is a check on the tools that guide real world plans.
plos-pone-0001619:
Alicia Fajardo and her co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE research article about a hard problem in medicine. Some germs are born able to resist antibiotics. Doctors call the full set of these built-in defenses the intrinsic resistome. Most experts had blamed two causes, cell walls that drugs cannot cross and pumps that push drugs back out of the cell.

Fajardo's team tested that view by studying transposon mutants, germs with single genes knocked out at random. Their work points to a wider set of genes behind built-in drug resistance than the usual two causes suggest. The full text sets out the mutant screen and the genes it flagged. It also shows why a fuller map of these defenses could guide the search for drugs that still work.
plos-pone-0001719:
Wenbin Ye and co-authors studied the fine shape of the bond between microRNAs and their targets in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. MicroRNAs guide the repression of messenger RNAs after they are made. Hundreds are known, but finding which mRNAs each one targets in mammals is hard, partly because the pairing rules are poorly understood.

The team focused on central loops, bulges in the middle of the miRNA to target duplex, and measured how they affect repression efficiency. The full text gives the pairings tested and the gene regulation readouts. Sharper pairing rules mean better computer predictions of microRNA targets, a step needed before these tiny regulators can be fully mapped or used as drugs.
plos-pone-0001819:
Paula H. A. Ronkainen, Eija Pöllänen, Timo Törmäkangas, and their co-authors studied a gene affecting muscle in older women in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Muscle strength declines on average by one percent a year from midlife. In postmenopausal women that decline coincides with a rapid drop in estrogen production. The genetics behind estrogen's effects on skeletal muscle remained unclear.

The team reports that a polymorphism in the COMT gene is associated with skeletal muscle properties in older women. The gene's full name is catechol-O-methyltransferase, and the effect appears alone and together with physical activity. The full text gives the muscle tests and the gene comparisons. Gene-activity interactions like this point toward exercise prescriptions tuned to a woman's genetic profile.
plos-pone-0001919:
Svetlana Novikova and co-authors studied what cocaine use in pregnancy does to the brains of mouse pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Past work had shown clear changes in how the young of cocaine-exposed mothers behave. The team tested a deeper idea: that the drug warps the fetal system that tags DNA, leaving lasting marks on brain chemistry.

They gave cocaine to pregnant mice and then checked pups at birth and before puberty. The focus was the hippocampus, a brain area for memory, where they measured DNA methylation and which genes were switched on. Lasting tags there could help explain why early drug exposure shapes later acts.
plos-pone-0002019:
Glen Duncan and co-authors used twins to sort genes from surroundings in exercise habits, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Regular physical activity is well known to protect health. Yet how much of a person's activity level is inherited, and how much comes from their setting, was still disputed. The team set a cut point of sixty minutes of total activity per week.

Twin data let them split the effects of shared genes, shared home life, and each person's unique setting. As the title stresses, unique environmental effects stand out in who takes part. If settings drive activity more than genes, changes to daily life may move people more than advice alone.
plos-pone-0002119:
Martina Proell and co-authors published a review in PLOS ONE in 2008. Its subject is the Nod-like receptor family, a group of proteins often shortened to NLRs. These proteins sit inside cells and help the innate immune system, the body's fast first line of defense, sense signs of infection and damage.

The review sets out what the family members share and where they differ. It covers how NLRs are grouped, how they are thought to switch on immune responses, and why they sit at the core of many diseases. Readers get a clear map of a protein family that was then drawing fast-growing interest in immune research.
plos-pone-0002219:
Alexandre Zenon, Suliann Ben Hamed, and Jean-René Duhamel tracked the focus of attention during hard visual searches, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spotting prey or a predator depends on pulling the right sight out of a busy scene fast. In the lab, visual search tasks copy that challenge: a subject must find one target among many distractors.

When the target is hard to tell apart, the search is slow and attention must be guided step by step. The team mapped how that guidance unfolds in space and time. Their results show the order in which the brain checks each part of a cluttered scene while hunting for a hard target.
plos-pone-0002319:
Flonia Levy-Adam and co-authors found a second job for an enzyme that chews up a common cell coating, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Heparanase cuts heparan sulfate, a sugar chain found on cell surfaces and in the matrix between cells. Its cutting helps tissues remodel and lets cancer cells spread.

The team reports that heparanase also works without cutting: it helps cells adhere and spread by clustering the heparan sulfate proteoglycans on the cell surface. Bringing those surface molecules together can fire growth signals. A non-cutting role matters for drug design, since blocking the enzyme's blade may not block this second activity.
plos-pone-0002419:
Prins led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Kurt W. Prins, Dawn A. Lowe, James M. Ervasti, among others. Its subject is skeletal Muscle-Specific Ablation of γ cyto -Actin Does Not Exacerbate the mdx Phenotype. We before documented a ten-fold increase in γ cyto -actin expression in dystrophin-deficient skeletal muscle.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002519:
Kondilis and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Barbara K. Kondilis, Ismene J. Kiriaze, Anastasia P. Athanasoulia, among others. Its subject is mapping Health Literacy Research in the European Union: A Bibliometric Analysis. To examine and compare the research productivity on selected fields related to health literacy of the current members of the European Union.

A bibliometric analysis (1991–2005). The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002619:
Betina Højgaard and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on waist circumference and body mass index as predictors of health care costs. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Betina Højgaard, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In the present study we analyze the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC) and future health care costs. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002719:
A 2008 study by Zhan Gao and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up substantial alterations of the cutaneous bacterial biota in psoriatic lesions. The catalog record names Zhan Gao first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. For psoriasis, an idiopathic inflammatory disorder of the skin, the microbial biota has not been defined using cultivation-independent methods. It goes on to note a further point. We used broad-range 16S rDNA PCR for archaea and bacteria to examine the microbiota of normal and psoriatic skin. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002819:
Arjan B. Brenkman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on mdm2 induces Mono-Ubiquitination of FOXO4. Authorship is credited in the record to Arjan B. Brenkman and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The Forkhead box O (FOXO) class of transcription factors are involved in the regulation of several cellular responses including cell cycle progression and apoptosis. It goes on to note a further point. Furthermore, in model organisms FOXOs act as tumor suppressors and affect aging. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002919:
Arach Goldar, Hélène Labit, Kathrin Marheineke and co-authors modeled DNA copying in early embryos in 2008. Cells seem unable to check that copying is finished during a normal S phase, yet they must finish on time. In early Xenopus frog embryos the problem is sharp, since copy start sites switch on at random.

Their dynamic stochastic model treats start site firing as a chance process and works out how reliable finishing still results. Stochastic here means driven by random timing. Published in PLOS ONE, the model helps explain how embryos copy a whole genome fast without a central checker.
plos-pone-0003019:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Konstantinos Kantartzis and co-authors tested new type 2 diabetes risk loci against prediabetic traits in 2008. Genome-wide studies had found a series of new risk loci, most later shown to affect insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells. A fresh meta-analysis had just revealed nine more loci with unknown roles.

The title reports those new loci do not determine prediabetic phenotypes. In other words, carriers did not show the expected early traits. Published in PLOS ONE, the gap between genetic risk and measurable early signs is itself informative for screening ideas. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003119:
Masashi Fujihara, Norihiro Nagai, Thomas E. Sussan and co-authors published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks whether long-term cigarette smoke can harm the retina in ways that look like early age-related macular degeneration, a common cause of vision loss in older adults. Two-month-old mice breathed either clean air or smoke in a chamber for five hours a day, five days a week.

The title reports the main result: smoke caused oxidative damage and cell death in the retinal pigmented epithelial cells, the layer that supports the light-sensing retina. Readers get a clear test of how smoke exposure links to eye damage, and why smoking may raise the risk of this eye disease.
plos-pone-0003219:
Yong Luo, Mauricio Alvarez, Lingchuan Xia and colleagues ask what happens to microbes when their host cell divides in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Macrophages can multiply, and certain microbes survive inside phagocytic cells. That raises the question of where the microbe cargo goes after the host cell splits. Using macrophage-like cells, the team checked how Cryptococcus yeast inside the cells is shared out after division.

The title reports that the outcome of phagocytic cell division with infectious cargo depends on single phagosome formation. Readers see lasting infection as a problem of cell division. If microbes cluster in one compartment, daughter cells may inherit them unevenly.
plos-pone-0003319:
Max-Philipp Stenner, Anne Waschbisch, Dorothea Buck and colleagues study a multiple sclerosis drug's effect on regulatory cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natalizumab is a monoclonal humanized antibody targeting the alpha-4 chain of very late activation antigen 4. It has strong healing effects in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. The goal was to study impacts of natalizumab therapy on Foxp3+ T regulatory cells.

Readers learn how a strong drug that blocks cell traffic affects the cells that calm immunity. That balance matters because blocking cell movement helps the brain but can raise infection risk. Tracking regulatory cells adds a safety layer and shows more of how the drug works.
plos-pone-0003419:
László Pecze and co-authors studied how skin cells react to chili compounds in this 2008 paper. Capsaicin, the heat in chili peppers, can also dull pain. A stronger cousin, resiniferatoxin, opens a channel called TRPV1 for good. That flood of calcium can remove pain-sensing nerve cells.

Oddly, the main cells of the skin did not react the same way. These cells, called keratinocytes, proved resistant to both compounds. Their toughness sets them apart from the nerves around them. Drug makers must weigh that split when designing skin-applied pain treatments. Nerves and skin, though close neighbors, answer these compounds in opposite ways.
plos-pone-0003519:
Elina Salmela and co-authors mapped population structure in northern Europe in this 2008 study. Genome-wide data can reveal fine patterns of human variation. The team analyzed almost 250,000 DNA markers per person. Samples numbered 945, from Finland, Sweden, northern Germany, and Great Britain.

Even within northern Europe, clear genetic clusters appeared. Eastern and western Finland differed, as history would suggest. Geography and past migration carved structure into the genome. Such maps matter when gene studies compare cases and controls. Such maps also serve as base lines for gene hunts in each region. Finnish groups proved especially rich in fine detail.
plos-pone-0003619:
Pascal F. Egea and co-authors solved a docking protein's structure in this 2008 paper. All cells use a signal recognition particle to guide new proteins to membranes. Its receptor catches those proteins at the membrane for secretion or insertion. The team worked with the receptor from Pyrococcus furiosus, a heat-loving archaeon.

They present the first X-ray structures of an archaeal FtsY receptor. The shapes clarify the targeting step at the membrane. A system conserved across all life can be read in this ancient version. Such structures anchor models of protein delivery.
plos-pone-0003719:
Gaoping Xiao, Eirik W. Lundblad, Mina Izadjoo, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. External guide sequences are short RNAs that steer an enzyme to cut a chosen target RNA. That trick can shut a gene off after it is read. The team aimed it at a dangerous bacterium's control gene.

They used the method in E. coli to block MglB, a virulence regulator of Francisella tularensis, the tularemia germ. Blocking the regulator shows the switch can be reached and silenced. The approach offers a programmable off-switch for probing how dangerous pathogens run their genes.
plos-pone-0003819:
Cyril Touboul, Wassim Badiou, Julien Saada, and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Heavy bleeding after childbirth can kill a new mother within hours. Selective arterial embolisation blocks the bleeding arteries from inside, using imaging to guide the block. The team assessed how well it works at scale.

They studied 102 patients with life-threatening post-partum haemorrhage who underwent the procedure. The results measure the technique's efficacy and help pin down its best indications. Knowing when embolisation works best guides emergency teams facing one of childbirth's deadliest complications.
plos-pone-0003919:
Leigh Anne Eller, Michael A. Eller, Benson Ouma, and co-authors set lab reference ranges in Uganda in 2008. Vaccine trials now run in many countries at once. Each site needs local ranges for normal lab values to judge safety. Values from other populations can mislabel healthy local volunteers.

Their PLOS ONE article reports ranges from healthy adult blood donors in Uganda. Those ranges show where local norms depart from imported ones. Using them keeps trials from excluding healthy people by mistake. It also sharpens safety checks while new vaccines are tested in the region. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004019:
Michael W. Miller, Heather M. Swanson, Lisa L. Wolfe, and co-authors assessed prion disease in deer in 2008. Chronic wasting disease spreads through deer family populations. Scrapie does the same in sheep flocks. Such epidemics seem able to threaten whole host populations.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs the ecological fallout in natural settings. Mountain lions prey on deer and may shape the epidemic. Predators could remove sick deer faster than healthy ones. The study asks whether prions, predators, and deer together decide population fate. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004119:
Mansour Aliabadian, Mohammad Kaboli, Vincent Nijman, and co-authors tested DNA barcoding in birds in 2009. Barcoding uses the COI gene to identify species by DNA. It has worked across many animal groups. Closely allied neighboring species, though, sometimes blur together.

Their PLOS ONE article tests distance-based barcoding across three genes. The target was delimiting parapatric species, neighbors with touching ranges. Performance varied in how cleanly the genes split those species. The study warns barcoding needs backup where bird ranges meet. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004219:
Shota Nakamura and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The SARS epidemic of 2003 and fears of bird flu pandemics showed the need for surveillance systems that catch new infectious diseases early. The team applied next-generation parallel sequencing, a high-throughput way to read DNA, directly to clinical samples.

Their unbiased approach reads whatever genetic material is present in nasal and fecal specimens, without first choosing which virus to look for. That direct metagenomic detection can name viral pathogens in a single run. The method points toward outbreak watch systems that do not need to guess the culprit in advance.
plos-pone-0004319:
Françoise Gondois-Rey and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I interferon during viral infection. Interferon alpha therapy clears hepatitis C virus in more than half of chronic patients. That success suggests the patients' own interferon production may be impaired.

The team compared how these cells respond to hepatitis C virus versus influenza and human herpesvirus type-1. They report that HCV is a weak inducer of interferon alpha in these cells. A virus that barely trips the alarm can explain how HCV settles in for decades.
plos-pone-0004419:
GB virus B, a close cousin of the hepatitis C virus, serves as a stand-in for human disease. Lucile Warter, Lisette Cohen, Yann Benureau, and colleagues used it in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The virus infects small primates, so it lets scientists study hepatitis C safely. Both viruses carry RNA ends that are not read as protein but fold into four loops with like shapes.

The study shows that these untranslated RNA stretches work together with a viral protein called NS5A. That teamwork makes a combined, or chimeric, virus fitter in a living host. Learning how the parts help each other points to weak spots that future hepatitis drugs might attack, and it sharpens the animal model used to test them.
plos-pone-0004519:
Mice lacking a sugar-binding protein fight a fungal infection with the wrong kind of immune response, report Luciana Ruas, Emerson Bernardes, Marise Fermino, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is galectin-3, which had recently been shown to help tune immunity to infections, largely by steering cytokine signals. The fungus is Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, a cause of serious disease in South America.

Immune responses lean toward Th1 or Th2 styles, which suit different enemies. The team infected mice without galectin-3 and measured that balance. Without the protein, the response tipped toward Th2, as the title reports, and resistance suffered. The result shows one protein acting as a traffic cop for immune style, with real effects on who wins against a fungus.
plos-pone-0004619:
Unknown gene sequences from genome projects can be named faster with help from their neighbors' functions, show Paolo Fontana, Alessandro Cestaro, Riccardo Velasco, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Large-scale sequencing had become routine laboratory practice. That flood of sequences created a need for tools that predict gene function, bringing such methods back to the fore.

The authors annotate anonymous sequences by semantic similarities, comparing the Gene Ontology terms, a structured vocabulary of gene functions, attached to related genes. A weighting scheme decides which similarities count most. Fast, reliable annotation turns raw sequence into biology. Without it, genome projects produce letters that no one has time to read, and the functions of most genes stay unknown.
plos-pone-0004719:
Kathrin Michelsen and colleagues linked gene variants to higher levels of an immune signal in bowel disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal, called TL1A, boosts output of other immune signals from T cells. Both TL1A and its receptor rise during long term gut inflammation in Crohn disease and related illness.

The team asked if the gene form a person carries sets how much TL1A they make. They found that forms linked to bowel disease do raise TL1A levels. That tie helps explain why some people face stronger gut inflammation. It also names a path that new drugs could calm.
plos-pone-0004819:
Sean Kim and colleagues took a computational approach to understand in vitro alveolar morphogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Primary human alveolar type II lining cells in Matrigel form alveolar like cysts using a step different from other studied lining types. Neither growth nor death is involved during cyst formation, making it a pure rearrangement process suitable for modeling cell movement and adhesion changes.

Models reproduce lumen formation dynamics from cell properties. Knowledge alveolar formation informs lung repair research. Computational tests can predict perturbations before tests. The system isolates morphogenesis steps. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004919:
Copper is a metal that every cell needs in tiny amounts. Its balance inside cells shifts as they grow old. Christian Scheckhuber and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on that shift. They tracked copper in ageing cells of the fungus Podospora anserina, a classic ageing model. They also tracked it in ageing human skin cells called fibroblasts.

Their measurements pointed to mitochondria as major players in the change. Mitochondria are the cell's energy producers. The same kind of shift appeared in the human cells, not just the fungus. That parallel suggests some features of cellular ageing are shared across very different forms of life.
plos-pone-0005019:
Lead in city air has fallen for decades. Even so, children need still lower exposure. This potent neurotoxin harms the developing brain. Nicholas Pingitore and colleagues hunted its remaining source. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used X-ray absorption spectroscopy on urban airborne lead.

The analysis fingered urban soil as the dominant source. Factories and traffic were not the main culprits anymore. Old lead settled in soil keeps rising into the air as dust. The finding points cleanup at the ground beneath cities. It also explains why air lead resists further decline. Soil is a long memory for past pollution.
plos-pone-0005119:
Viruses engineered to kill cancer are called oncolytic viruses. Some replicate only in tumor cells. Their clinical efficacy is still limited by poor infection of the tumor mass. Verónica Lopez and colleagues studied a missing factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor is the tumor's stromal cells. These support cells talk constantly with malignant cells.

Tumor-associated stromal cells play a critical role in the outcome. They can shield the tumor from the viral attack. Beating cancer with viruses means beating its neighborhood too. The study used conditionally replicative adenoviruses. It shows efficacy depends on more than the virus and the cancer cell. Trial designers should measure the stroma's role. Patients might be chosen by stromal features.
plos-pone-0005219:
Melanoma that has spread is hard to treat and lacks reliable blood markers to track it. Tumors shed tiny vesicles called exosomes, which carry proteins from the cells that made them. Logozzi and colleagues measured those vesicles in melanoma patients in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Patients carried high levels of exosomes marked with the proteins CD63 and caveolin-1 in their plasma. Healthy tumor-derived vesicles also play roles in cancer growth, so the signal is biologically plausible. A blood test based on vesicles could track disease without repeated tissue samples. A test built on these tiny packets would be easy to repeat, which is just what doctors need when they track a fast-moving cancer.
plos-pone-0005319:
Human attention is not spread evenly across space, and that bias shows up in both patients and healthy people. Turriziani and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the same spatial biases shape language processing. Their study explores the relationship between semantics and space.

Meaning and space may share mental machinery, so a skew in one could tilt the other. The work investigates how representations of space affect aspects of processing words. Links like these matter for understanding language disorders that follow brain injury to one side. Ward care for stroke cases with one-sided neglect may gain from this link, since drills that join words and space could train both at once in the same task.
plos-pone-0005419:
Caroline Kulangara and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE study on the search for a malaria vaccine. The genome of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum had opened new ways to hunt for vaccine parts. One new method picked out short repeating patterns that form coiled shapes in parasite proteins.

The authors checked how much those coiled parts stay the same across parasite strains. A part that does not change much makes a better vaccine target, since the parasite cannot easily escape it. Their checks help narrow the list of parts worth testing in future vaccine work.
plos-pone-0005519:
Renee Tsolis and co-authors read the genome of a sheep pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Brucella ovis causes a disease of the breeding organs in sheep. Unlike its close kin, it does not infect people.

The team's genome study found many broken and missing genes compared with its kin. That decay matches the germ's narrow life: one host and a narrow range of tissues. Reading which genes were lost helps explain why this Brucella stayed a farm problem while others became a threat to people as well. Its broken genes read like a record of a germ settling into a narrower and safer niche.
plos-pone-0005619:
Yosuke Kumamoto and co-authors studied skin immune cells and allergy in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Dendritic cells are the immune system's strongest teachers, showing T cells what to attack. In skin, two groups share that job: cells in the top layer and cells in the layer below.

The team showed that one group of the deeper cells, marked MGL2, is enough on its own to start contact allergy in mice. Knowing which teacher cell starts the reaction helps target allergy treatments to the right place in the skin. Skin allergy to metals and chemicals is common, so the cells that start it are a natural drug target.
plos-pone-0005719:
Akito Kawahara and colleagues built a family tree for hawkmoths in 2009 using five nuclear genes. Hawkmoths number about fourteen hundred species and serve as test cases across biology. Yet their family links, built mostly on body form, were shaky.

Gene data gave the team a firmer tree and a view of how the moths spread across the globe. A solid tree lets other work, from flight studies to pest control, rest on real kinship. The study replaces guesswork about hawkmoth history with evidence from the moths' own DNA. It covers one of the most watched moth families in science.
plos-pone-0005819:
Nishaki Mehta and co-authors made HIV testing cheaper in 2009 by validating diagnosis from dried blood spots. A spot of blood dried on paper is easy to collect, store, and ship where labs are scarce. Real-time PCR can then measure the virus from that spot.

Their method both detects HIV and counts its load at low cost. Early treatment of infected infants is now advised, which needs exactly this kind of test. The approach fits clinics that lack freezers, couriers, or big budgets. The team shows performance data to back its use in limited-resource settings.
plos-pone-0005919:
Food sharing keeps an ant colony alive, yet who hands food to whom is hard to watch. In 2009, Aurélie Buffin, Damien Denis, Gaetan Van Simaeys and their co-authors took up that puzzle in PLOS ONE. They fed ants food marked with a mild radio label so that each meal could be traced through the colony.

By tracking the label, the team could see how food moved from ant to ant and where it ended up stored. The maps point to set exchange patterns rather than random sharing among nest mates. Work of this kind helps explain how a colony feeds queens, larvae and workers with no central control at all.
plos-pone-0006019:
Learning needs the right proteins in the right neurons at the right time. Attila Stetak, Frederic Hörndli, Andres Maricq and colleagues pinned one such protein down in the worm C. elegans in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies MAGI-1, a scaffold protein at synapses, and its neuron-specific role in associative learning and memory.

A scaffold holds signaling parts in place so a synapse can change with experience. Finding that MAGI-1 acts only in certain neurons sharpens the map of the worm's learning circuit. The worm's small nervous system lets each cell be named, so a cell-specific result like this gives memory research unusually firm ground.
plos-pone-0006119:
A signal that fights tumors elsewhere in the body may reach lung tumors too. Irma Airoldi, Emma Di Carlo, Claudia Cocco and colleagues studied interleukin-12 in lung cancer in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper builds on mice lacking the IL-12 receptor part rb2, which develop lung adenocarcinomas on their own, and examines the receptor in human primary lung tumors.

IL-12 can target both the cancer cells and the normal bronchial cells around the lesions, the title reports. Non-small-cell lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, so a signal with that reach earns attention. The receptor's pattern in human tissue helps judge where IL-12 therapy might act.
plos-pone-0006219:
Cells talk through signals and direct touch, but passing whole genetic messages between cells was thought rare. Amy Skinner, Lee O'Neill, and Peter Kurre studied tiny bubbles called microvesicles in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Similar RNA transfer by small vesicles had been reported in immune cells.

The team shows these pathways can be aimed to carry genetic information between non-immune cells. Deliberate targeting turns a natural parcel service into a delivery tool. That opens ideas for moving therapeutic genes without viruses. It also suggests cell messages in the body may travel further than textbooks assumed.
plos-pone-0006319:
Naming a plant pathogen wrong can misdirect quarantine and crop protection. Markus Goeker and colleagues used Peronospora, a genus of downy mildew fungi, as a case study in molecular taxonomy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Sensible species limits are crucial for plant protection and biological control.

DNA-based analysis redraws species boundaries in the genus more sensibly. Poorly drawn taxa have severe consequences across research and farming. Model organisms chosen for comparison also depend on correct names. The case study shows molecular data settling disputes that appearance alone could not.
plos-pone-0006419:
Steroid treatment can starve bone of blood until the bone dies, a condition called osteonecrosis. Ge Zhang and colleagues tested flavonoids from the herb Epimedium in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Two events interrupt bone blood supply: clotting inside vessels and fat deposits outside them. No clinical agent targets both at once.

The Epimedium flavonoids reduced the incidence of steroid-associated osteonecrosis in a dose-dependent way. The effect did not come via direct action on the expected cellular targets, the title notes. The compounds may act through circulation rather than bone cells. A plant-derived candidate for an untreatable side effect deserves the attention.
plos-pone-0006519:
Hridayesh Prakash and co-authors studied a protein that helps infected lung cells stay alive, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ Chlamydophila pneumoniae infects the lung and lives inside its cells. Cells it infects resist apoptosis, the built-in death program of cells. That stand has been tied to a protein called cIAP-1, which blocks cell death.

The team asked how cIAP-1 shapes the first immune response to this lung germ. A germ that keeps its host cell alive gains a safe home. If that shield could be lifted, the body might clear the germ more fast. The work shows the push and pull between the germ and the cell it lives in.
plos-pone-0006619:
Isabel Calvo and co-authors ran a genome-wide screen for caffeine tolerance in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. An excess of caffeine is cytotoxic to all eukaryotic cell types. The team aim to study how cells become tolerant to a toxic dose of this drug. They also study the relationship between caffeine tolerance and other stresses.

A genome-wide screen of genes required for caffeine tolerance tests every gene for its contribution. Yeast screens are fast and complete, giving a parts list for drug defense. Many tolerance genes will have human counterparts. The work also illuminates how caffeine affects cells beyond its stimulant fame.
plos-pone-0006719:
Enas R. Yassin and colleagues dissected how a fusion gene transforms blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is NUP98-HOXA9, a hallmark of acute myeloid leukemia. It joins part of NUP98 to the DNA-binding part of HOXA9. The fused protein likely acts as a faulty transcription factor. It binds DNA and switches the wrong genes on or off.

The team introduced the fusion into primary human blood-forming cells. They then took its transforming action apart step by step. Watching healthy human cells turn cancerous shows which parts are essential. That knowledge can point to drug targets in this leukemia. It also clarifies how one fusion protein can drive a whole cancer.
plos-pone-0006819:
Lavinia Nardinocchi and colleagues targeted low-oxygen survival in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Solid tumors often contain hypoxic, oxygen-starved zones. A factor called HIF-1α helps cancer cells survive there. It also restrains blood vessel growth and drug response in tumors. A kinase called HIPK2 normally opposes HIF-1α and supports the guardian p53.

Restoring HIPK2 and p53 activity suppressed HIF-1α in their experiments. That suppression attacks the hypoxia program cancer cells depend on. The combination offers a strategy against resistant tumor cores. Hypoxic zones often survive chemotherapy, so targeting them addresses relapse at its source.
plos-pone-0006919:
Nassima Temime-Smaali and her team used a plant-made drug to strike cancer cells that stretch their gene caps in an odd way in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some cancers stretch caps by a path called ALT, in place of the stock path. Their caps crowd in odd hubs in the cell core, with tools for gene swaps. One tool, topoisomerase III alpha, is a must for that path. The drug telomestatin grips four-strand knots in DNA, called G-quadruplexes.

The drug kept the tool from gripping those knots. It also stripped the caps bare in ALT cells. Bare caps read as harm, and harm can kill the cell. The strike is a made-to-fit blow at ALT cancers.
plos-pone-0007019:
He-Ge Chen, Wen-Jun Han, Mi Deng, and colleagues mapped control of a widespread enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protein phosphatase 2A removes phosphate tags from proteins. It supplies more than half of that activity in many cells. The enzyme is built from scaffold, catalytic, and regulatory parts.

The team studied how the scaffold part's gene, PP2A-A alpha, is switched on. Several transcription factors shared the job, including AP-2α, CREB, ETS-1, and SP-1. Knowing its controls helps explain how cells tune this master regulator. Faulty tuning is linked to cancer and other diseases.
plos-pone-0007119:
Liwen Chen, Edward Tredget, and Chenxiong Liu tested donated stem cells in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow can aid tissue repair. Donor, or allogeneic, cells would be easier to stock than a patient's own. Yet immune rejection might destroy them and cut engraftment. The team compared donor and matched cells directly.

They measured engraftment and wound healing in mice for each type. The comparison tests whether off-the-shelf cell therapy is realistic. If donor cells survive long enough to help, banks of ready cells become practical for wound care.
plos-pone-0007219:
Lucia Colombo and Jason Zevin investigated how readers assign word stress in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They ran four experiments using priming methods. Their language focus is Italian, where word stress is unpredictable and often needs lookup in memory rather than simple rules.

Readers can use lexical routes based on whole words, or sub-lexical routes based on parts. The authors study how stress priming changes each route during reading aloud. Their findings show selective effects on the two pathways. Psychologists of language can use the work to model how pronunciation is planned.
plos-pone-0007319:
Melissa Garren, Laurie Raymundo, James Guest, and colleagues tested coral microbes under fish farm pollution in PLOS ONE in 2009. A coral holobiont includes the coral animal, its algal symbionts, and its microbes. Those microbes help keep the whole system balanced, so robust microbial communities support long-term reef survival.

Coastal pollution threatens that balance. The authors expose coral-associated bacterial communities to fish farm effluent. They measure how resilient the communities are to that exposure. Their results show whether farm waste can destabilize the microbes corals depend on in reef ecosystems.
plos-pone-0007419:
Ole Hartvig Mortensen, Anders Rinnov Nielsen, Christian Erikstrup, and colleagues proposed an inflammation protein as an obesity marker in 2009. Two inflammatory molecules, S100A8 and S100A9, form a combined protein called calprotectin. Plasma calprotectin levels are elevated in various inflammatory disorders, from arthritis to inflammatory bowel disease in clinical practice.

The authors hypothesize levels would rise in low-grade systemic inflammation as well. That state accompanies obesity. They test calprotectin as a novel marker of obesity. Their PLOS ONE paper evaluates whether a simple blood measure can capture the hidden inflammation that links obesity to disease.
plos-pone-0007519:
Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the fragility of personal memories. A new memory starts out labile, then settles into stable storage. Recalling a settled memory makes it fragile again until it re-stabilizes, a step called reconsolidation. The team asked whether learning something new during that window interferes. Their test used autobiographical memories, the stories of a person's own life.

Fresh episodic learning did interfere with the reconsolidation of the recalled personal memories. The old memories came back altered by what was learned in between. That finding carries real stakes for therapy and for eyewitness accounts. It shows that remembering is not replaying a fixed record. Each recall opens a brief chance for the record to be edited, for better or worse.
plos-pone-0007619:
John Lukens and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the liver's unusual immune character. The liver is constantly exposed to bacterial products and food antigens from the gut. To avoid constant inflammation, it leans toward tolerance. The mediators that shape immune responses in that environment were not fully known. The team tested whether the liver itself can activate naive killer T cells in mice.

The liver can activate those CD8 T cells. The cells it produces, though, show dysfunctional antiviral activity. That is the tolerance trade-off made visible: response without full fighting power. Such a compromise protects the organ from friendly fire. It may also explain why some viruses persist in the liver. The study pinpoints the liver as an active teacher of T cells, not a passive bystander.
plos-pone-0007719:
Masaaki Adachi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at what happens when cells face heat and oxidative stress at once. Pollution and ozone loss raise oxidative stress, while warming raises heat exposure. People now risk meeting both at the same time.

Cells defend themselves with a heat stress response that rescues folded proteins. The authors found that oxidative stress weakens that defense. It also slows the recovery of proteins after heat damage. The result helps explain why combined stresses can harm health more than either one alone.
plos-pone-0007819:
David Gallego-Ortega and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares two sister enzymes that start a key fat-building path in human cells. Choline kinase is the first enzyme of the Kennedy pathway branch. That branch makes phosphocholine, a main part of cell membranes.

Humans carry two forms, alpha and beta, with different jobs. The authors map their differential roles in lipid metabolism. The split matters for cancer, where choline use runs high. It also matters for treatment, since blocking the wrong form could cause harm. The study guides which enzyme drug makers should target.
plos-pone-0007919:
Murugesan Rajaram and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows a dangerous bacterium's escape from the cell compartment meant to kill it. Francisella tularensis infects macrophages, the immune cells that eat germs. It breaks out of the phagosome and multiplies in the cell body.

Infected cells then die through the Fas-mediated death pathway. The authors show that pathway switches on as the bacterium escapes. Two cell proteins, Akt and SHIP, modulate the escape. The tug-of-war between germ and host decides the infection's course. Each control point is a possible therapy target.
plos-pone-0008019:
David Lambert and colleagues read DNA from museum skins of an extinct New Zealand bird in PLOS ONE in 2009. The huia was famed for its beak: the male's was short and stout, the female's long and curved, the widest such gap known in birds. The last birds died out a century ago.

Gene tests, sex checks, and careful measures of the old specimens let the team rebuild parts of the bird's family life and variety. Museum skins thus still speak. What they say can guide care for the huia's living kin and sharpen how we read other lost species.
plos-pone-0008119:
Aimee Shen and colleagues simplified protein cleaning with a tag that cuts itself off in PLOS ONE in 2009. Labs grow useful proteins in bacteria, then must fish them out pure. Tags help the fishing, but cutting the tag off usually adds steps and cost.

Their tag borrows a cutting enzyme from the cholera germ that snips only at one exact spot, its own joint. A trigger makes it cut on command, freeing the clean protein. Fewer steps mean less loss and fewer chances to spoil delicate proteins, a gain for labs large and small.
plos-pone-0008219:
Sean Myles and colleagues presented fast genome methods for grapes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The genus Vitis includes the grapes used for wine and table fruit. New sequencing tools promise to speed the use of genetic data in crop improvement. Mapping genes for useful traits is a key step in breeding. Good study design comes before that mapping work.

The team showed how rapid genomic characterization can be done across the genus. A broad genetic picture helps breeders plan crosses and mapping studies. It can reveal diversity that breeding programs might otherwise miss. The work supports faster, smarter improvement of grape varieties.
plos-pone-0008319:
Carney D. Matheson and colleagues investigated an ancient tomb in Jerusalem in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Tomb of the Shroud dates to the first century of the common era. It was discovered in Akeldama, Jerusalem, and had been looted before study. An interdisciplinary team began investigating it in 2000. More than twenty stone ossuaries held human remains there.

Molecular methods were used to explore the tomb's contents. Ossuaries are boxes for collecting bones after burial. DNA and other traces can reveal kinship and disease among the dead. The work connects archaeology with laboratory science.
plos-pone-0008419:
Zhe Ji and Bin Tian studied messenger RNA endings in stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The 3 prime untranslated regions of mRNAs contain elements that regulate gene expression after transcription. Over half of mammalian genes have multiple polyadenylation sites. Alternative choices produce different 3 prime regions for the same gene. The team examined this during generation of pluripotent stem cells.

Reprogramming cells from different types reshaped their mRNA endings. Shorter or longer tails change how messages are controlled. Such reprogramming may be part of how stem cells reset identity. The work links RNA processing to cell fate.
plos-pone-0008519:
Otto Erlwein and co-authors test a claimed virus link in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In October 2009, a study reported a new retrovirus in chronic fatigue syndrome. The virus, called XMRV, had also been linked to prostate cancer. It was reported in most US patients in that study. If confirmed, the claim would reshape understanding of the syndrome. Erlwein's team try to detect XMRV in their own patient group.

They fail to detect the novel retrovirus in chronic fatigue cases. Their methods were able to find the virus if present at reported levels. A negative result of this kind tempers a high-profile claim. It shows why independent replication is essential in science.
plos-pone-0008619:
Khatira Anwari and co-authors describe a membrane machine in a germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria, the power units of our cells, came from a free germ long ago. They still build their outer membrane much as that germ did. The germ studied here is Caulobacter crescentus, a model species. The team study its BAM complex. That machine inserts barrel-shaped proteins into the outer membrane.

They find the germ BAM complex is built from modules. Its modules echo the machine still used in mitochondria. Study of the germ version clarifies how mitochondria arose. It also reveals weak points in germ membranes that drugs could target.
plos-pone-0008719:
Soumyajit Banerjee Mustafi, Prabir Chakraborty, and Sanghamitra Raha traced how a grape compound attacks leukemia cells. Their work ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. Resveratrol is found in grape skins and red wine. It lowers levels of Hsp70, a protective protein, in chronic myelogenous leukemia cells. Lower Hsp70 helps push those cells to die. The route from compound to protein drop was unclear.

The team followed two signaling paths, Akt and ERK1/2, inside K562 leukemia cells. Resveratrol shifted both paths, and Hsp70 fell as a result. Mapping the route shows where similar drugs might strike leukemia cells.
plos-pone-0008819:
Koichi Matsumura, Maryanne Opiekun, Hiroaki Oka, and colleagues sniffed out lung cancer through urine odor. Their proof-of-principle study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung cancer is the top cancer killer worldwide. It often grows silently until late stages. The body releases volatile compounds that change with disease. Breath studies had hinted such odor signatures exist.

Mouse models of lung cancer carried distinct urinary odor profiles. Trained detection could separate cancer urine from healthy urine. A urine test would be painless and cheap to repeat. Much work remains before human screening, but the principle held in mice.
plos-pone-0008919:
Martin Peifer, Jonathan Weiss, Martin Sos, and colleagues built a math method for judging drug pairs in fast cell screens. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Single cancer drugs often shrink tumors only briefly. Pairs of drugs can control tumors longer and better. Finding pairs that truly synergize, though, is slow. High-throughput screens test thousands of combinations on cells. Scoring synergy fairly across a whole population is the hard part.

Their lifetime modeling scores synergy from how cell populations fare over time. Population-level scoring resists the noise of single snapshots. Combination hunting for cancer drugs gets a sharper tool. Better pairs can reach animal testing sooner.
plos-pone-0009019:
Thomas Ray charted where psychedelic drugs attach across the whole human receptor set, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Psychedelics are thought to work mainly through two serotonin receptors, 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C. Drugs like the phenylalkylamines seem fairly choosy for those two. But a full census of their binding had not been assembled.

Ray mapped the drugs against the human receptorome, the full set of receptors. The chart shows which receptors each compound touches beyond the famous two. Some side targets may help explain differences between these drugs. A complete map warns against assuming one receptor explains the whole experience.
plos-pone-0009119:
Adriane Martin Hilber and co-authors pooled dozens of studies on vaginal practices and HIV risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many women use intravaginal practices to manage their health and sexual life. Cleansing the vagina and inserting substances are common in many regions. Such practices could harm the vaginal lining and invite infection, though.
