Combined with the earlier toxicology review, the panel concluded the extended uses raise no safety concern under the stated conditions.
pmc-13249619:
Barril and Vegué model how a mixed population of hosts steers pathogen nastiness, in a 2026 mathematical biology paper. Their model links two scales: how germs multiply inside one body, and how infection spreads through a population. Hosts differ in immune strength, and that difference turns out to decide which level of virulence evolution favors.

When hosts reliably clear infections fast, germs evolve to be more virulent. When hosts are doomed once infected, gentler germs win instead. Mixing the two host types, with a share of vulnerable individuals, produced richer behavior between those extremes. The authors use the results to argue that immune diversity in a population is itself an evolutionary force.
pmc-13250019:
Rodríguez-Belenguer and a European team propose a shared catalog format for imaging biomarkers, in a 2026 paper. A biomarker here is a number pulled from a scan that signals disease state or treatment response. Every group describes such numbers in its own way, which blocks comparison and reuse. The team mined official and scientific sources, then merged the overlapping fields by expert agreement.

The result is a five-part template. It covers identity, clinical context, technical imaging details, proof of validity, and upkeep, all aligned with the FAIR data rules for findable, reusable data. Test entries for inflammation imaging, from diffusion measures to PET scans, fit the scheme cleanly. The authors aim the catalog at researchers, regulators, and clinicians alike.
pmc-13250219:
Nishikawa and colleagues build a non-invasive way to sort heart failure patients into classic wet-or-dry and warm-or-cold profiles. Their 2026 Open Heart study replaces catheter measurements with two bedside tools: body water analysis and pulse wave timing. Patients admitted to one cardiology department between 2020 and 2022 were grouped by these measures.

Among five hundred fifty-eight patients, the warm and dry group fared best over follow-up, with the fewest major heart events. Wet groups were older, with weaker muscles, lower blood counts, and more kidney trouble. Cold groups had weaker heart pumping strength on imaging. The authors say the paired tests give a practical, repeatable profile that could guide care without invasive procedures.
pmc-13251119:
Stalberg Ostwald and colleagues compare two trigger finger releases at a Swedish regional hospital where the needle method was new. Their 2026 Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research study covers one hundred ten patients treated between 2018 and 2020. Open surgery is the standard fix, while percutaneous release promises lower cost and faster recovery.

Open surgery freed almost all treated fingers from triggering, against only about half for the needle method. Nearly two in five needle cases needed further treatment, versus almost none after open surgery. Neither approach caused a major injury, and the needle method cost far less per patient. Most needle patients would still choose it again, but the authors judge open release clearly more reliable here.
pmc-13251519:
Liu and co-authors scan dozens of environmental chemicals for links to obstructive sleep apnea in United States adults. Their 2026 Future Science OA study uses two national health survey cycles covering more than thirteen thousand participants. Fifty-six toxicants in six chemical families were measured in blood or urine samples.

About half the participants met the study's symptom-based definition of sleep apnea. Nine toxicants stood out, including cadmium in blood and urine and several solvent-related breakdown products. Women and adults under sixty-five showed stronger susceptibility to some of the exposures. Dose patterns for cadmium and related compounds bent rather than rising in a straight line. The authors flag these chemicals as targets for mechanism research and prevention.
pmc-13257019:
Parra and a large South American team review the rules governing bacteriophage products used against foodborne germs from farm to fork. Phages promise help against contamination and antimicrobial resistance, but uptake in the region lags. The review maps the scientific landscape, then pinpoints why classification, approval, and labeling stall.

Research and patents are growing yet concentrated in a few areas, and regulatory frameworks still leave product categories and safety monitoring vague. The authors propose risk-based guidelines defining categories, claims, safety standards, traceability, and post-market surveillance. They suggest a new Codex Alimentarius project to harmonize rules globally, easing both safety assurance and food trade.
pmc-13258019:
Yan Shao leads a 2026 study building a computer model to predict which genes microRNAs target. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules that help control gene activity, so their targets matter for understanding disease. The model treats input features as linked random values and uses statistical tools, including Gaussian mixture models and a vine copula, to estimate their joint patterns. Extra virtual samples were created to fix small and unbalanced training data.

The model kept high predictive performance even when only thirty percent of the training data were used. As a real-world check, the team tested one predicted pairing, miR-8485 targeting the gene JAK2, with lab and animal experiments. The tests confirmed that this predicted interaction is real. The authors offer the model as a tool for studying microRNA function and disease mechanisms.
pmc-13258119:
An Thinh Nguyen leads a 2026 machine learning study of how farm land use affects carbon dioxide emissions in Vietnam. The team built a four-layer artificial neural network, a computer model loosely modeled on brain networks, using data from 1990 to 2019. It linked twenty-one types of agricultural land use, covering crops, meat, and vegetables, to national carbon dioxide emissions over that period.

Most land-use types were positively associated with emissions, including bananas, dry beans, cabbages, cashew nuts, cassava, coconuts, coffee, tea leaves, and sweet potatoes. Five types showed negative associations: horse meat, unmanufactured tobacco, soya beans, sesame seed, and rice. National emissions rose sharply in the background, from 62.9 million tons in 1990 to 263.6 million tons in 2019. The authors say the results can guide targeted policy to cut farm greenhouse gas output.
pmc-13258719:
Jelena Bogdanović and colleagues review whether Nogo proteins could flag type 2 diabetes trouble before it strikes. Nogo, also called RTN4, helps run cell membranes and blood vessel behavior. Their 2026 systematic review weighs clinical cohorts and lab studies from two thousand to twenty twenty-five.

Lab work ties Nogo forms to insulin release, gut hormone processing, and vessel leakiness through known signaling routes. Blood and tissue studies link higher Nogo signals to faster diabetes progression and vascular damage. Genetic tests for cause and effect, however, offer little support so far. Mixed directions across tissues mean far more validation is needed before any clinic-ready test.
pmc-13259619:
Saya Furukawa and colleagues watch a salamander regrow its hand and find the instructions move. Axolotls rebuild limbs using the same SHH and FGF8 signals other vertebrates use, but deployed in a different place. Their 2026 study tracks the signaling loop as digits appear.

Instead of staying put, the loop's active zone slides steadily toward the rear of the growing limb. Digits are switched on one after another as it passes, back to front. That is the reverse of the amniote order, yet the finished limb looks the same. Conserved toolkits, they conclude, can reach one shape by different routes.
pmc-13260019:
Edis Kahraman and colleagues wrote a 2026 reply letter about their study of single against double-suture cervical cerclage. Cerclage is a stitch that holds the cervix closed during pregnancy. Commentators Park and Park had argued that mixing reasons for cerclage could hide varied effects, since stitches placed for past history, ultrasound findings, or exam findings serve different situations. The authors agree that the reason for the stitch is a key source of difference.

Their original study used a simple prophylactic against emergency split, reflecting urgency and operative context, because finer groups left too few cases per cell. They then rechecked the records and sorted all cases into three groups by reason: twenty-four placed for past history, fifty-nine placed for ultrasound findings, and forty-two placed for exam findings or emergency. This new sorting supports a post-publication sensitivity analysis, not a replacement of the original framework.
pmc-13260319:
Lin Li, Xiaoyue Zhao, and Xiaobin Ding wrote a 2026 cross-sectional study of anxiety and reasons for living in Chinese college students. Reasons for living are the beliefs that protect against suicide risk. The study surveyed 416 undergraduates on anxiety, reasons for living, self-inconsistency, meaning a gap between the real and ideal self, and adult attachment styles. Statistical analyses with repeated resampling tested which factors carried or changed the relationship.

Higher anxiety was associated with fewer reasons for living. That link ran partly through self-inconsistency and through attachment avoidance, the tendency to keep emotional distance from others. Attachment anxiety, the fear of being abandoned, changed the strength of the link: the negative effect of anxiety was stronger in students with higher attachment anxiety. The authors highlight both self-system disruption and attachment coping as targets for support.
pmc-13262819:
Muhammad Umair Khan and colleagues track deaths recorded as involving antipsychotic medicines in England in a 2026 journal article. These drugs treat severe mental illness, but their link to death rates is debated. The team used national prescription data from 2015 to 2023 across seven regions, and modeled how rates vary with deprivation, ethnic mix, and place.

Recorded deaths rose from 10.33 to 13.85 per million prescription items over the period, an average yearly rise of 3.56 percent. London saw the steepest increase, while the Midlands saw a decrease. Areas with more deprivation had higher death rates, and areas with higher Asian population shares had lower rates. The authors call for safer prescribing, closer monitoring, and fairer care.
pmc-13263019:
Ishreen Kaur Dhillon and colleagues test faster ways to grade dental students' handling of child patients in a 2026 journal article. Personal feedback helps students guide children's behavior, but watching full videos takes too long. The Singapore team compared scores from written transcripts of 40 recorded sessions with video scores, and also let two versions of ChatGPT score the transcripts.

Scoring a transcript took about 12 minutes on average, versus 73 minutes of video. Transcript scores agreed well with video scores. The language models agreed only moderately with the human scorer and were inconsistent, giving the same score on all repeats in few cases. The authors back transcripts for teaching, but say the models need work first.
pmc-13263719:
Ming-Yi Zhang and colleagues describe three new fungi from Chinese city soils, an overlooked hunting ground. Urban soil fungi keep soil healthy and cycle nutrients, yet taxonomy there lags far behind forests. Their 2026 survey cultures eight isolates of the family Sympoventuriaceae.

Five genetic markers plus detailed morphology separated the finds from known relatives. The new species are Scolecobasidium campestre, Verruconis obovatus, and Veronaeopsis sinensis, each illustrated and compared with its nearest kin. Two belong to genera whose status has been unsettled, so the data also steady the family's family tree. City dirt, they show, still hides unnamed species.
pmc-13264819:
Sally Abd-Elrahman Mohammed and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on home yoga for women after childbirth. The weeks after birth often bring pain, stress, and a drop in quality of life. Yoga mixes gentle movement, breathing, and relaxation, and doing it at home keeps costs low. The team tested a home program at a university hospital in Egypt.

Three hundred women were split evenly into a yoga group and a control group. The yoga group used a schedule card to guide and log practice, and both groups answered quality of life surveys. After the program, quality of life scores differed sharply between groups, and every woman in the yoga group reported some satisfaction, against none in the control group. The authors urge adding home yoga to routine care after birth.
pmc-13265019:
Wenshen Mo and Zhan Wang wrote a 2026 genetic study on blood proteins that may cause basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer. Using protein data from the UK Biobank and an Icelandic group, they applied Mendelian randomization, a genetic method for testing cause, and traced chains where one protein acts through another.

The analysis found blood proteins affect cancer risk in one direction only, with no reverse effect, and the proteins clustered in immune and inflammation pathways. Thirteen UK proteins acted through six Icelandic-set proteins. Two hubs, STAT3 and GUCA1A, sat at the center of many chains, with the strongest single mediation reaching 15.2 percent. Sensitivity checks supported the results. The authors say the hubs could guide patient sorting and targeted treatment research.
pmc-13267019:
Qing-Dong Ma and colleagues report the full chloroplast genome of a medicinal plant variety in a 2026 paper. The plant is a form of Paris polyphylla, a herb used in Chinese medicine and listed in drug standards of Gansu and Zhejiang provinces. Chloroplasts are the green parts of plant cells that carry their own small genome.

The genome is about 165,000 DNA letters long, with the usual four-part layout of plant chloroplasts. It holds 134 genes in total. Family-tree analysis placed this variety as sister to one close relative and near another well-known variety. The authors say the sequence gives a resource for future work on this herb, including checks of identity and kinship.
pmc-13267619:
Yun Zhang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of soil quality under mangrove planting on China's coast. An invasive grass, Spartina alterniflora, has spread through coastal wetlands there. The team compared soils down to one meter under a native sedge, the invader, a restored mangrove called Kandelia obovata, and mixed stands in the Oujiang Estuary. They also compared four mangrove sites across Zhejiang Province.

Plant type and soil depth both strongly shaped soil traits. Mangrove soils held the most nitrogen and usable phosphorus, yet their ratios hinted at phosphorus shortage. A combined quality ranking put mangrove first, then the invader, mixed stands, and the sedge. Two bays ranked as the best mangrove sites. The authors say planting improves soil but will need added phosphorus over time.
pmc-13269519:
Vincent Leclercq published a review article in 2026 on careful use of two biomarker tests in parkinsonism, a group of movement disorders that can look alike early on. One test detects clumping activity of a brain protein, alpha-synuclein. The other measures a protein released when nerve fibers are damaged.

The first test identifies Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia with high accuracy, but misses more cases in some genetic and early forms. The second test helps separate those diseases from atypical disorders, though cut points vary with age and test platform. Leclercq proposes step-by-step paths that combine test results with scans, genes, and prior likelihood. He also stresses explaining positive and negative results clearly to patients.
pmc-13270019:
Qingling Chen, Zhaohui Liu, and Guanfeng Shi published a journal article in 2026 on moral leadership and negative workplace gossip. Moral leadership has two sides: being a moral person and actively managing ethics at work. The study asked what happens when those two sides match or mismatch in the same leader.

Using surface analysis of survey patterns, aligned leaders drew less negative gossip from staff. Leaders strong on both sides faced the least gossip of all. A leader seen as moral personally but weak on managing ethics fared better than the reverse profile. Perceived hypocrisy explained much of the effect. The authors say splitting the two sides exposes a hidden cost of virtuous leadership.
pmc-13271419:
Haoyun Zhao is lead author of a 2026 case report of a primitive neuroectodermal tumour, a rare and aggressive cancer, arising in the endometrium, the lining of the womb. Such tumours have vague symptoms and images, so they are often mistaken for harmless growths and treated late.

The patient was a 26-year-old woman with persistent abnormal womb bleeding, first diagnosed after scraping as a benign polyp. Later scans showed a large mass inside the womb, and tissue tests, including a marker called CD99 and characteristic rosette patterns, confirmed the rare tumour. She had major surgery with lymph node removal, then chemotherapy, which was stopped because of severe side effects. The authors stress early, definite diagnosis.
pmc-13272619:
Per Flodbring Larsson leads a 2026 study of a new antibody treatment for prostate cancer that has spread and no longer responds to hormone therapy. The target is a growth signal receptor called TbetaRI, which an enzyme can cut so a fragment enters the cell nucleus. That fragment helps cancer invade and spread.

The team made human antibodies that block the cut by covering the site. In mice carrying human tumors, the antibodies stopped the fragment reaching the nucleus and curbed growth, invasion, and spread. The effect matched a standard chemotherapy drug, with no clear harm to body weight, aorta, or heart in the mice tested.
pmc-13272719:
Weihua Hu leads a 2026 study of a gene called SOAT1 in glioma, an aggressive brain tumor. The team asked whether levels of this gene track with survival, immune cells in tumors, and blood test results. They used two large glioma databases and a hospital group of 195 patients who had surgery from 2016 to 2020.

SOAT1 levels rose with tumor grade, and high levels meant a worse outlook, even after other factors were counted. High levels also linked to more immune cells in tumors, especially macrophages and neutrophils, and to higher inflammation scores in blood. Salt levels in blood were lower and bilirubin higher in the high group.
pmc-13273519:
Qian Shen leads a 2026 review of inherited DNA damage response gene mutations in multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Faults in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, and CHEK2, which normally repair DNA, can raise myeloma risk and shape how the disease evolves and responds to treatment.

Inherited repair defects promote chromosome instability, reshape the immune setting around tumors, and aid therapy-driven progression, the authors summarize. New tools such as multiomics profiling, single-cell sequencing, and liquid biopsy improve monitoring of these changes. The faults also create vulnerabilities that precision therapies can exploit, including PARP inhibitor strategies that kill cells lacking backup repair paths.
pmc-13274019:
Ruth Cowlishaw and colleagues wrote a 2026 semi-systematic review of threadworm infection in baboons. The worm Strongyloides fuelleborni can infect both baboons and people, so baboon infections may matter for human health. Baboons are Africa's most widespread non-human primate, yet this risk is little studied.

The team searched three databases through December 2025, screening 1,588 articles down to forty-four for summary. Infection rates differed across the six baboon species, highest in yellow baboons at about sixty-nine percent and lowest in Guinea baboons. More than two thirds of papers never named the worm to species level. The authors urge better species identification so the true risk to people can be judged.
pmc-13274119:
Eman M Othman and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on cytokinins, chemicals long known as plant growth hormones, inside mammals. Whether these small molecules occur in animals, and where they come from, was largely undefined. The team combined chemical profiling of blood and tissues with studies of gut microbes.

Blood from five animal species consistently held several cytokinin forms, led by a storage form called zeatin-O-glucoside, at levels far below plants. In mice, fasting sharply lowered cytokinin levels in blood, gut, and urine, showing diet is a major source. Germ-free mice had much lower levels than normal mice, proving gut microbes also contribute to the supply.
pmc-13274819:
Hannah Healey, Claudia Susana Caxaj, and Elysée Nouvet present a 2026 qualitative journal article on who gets recognized as having an eating disorder. Beyond clinic wait lists, the authors argue, people face symbolic barriers: being disbelieved, misread, or ruled out by narrow ideas of what these illnesses look like. They used narrative methods informed by lived experience.

One theme ran through the accounts, summed up as 'Who Gets Seen.' Participants described struggling for legitimacy, being seen, misread, or overlooked by family, friends, and clinicians, and learning to recognize their own illness. The authors frame this as epistemic injustice, where a person's credibility is unfairly discounted. They urge reimagining who counts as deserving of care.
pmc-13275919:
Ulrike Hendgen-Cotta and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on protecting mitochondria, the tiny power stations inside cells. When mitochondria are damaged, cells can die, driving injury in the heart, brain, and liver. A protein called BNIP3 helps trigger that death, but its controls were poorly understood.

The authors worked backward from BNIP3's structure to find the short stretch that switches on cell death proteins. They then built a peptide, a small protein fragment named B-017, that blocks BNIP3 from binding those partners. In human cells the peptide stopped death signals while leaving other functions alone. In animal models it reduced tissue damage in the heart, brain, and liver. The team offers it as a candidate drug for diseases tied to failing mitochondria.
pmc-13276219:
Massrehaw Assnakew Abebe and co-authors report a 2026 computer-based study designing test proteins for epidemic typhus. This louse-spread disease, caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, still threatens many poorer regions. Current blood tests for it are often insensitive or unreliable, delaying treatment.

Using gene and protein data, the team picked two bacterial surface proteins as the most promising targets. They then designed two engineered proteins on the computer. One strings together short immune-triggering fragments; the other uses larger chunks of the natural proteins. Checks suggested both designs would be stable, soluble, and strong at provoking immune recognition. They also barely resemble human proteins, which lowers false alarms. Computer docking tests indicated steady binding to an immune receptor. Lab validation still lies ahead.
pmc-13276319:
Salma El Aouadi and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a newborn whose breathing failed because of a rare bone disorder. Jeune syndrome narrows the chest cage so much that the lungs cannot expand. It is inherited and can also affect the pelvis and other organs.

The full-term baby boy was admitted on his first day of life in acute respiratory distress. Imaging showed a markedly narrow chest with short ribs and raised collarbones. His pelvis showed the syndrome's signature shape, with trident-like hip sockets and short iliac bones. Despite intensive support and a breathing machine, his respiratory failure worsened. He died after seven days. The authors use the case to highlight the imaging signs that let doctors recognize this rare, life-threatening condition early.
pmc-13276819:
Jackline A Odhiambo leads a 2026 survey of widowed women in Siaya County, Kenya, an area with high HIV rates. The team asked when women living with HIV may have been exposed and what risk behaviors had occurred since widowhood. A random sample of 480 widows took part, grouped by age.

About thirty-seven percent of the women had HIV, and many infections may have come after widowhood began. At least half reported sex without a condom since becoming widows. Becoming widowed before age thirty was strongly tied to condomless sex and to customs such as widow inheritance and sexual cleansing. The authors urge testing, preventive drugs, and safer practice within those customs.
pmc-13277019:
Jade Cartwright leads a 2026 study of a new mealtime model in one Australian residential aged care home. Older residents face high risk of malnutrition, poor nutrition that weakens health. The model, called Maggie Beer's Big Mission, aimed to improve food, access to meals, and the dining setting through work across many staff roles.

Interviews, audits, and meal observations ran over ten months at three points in time. Staff and residents welcomed the model and reported better meal quality and a calmer, more home-like dining room. Shared vision, training, and leadership helped the changes stick in daily routines. The authors say longer studies should test whether the gains last and what they cost.
pmc-13278019:
Soledad Gómez-Escalonilla Lorenzo leads a 2026 pre-post study of how COVID-19 lockdowns affected patients with high blood pressure and diabetes in central Spain. Restrictions cut activity and disrupted daily disease management. The team measured 152 patients from March 2019 to June 2021, before and after lockdown, tracking blood pressure, weight, blood sugar, activity, drug adherence, and quality of life.

A year after lockdown began, systolic blood pressure had risen, while activity, adherence, and mental quality of life had fallen. Patients in the least active group fared worst on adherence and mental quality of life. The most active patients actually improved their adherence. The authors caution that the design cannot prove lockdown caused each change.
pmc-13278419:
Sei-Woong Choi leads a 2026 genetic study comparing mainland and island moth populations in southern South Korea. Island populations are often expected to lose genetic diversity. The team sampled two moth species along mountain slopes on mainland Mount Jirisan and island Mount Hallasan, analyzing 155 individuals and their mitochondrial DNA.

One species kept similarly high diversity in both places, with strong gene flow across regions. The other showed lower overall diversity but, against expectation, higher diversity on the island, plus strong geographic structuring and little migration. Both species split clearly between mainland and island, but not within each mountain. Island diversity loss is not universal; species traits and setting decide the pattern, the authors conclude.
pmc-13279019:
Ke Cheng and co-authors report a 2026 study of colon and rectum cancer spread under low oxygen. Low oxygen zones are common in fast growing tumours. A master switch called HIF-1 turns on genes that help tumours grow new blood vessels and spread. The team asks how a protein called TDP-43 fits in that chain.

Lab and animal work showed HIF-1 turns on the gene for TDP-43. TDP-43 then holds steady a message for a second protein, TRIP6, which helps vessel growth. Cutting TDP-43 slowed spread and vessel growth. Restoring TRIP6 brought the harmful traits back. The chain gives drug makers a clear new target to test.
pmc-13280619:
Luca Persani and Leonidas H. Duntas present a 2026 article on diet as a supportive yet critical factor in managing thyroid disorders. The thyroid is framed as a metabolic engine converting nutrients in energy for the entire body. Macronutrients build and repair muscles and support cellular structure, while micronutrients serve growth, immune function and disease prevention. Thyroid health depends on adequate, synergistic intake of iodine, selenium and iron, termed the critical bodyguards of thyroid function.

Iodine enters the circulation as iodide and is taken up in the thyrocyte by a sodium iodide symporter. Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes it, and iodinated residues in thyroglobulin drive formation and release of thyroxine and triiodothyronine, the T4 and T3 hormones. Daily iodine sources include seafood, seaweed, dairy, eggs and iodized salt. Balance is needed: low intake promotes goiter and possibly thyroid nodules, while high regular amounts can be toxic to the thyroid.
pmc-13281919:
Mathilde Boussac and colleagues scanned the brains of people with Tourette syndrome in a 2026 study. Tourette brings tics, sudden movements or sounds the person cannot fully control. Its brain roots stay murky, with dopamine long blamed. The team used a scan tracer that lights up active NMDA receptors, doors for the signal chemical glutamate. Twelve patients and twelve healthy peers were scanned. Patients also took scales for tic severity, urges, and mood.

Patients showed higher receptor activity in five brain spots. They included a mood-and-conflict hub at the front and a movement hub deep inside. The front hub's activity rose in step with tic severity scores. The authors read this as a glutamate system running hot. A hot signal may overdrive the direct movement path and loose tics. The finding points to glutamate-calming drugs as a route worth testing.
pmc-13283219:
Salmon farms in a Chilean fjord nudge coral microbes toward drug resistance, Anna Berezkina's sampling team reports for 2026. Heavy antibiotic use in salmon farming may affect nearby sea life. Cold-water coral banks grow in fjords close to many farm sites.

Coral samples came from sites near and far from farms in Comau Fjord. Cultured coral bacteria near farms resisted slightly more drugs on average. Dominant bacteria shifted near farms in both culture and gene tests. Common farm drugs still cut growth of most isolates in lab tests. One drug, tilmicosin, was the main exception in the results. The authors call for wider checks across space and time.
pmc-13283619:
Faking on personality questionnaires is the problem at the heart of a 2026 simulation study by Julius David Kleinbub and Timo Seitz. Their model tries to split true trait scores from answers warped to look good. One key premise says all test takers judge what looks good in much the same way.

Computer runs broke that premise in three distinct ways to test model strength. Recovery of true scores held up well when faking matched each persons own view of what looks good. Trouble grew when people faked toward views they did not hold themselves. Test users can trust the model within limits, but those limits depend on honest alignment.
pmc-13283919:
Lasting tumor shrinkage on a targeted drug conjugate is reported for bladder cancer in a 2026 case by Zhi-ruo Jin and colleagues. The drug, disitamab vedotin, links an antibody to a cell-killing payload. It aims at HER2, a growth signal found on some bladder tumors.

The patient had advanced disease that grew after first-line chemo plus immune therapy. Tumor tests showed mid-level HER2 with a negative gene amplification test. Response held as a partial shrinkage for more than eight months. Bladder cancer struck over six hundred thousand people worldwide in 2022 by cited counts. Wider HER2 testing could open this option to more patients.
pmc-13284019:
Three bowel control scores disagree often enough to mislead follow-up in a 2026 study by Galib Bairamovi and colleagues. Children born with anorectal malformations need lifelong checks on continence after repair. Kelly, Holschneider, and Templeton scores each grade control differently.

Records covered 110 surgically treated patients seen from 2007 to 2017. All three scores were applied at the latest follow-up visit for each child. Score links were moderate, and category agreement ranged from moderate to substantial. Poor control rates shifted noticeably depending on which score was used. Predictors of poor control also changed by scoring system. Combined scoring is advised.
pmc-13284419:
Franziska Richter and colleagues report a 2026 study of diabetes risk in young cancer survivors who had radiation to the brain and spine. Such survivors face higher risk of metabolic problems, but brain tumor groups have been studied less than leukemia groups. The team drew on a survey cohort and a late-effects clinic cohort.

In the survey group of 197 respondents, diabetes was reported by about 3 percent of survivors, a rate close to the matched general public. In the clinic group that had craniospinal radiation, about one third showed poor glucose control, split between diabetes and prediabetes levels. The authors call for planned, risk-based long-term checks of blood sugar in this survivor group.
pmc-13285419:
Breathing tiny plastic bits into rat lungs leaves clear marks, a 2026 toxicity study by Hyoung-Yun Han and co-authors finds. Micro and nano polyethylene bits are rising as a lung risk worry, yet safety proof is thin. Rats got weekly doses into the windpipe for thirteen weeks at four dose levels, then a four-week rest phase checked if harm faded.

Swelling cells ringed vessels and airways in both sexes at even the lowest dose for both bit sizes. Thick airway walls and lining overgrowth showed at higher doses, sooner in females for some signs. pmc-13285919:
Mingrong Cheng and colleagues review nanotechnology for liver cancer care in a 2026 survey of metabolism and immunity. Liver tumors rewire how they burn sugar, fat, and amino acids, and that rewiring also muffles immune attack. Drugs alone rarely break the loop, since targeted agents meet resistance and immune drugs answer in few patients.

Tiny carriers can land in tumors, sense acid or stress cues there, and release several drugs at once where they matter most. By tuning sugar, fat, and amino acid paths together, such platforms may lift the immune brake and boost checkpoint drugs or local care. Carrier quality, shared test standards, and proof in patients remain the hurdles the authors flag for the field.

pmc-13287219:

pmc-13287419:

The authors see the method as workable for this group.
pmc-13288719:
Sung Woo Joo and Jungsun Lee map brain wiring in schizophrenia to gene activity in 2026. Their study uses MRI scans. It holds 1,216 people. Networks were built from cortex shape likeness. Patient and control maps were compared. Gene data came from the Allen atlas.

pmc-13289119:

The model marks four fluid zones in the brain. Fake CT images from MRI were tried first. They proved too weak for training. Hand-marked real CT scans worked better. pmc-13289219:

Fieldwork covered 360 randomly chosen households in Panini Rural Municipality, Arghakhanchi district, in July and August 2022. Knowledge about the program proved a strong predictor of joining, as did feeling that premiums were affordable for the household. Recent illness and worry about poor family health also raised the odds of joining. Encouragement from neighbors, peers already enrolled, and agreement within the family mattered a great deal as well. pmc-13290019:
Hannah M Cranford led a 2026 implementation report on modernizing disease surveillance in the United States Virgin Islands. In January 2024 the health department needed to sustain its cloud surveillance system while advancing local data modernization. Leaders chose to move the national surveillance platform to Amazon Web Services under local control and upgrade to the newest version, called NBS 7, with federal partner advice.

Phased work covered planning, cost review, deployment, database transfer, validation, and staged reconnection of reporting sites. The system went live on May 6, 2025, making the territory the first jurisdiction on that cloud host for this platform. Cost savings neared 90 percent, with faster data flow and stronger local informatics skill.
pmc-13290519:
Advanced clot-removal care leaves the heart's right side working better months later, Hammad Sheikh and colleagues report in 2026. The study covers survivors of acute pulmonary embolism treated at the Mount Sinai Health System in New York between 2021 and 2023.

Of 122 patients with scans at the start and at follow-up, some had clot removal by catheter or surgery, and the rest had blood thinners alone. In matched, adjusted comparisons, the treated group pumped more blood from the right ventricle and had triple the odds of a better tricuspid valve grade. Follow-up came at a median of 26 weeks. Sheikh and colleagues say the results back aggressive treatment for higher-risk embolism, at least among survivors.
pmc-13291119:
A hyaluronate nose spray is compared with saline by Weizheng Zhao and colleagues in a 2026 mouse study. Saline rinses are a staple for nasal disease. Plain salt water cannot copy the airway surface liquid. That gap may cap long-term rinse gains.

Mice breathed mugwort allergen through the nose. They then got saline or the test spray for days. Scratching, crusting, and tissue state were scored. Spray mice scratched less and crusted less. Allergy signals fell in tissue and blood. Mucus depth and clearance speed held up better. Cell barrier proteins stayed the same in both groups.
pmc-13291219:

Four feeding plans were compared in the trial. One gave nitrogen alone, one gave phosphorus alone. A third gave both, and a fourth gave none. Leaf color, shape, and light use were tracked. Both nutrients together raised leaf green and light scores most. Leaf size also grew under the combined plan. Feed protein and nutrient levels rose with it. Mixed feeding thus looks best for quality grass here.
pmc-13292019:
Mehrgan Shahryari and co-authors tell a 2026 diagnostic case story about a brain mass that looked like glioblastoma but was not. A 65-year-old man arrived with tingling, slowed thinking, and slurred speech, and MRI showed a lone enhancing mass in the right caudate head with wide swelling around it. Before surgery, he also received multifrequency magnetic resonance elastography, which maps tissue stiffness and viscosity.

The scan showed unusually high stiffness and viscosity, a signature tied to metastases or meningioma rather than soft glioblastoma tissue. Tissue testing then confirmed a metastasis from squamous cell carcinoma, and PET-CT located the primary tumor in the right lung hilus. The authors suggest elastography could serve as an easy extra contrast that rules glioma out when a lesion feels stiff.
pmc-13292319:
Jingyang Zhang, Qin Zheng, and Mulin Liu write a 2026 letter commenting on a single-cell study of DUSP9 in liver cancer by Xu and colleagues. That study mapped DUSP9-positive, stem-like tumor cells sitting beside cancer-associated fibroblasts and floated an inhibitor, AKOS000434153, as a candidate drug. The letter writers praise the spatial finding but question how the follow-up experiments were run.

Their core point: knockdown and drug tests happened in flat monocultures of HepG2 and Huh7 cells, cut off from the fibroblast niche the authors say sustains the stem-like state. Stromal signals often shield tumors from therapy, they argue. They propose testing the inhibitor in co-culture, 3D spheroids, or fibroblast-conditioned media instead. Those designs, they say, would show whether blocking DUSP9 survives contact with its protective soil.
pmc-13292519:
Mohammed Yousef Almulhim and Samah Faisal Fakhry interview a 2026 group of intensive care nurses in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, about learning to run continuous dialysis machines without formal training. Twenty nurses with direct responsibility for continuous renal replacement therapy described their experience in depth interviews, analyzed thematically.

Four themes structure the findings. Nurses figured things out on the floor, learning by watching and doing at the bedside. Colleagues served as the real textbook, passing know-how through demonstration and stories. Fear of making an error shadowed the machines until repetition slowly built competence. Finally, nurses named the invisible gap: no structured program exists, and they want simulation training, written protocols, and competency checks. The authors urge leaders to lift this hidden teaching burden from frontline staff.
pmc-13293419:
Ellen A. M. Kuipers and co-authors sort, in a 2026 study, people awaiting weight-loss surgery into groups by behavior and mental well-being. Knowing how patients differ before surgery could help clinics tailor support to each person's needs.

Surveys from 272 patients covered health, quality of life, social support, eating habits, and low mood before surgery. Four groups emerged: one strong on all fronts, one with weaker body health, one with weaker mood yet stable body health, and one weak on both fronts. The largest group held 122 people with no deficits, based on counts the authors give. Follow-up work should test how groups fare later.
pmc-13293819:
Qiujian Liang and co-authors link, in a 2026 study, a skeleton protein called CORO1A to inflamed cartilage cell groups and immune shifts in osteoarthritis. Joint cartilage holds varied cell types, and what ties some groups to immune change was unclear.

Gene data from many sources, plus single-cell reads, placed CORO1A mainly in inflamed and growing cartilage cells. High levels went with more immune cells in tissue and with active inflammatory signaling paths. Human and mouse diseased cartilage both showed raised levels, and cutting the protein in lab cartilage cells lowered a damaging enzyme and cell movement. CORO1A may drive part of joint inflammation.
pmc-13293919:
Huiping Tian, Yue Wang, and Song Guo follow resilience over time in a 2026 longitudinal study of 223 breast cancer patients. Resilience and meaning in life were measured right after surgery and again 3 months later. Latent profile and transition methods sorted patients into low and high resilience groups and tracked who moved between them.

Two groups appeared at both times. About 38.63% moved from low to high resilience, while 5.64% slipped the other way. Others stayed put, split between lasting high and lasting low groups. Meaning in life related closely to which path patients took. The pattern shows recovery is uneven and support needs change after surgery.
pmc-13294219:
Stephanie Casey and coauthors build a fungal bioreactor for DDT-tainted soil in a 2026 study. DDT and its breakdown products, called DDX, still linger in Swedish soils over 50 years after the ban and cling to organic matter. Their bench system washes soil with surfactant, then passes the freed chemicals over woodchips colonized by the white-rot fungus Ganoderma lucidum.

In liquid tests the fungus broke down 73% of total DDX within 10 days, give or take 6 points. Over 28 days in the reactor, soil totals fell far more with fungus than in the control run, about 45% lower in relative terms. Coupling washing with fungal breakdown scales the cleanup idea.
pmc-13294419:
Katie L. Boncella joins Micah Brown, Jonathan P. Beausejour, and Michael O. Harris-Love to introduce a 2026 research topic editorial on muscle health. Muscle does far more than move limbs: it regulates metabolism, sends hormone signals, steadies posture, and shapes immunity. Decline feeds frailty, falls, and lost independence, yet studies measure health with clashing tools and cutoffs.

A framework grounded in the World Health Organization functioning classification links body systems to daily activity and participation. Shared language could help therapists and doctors compare studies and adopt measures in clinic. The editorial synthesizes where models agree, where they split, and how to use the common base.
pmc-13295119:
Yilin Wang, Wenbing Wu, and Fuli Yao review ball-shaped nucleic acid particles for precise cancer care in a 2026 article. Each particle wears a dense shell of short genetic strands pointing outward, a shape cells absorb without extra carriers. The shell also resists breakdown, aiding stable delivery.

Design choices add antibodies, aptamers, or gene-silencing strands aimed at targets such as HER2 and PD-L1. Responsive, self-built, and peptide based carriers release cargo on cue and reshape the tumour surroundings. Uses span sensing of cancer markers, combined drug and immune delivery, and vaccine support. Early human work looks safe, though delivery strength, targeting, scale-up, and long-term safety still need work.
pmc-13295919:
Add-on blood treatments are tested in 2026 by Neusvaldo de Medeiros Caldas Júnior and co-authors in dogs with a contagious tumour spread mainly by mating. Standard chemotherapy works but can need many sessions and cause side effects, so the team try reinfusing the dog's own blood, with or without ozone.

Dogs receiving these add-ons alongside chemotherapy reached full remission in fewer sessions, without extra side effects appearing. The authors suggest the approach may make treatment quicker and easier on the animals. They stress that larger studies must confirm the benefit before wider use.
pmc-13296919:
Zarrin Moghaddam and a large materials team craft, in 2026, porous glass fibres loaded with gallium and coated in clove oil as a wound dressing candidate. The fibres were spun with a template leaving fine pores, then tested for antioxidant power, germ killing and skin cell friendliness.

One recipe, with a small gallium share and the stronger clove coating, scavenged harmful radicals best and held the most plant phenolics. Its breakdown products lowered stress chemistry inside skin cells while keeping them alive for three days, and it cut E. coli growth clearly. Gallium ions likely drive the antibacterial side, clove the antioxidant side.
pmc-13297919:
Family doctors now have a step-by-step pathway for finding dangerous fatty liver disease, summarized by Mitchell P Wilson and colleagues in a 2026 primer. The guidance distills recent Canadian consensus recommendations on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease for front-line practice.

Screening starts with the FIB-4 blood score. Patients landing in the middle zone, between 1.3 and 2.67, move on to a stiffness scan by transient elastography, ultrasound shear wave, or magnetic resonance elastography, which perform about equally. The primer supplies thresholds, an algorithm, and notes on the practical hurdles of running this pathway in community clinics, where most patients with the condition are actually seen.
pmc-13298019:

They aged 120 specimens from three bulk-fill composites and one nanofilled reference material under combinations of mechanical wear, pH cycling, and heat cycling.

Roughness climbed and hardness fell as aging accumulated. The harshest changes came from wear plus acid cycling, while wear alone did least damage. Two materials, Filtek One Bulk Fill and the nanofilled Filtek Supreme Ultra, held up best, and Venus Bulk Fill fared worst. Roughness and hardness did not correlate. The authors advise matching material choice to patients facing acidic challenges.
pmc-13298519:

pmc-13300019:

pmc-13300919:
Plant oils may help beekeepers fight hive disease with fewer synthetic chemicals, Yordan V. Hristov and colleagues conclude in a 2026 review of essential oils for honey bees. pmc-13301519:

pmc-13302319:

pmc-13302419:

pmc-13302819:

pmc-13303919:

pmc-13304819:

pmc-13306119:

The piece calls for faster, sharper diagnostics and wider recognition that toxoplasmosis may sit behind many hospital deaths.
pmc-13307719:

pmc-13308319:

pmc-13308919:

pmc-13309419:

The authors present the paired system as a candidate for slow, local mouth treatment.
pmc-13309619:
Laurence J. Kirmayer writes on diversity, equity, and inclusion in cultural psychiatry in a 2026 article. Fair critiques of current programs are weighed beside the scope and effects of the backlash, with Canada and the United Kingdom used as contrasts. pmc-13310819:
Seo-Ho Cho and colleagues compare add on health questions for a standard life quality scale in China and the Netherlands in a 2026 study. pmc-13310919:
Paula Helena Gomes de Moraes Ruiz and colleagues draft a group program to boost diabetes self care in a 2026 concept paper. pmc-13311219:

pmc-13311319:

One year on, the limb stayed open and the course was smooth.
pmc-13311619:

pmc-13311719:

The team surveyed 1085 dialysis patients at 17 sites in northeast Ohio from 2018 to 2023 with standard mood, anxiety, and body symptom scales. About 14.3 percent screened positive for depression in this group. Models that kept the three problems apart fit slightly better than one merged distress score. The three still correlated strongly, which supports screening for all three together in dialysis care.
pmc-13311819:

Arbor Acres broilers ate cadmium-laced feed with or without lycopene for 42 days. Lycopene reversed the growth drag and kidney tissue damage the metal caused. Deeper checks tied the protection to steadier mitochondria, the cell power units, across their birth, movement, and cleanup systems. The work suggests a feed additive route to safer poultry production on polluted land.
pmc-13311919:
Rosa Amalia and co-authors map Indonesian social media talk about oral health in a 2026 content analysis. Posts from Quora and Threads over eighteen months supply the material.

The team coded 858 posts from July 2023 to January 2025 into 19 topic classes and ran topic modeling on the text. Mouth ulcers and toothache drew the most talk. Ten themes emerged, from hygiene habits to children's dental visits and post-surgery recovery. Quora posts leaned toward symptom questions, while Threads posts read more personal and emotional. Set against national survey data, the chatter shows what worries the public most.
pmc-13312019:
Mohammad Amin Khalilzad and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how fine air particles known as PM2.5 may drive disease by switching on controlled forms of cell death. These particles, breathed in from traffic, industry, fires, and other sources, are tied to illness and death worldwide.

The same pathways appear across heart, brain, lung, kidney, liver, and eye disease in the studies surveyed. The authors map where the evidence is thin and name candidate treatments, aiming to guide later work that moves lab findings toward clinical trials.
pmc-13312419:

Their system, Ortho PeriFT, predicts risks, suggests fluid, vasopressor, and anesthetic adjustments through a decision module fenced by guideline rules. It monitors patients continuously, attaching calibrated uncertainty ranges so it can hold back when unsure. In internal and outside patient groups it beat classical and neural comparison models on accuracy and calibration. Off-policy estimates suggested its suggestions would have outperformed actual clinician behavior without breaking safety guardrails. The authors also report earlier warnings at the same false alarm rate.
pmc-13313019:
Yui Sasaki and co-authors offer a 2026 perspective on designing chemical sensor arrays that run from molecules floating in water all the way to paper test strips. pmc-13314519:

pmc-13318819:

pmc-13319719:

pmc-13321819:

pmc-13323819:

pmc-13328419:

pmc-13329219:

pmc-13329519:

pmc-13332119:

pmc-13333719:

pmc-13334319:

pmc-13334519:

pmc-13334819:

pmc-13336819:

pmc-13363219:
