Petr Danecek and colleagues looked back in 2021 on twelve years of SAMtools and BCFtools, two program suites used to handle DNA sequencing data. The tools manage the standard file formats of the field, converting, sorting, and querying the huge files that sequencing machines produce. They also call genetic variants and analyze their effects.

The article describes what the suites do, how they grew from their first versions, and the standards they helped establish. Almost every genome study of the past decade has passed its data through these programs at some point. The retrospective doubles as a short history of how high throughput sequencing became routine science.
pmc-8866119:
Yunlong Cao and co-authors reported in 2021 that the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 could escape most of the neutralizing antibodies then known. Omicron carried an unusual cluster of changes in its receptor binding domain, the spike region that antibodies target most. The team set out at once to learn how those changes affected antibody defenses.

Using a high throughput screening method that tests many antibody interactions at speed, they mapped which antibodies kept working and which failed. Most existing antibodies lost their grip on the variant, while a few broader ones held. Coming within weeks of Omicron's emergence, the results warned that many antibody medicines would need replacing, and that vaccine strategies had to account for this escape.
routledge-mystery-easter-island-1919:
Katherine Routledge led the Mana trip to Easter Island in 1914. Her book The Mystery of Easter Island came out in 1919. The trip made the first full study of the isle and its great stone heads, the moai. Routledge writes as both sailor and field worker.

She tells how the heads were cut, moved, and raised, and what the isle folk said of them. Strange carved birds, caves, and old rites fill the tale. The ship's tale frames the work: storms, waits, and war news from far off. The book stands as the base study of the isle.
royce-lectures-modern-idealism-1919:
Lectures on Modern Idealism, published in 1919, three years after Royce's death, prints the last lecture course he built on the idealist tradition. Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel are his subjects, the four Germans who made modern idealism.

Royce treats each thinker as a stage in one argument about selfhood and the absolute. His sympathy is with Hegel, but his exposition stays fair to all four, in the clear style of a practiced lecturer. The course sums up the tradition he had spent his life extending. It is his last word on idealism, and a graceful one.
russell-intro-mathematical-philosophy-19:
Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy, published in 1919, is Russell's plain-language account of the ideas behind Principia Mathematica. He wrote much of it in Brixton prison, where he was held for an anti-war article, working without a library.

Russell explains number, infinity, series, and the theory of descriptions for readers with no training in symbols. The paradox that shook the foundations of logic gets a clear, almost cheerful hearing. His aim was to show that the great work's ideas could live outside its notation. The book remains the friendliest door into mathematical logic ever written by one of its makers.
russia-in-1919: Arthur Ransome, later of Swallows and Amazons, went to Russia in 1919 and wrote what he saw: Lenin, Trotsky, and a land in upheaval. His kind view of the Reds caused a storm at home. A vivid, disputed eyewitness record.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol1-1819:
Say's Treatise on Political Economy reached its fourth French edition in 1819, and the first volume opens the work. Say was Adam Smith's great French interpreter, who recast the master's teaching into a clearer system. His Treatise became the most influential economics textbook of its age across Europe and America.

Volume 1 treats production: how wealth is created by industry, capital, and natural agents working together. Say gives the entrepreneur, the organizer who joins the factors and bears the risk, a central place that Smith had left vague. His famous law of markets, that supply creates its own demand, is stated in these chapters. The book taught Europe economics after Smith, in prose students could actually follow. The 1819 edition shows the system in its mature, author-revised form.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol2-1819:
Volume 2 of Say's Treatise, from the same 1819 fourth French edition, completes his system of political economy. The Treatise as a whole had already passed through many printings and translations, an honor no economics book of the age could match. Say revised each edition, and the fourth was his definitive statement.

The second volume carries the argument from production into distribution and consumption: how income is shared, and how wealth is used or wasted. Say treats public spending and taxation with the same wish for clarity that marks the first volume. The applied chapters show the doctrine meeting the facts of French economic life. Read with volume 1, the book gives the French master's full doctrine in its final form. It is the textbook that taught a generation, closed and complete.
shackleton-south-1919:
Ernest Shackleton published South in 1919, the story of his last great expedition of 1914 to 1917. His ship Endurance sailed to cross Antarctica from sea to sea. Instead, the ice caught the ship, crushed it, and sank it, leaving 28 men on the floes.

Shackleton tells how the crew camped on drifting ice for months, then sailed lifeboats to Elephant Island. From there he made the famous open-boat run to South Georgia and crossed its peaks to find help. Every man lived. The book is the leader's own record of endurance and command.
shelley-cenci-1819:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote The Cenci in Italy in 1819, basing it on a true Roman story from 1599. Shelley hoped the play could be staged in London, but its subject made that impossible in his lifetime. He modeled its plain, forceful style on Jacobean tragedy.

Count Francesco Cenci is a monster of cruelty who rejoices in tormenting his family. His daughter Beatrice, driven past endurance, arranges his murder with her mother and brother. The law then punishes the victims more harshly than it ever punished the tyrant. Shelley explores how violence corrupts even the innocent. The play is his most stage-worthy drama.
sinclair-brass-check-1919:
Upton Sinclair published The Brass Check in 1919, at his own expense, after no commercial house would take it. Sinclair had spent twenty years fighting editors who trimmed his socialism, and this book names names. Its title comes from the brass checks men once bought in brothels, his metaphor for bought journalism.

The book documents, case by case, how American newspapers served their owners and advertisers: suppressed stories, planted lies, and crusades steered by business interests. Sinclair draws on his own clashes with the press over The Jungle and his later campaigns. He proposes reforms, from public ownership to reader-funded papers. The Brass Check is the first systematic American critique of the press, and its charges still start arguments.
the-hermetic-art-an-introduction-to-the-: The Hermetic Art, an introduction to the art of alchemy, 1919. The introduction. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-works-of-thomas-vaughan-eugenius-phi: The Works of Thomas Vaughan, Eugenius Philalethes, 1919. The Vaughan works. This book preserves that collection. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
tob-0019:
Peter leads a tour of the world to come in the Apocalypse of Peter, one of the earliest Christian visions of the afterlife. This entry rests on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition. Some early churches read the work nearly as Scripture before later ages set it aside.

Heaven shows its brightness, and hell shows punishments fitted closely to each sin: liars, murderers, and the cruel each meet a matching torment. Later ages borrowed the pattern freely, down to the great infernos of medieval poetry. The vision is stern, vivid, and oddly hopeful, since mercy keeps breaking in. Few short texts cast so long a shadow.
tob-0119:
Laurence Dermott wrote the Ahiman Rezon for the Antient Grand Lodge, the rowdy rival of Anderson's Masons. First issued in the 1750s, his constitution defends older customs against what he saw as modern tampering. Waite's scholars and traditionalists alike still argue over its claims.

Dermott writes with wit and earthiness where Anderson is stately. Charges, rules, and songs fill the book, along with sharp words for the other side. The schism between Antients and Moderns shaped Masonry for sixty years. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, this abridged copy gives the other founding text of English Freemasonry, the one with jokes.
tob-10019:
Joshua, the sixth book of the Bible in King James translation, begins after the death of Moses. Joshua takes command of the Israelites and leads them across into Canaan, the land they believed had been promised to them. Battles, alliances, and the settling of territory fill most of its chapters.

Readers find the fall of Jericho, the division of land among the twelve tribes, and cities set aside for refuge and for the Levites. Near the end Joshua gathers the people, recalls what God has done, and charges them to stay faithful. The book works both as a conquest account and as a record of a covenant people taking shape.
tob-4019:
Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, amid England's civil war, and founded modern political philosophy on fear and contract rather than divine right. Without a sovereign, he argues, human life in the state of nature is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. War of every man against every man is his diagnosis.

The cure is surrender: subjects covenant to obey an absolute power, the Leviathan, in exchange for security. Hobbes builds the case with geometrical confidence through human nature, language, religion, and the church's proper subordination. Readers may reject his remedy, but his question, what justifies obedience, still organizes political argument.
tob-4219:
Jan van Ruysbroeck, prior of Groenendaal near Brussels, wrote the three works gathered here in the fourteenth century. The Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage maps the soul's active, inward, and God-seeing lives. The Sparkling Stone and the Book of Supreme Truth press further, into union without difference.

The 1916 English volume puts his masterworks between one set of covers. Ruysbroeck writes in images of fountains, bees, and summer valleys, then suddenly in hard paradox. Contemporaries called him the Ecstatic Doctor. Verified from the 1919 edition, the triple volume gives the Flemish mystic whole, at the height of his strange and beautiful powers.
tob-4319:
Meister Eckhart, the German Dominican of about 1260 to 1328, preached sermons that still startle. C. de B. Evans translated them in a modern version of 1924, and volume one gathers sermons and treatises on the Godhead beyond God. The church condemned some of his claims after his death.

Eckhart teaches detachment so complete that the soul lets go even of God as an idea, and speaks of the Word being born in the soul as in Bethlehem. Paradox is his native tongue. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Evans's first volume gives medieval mysticism's boldest voice in English built for modern ears.
tob-9219:
Around the year 140, a Roman Christian known as Hermas recorded a series of strange visions. His work, the Shepherd of Hermas, appears here in William Wake's translation, in a set of early Christian writings once left outside the New Testament. Some early churches read it almost as Scripture.

Hermas sees a tower being built from living stones, a picture of the church, and meets a shepherd who gives him strict commands. The great question is whether Christians who sin after baptism can be forgiven, and how. The visions answer with both warning and hope, and they show a young church working out its rules.
treaty-of-versailles-1919:
The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919 in the palace's Hall of Mirrors, set the peace terms between the Allies and Germany after the First World War. Germany had no real part in drafting the terms and signed under protest. The treaty was one of several settlements that redrew the map of Europe after four years of slaughter.

Its articles placed sole blame for the war on Germany, demanded huge payments for war damage, and cut the German army to a small force. Germany lost land on its borders and all of its overseas colonies, and the League of Nations was created in the treaty's opening part. Many historians link the harsh terms to the anger that later fed the Second World War.
un-ga-res-19: Pay for the judges of the International Court of Justice was fixed line by line in Resolution 19, passed on 6 February 1946. The president and the other judges draw a salary of 54,000 a year, in the florins of the day, and the president adds a special grant of 15,000. A vice-president acting as president earns 100 florins a day, capped at 10,000.
un-ga-res-a-69-19:
Memory of slavery and the Atlantic slave trade is kept by Resolution A/69/19, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the 2006 vote that marked two hundred years since the trade's abolition, and the votes since on a lasting memorial to the victims. Each 25 March serves as the world day of memory for the victims of slavery and the trade.

Too little is known of the trade and its long shadow, the text holds, a shadow felt across the world. The yearly rite of memory has drawn fresh eyes to the crime. States are praised for acts that fight the trade's legacy, in line with the pledges of the 2001 Durban meeting on racism.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
George W. Bush, president of the United States, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 19, 2006. He spoke while the Iraq war, launched by his government in 2003, faced sharp criticism around the world. The yearly general debate gave him a direct line to friend and critic alike.

Bush defended his freedom agenda and said the war on terror served all free states. He spoke to the people of Iraq, Iran, and Syria over the heads of their rulers. He also backed aid, debt relief, and talks on trade. The speech is a clear record of his case, in his own words.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 19, adopted on 6 February 1946 at the twenty-third plenary meeting, fixed the pay of the judges of the International Court of Justice. The president and members were each set a yearly salary of 54,000 florins. The president drew a special allowance of 15,000 florins. Extra judges called in for a case were paid by the day, with a daily living allowance.

In resolution 69/19 (2014), the General Assembly follows up its long-running project for a permanent memorial at United Nations Headquarters honoring the victims of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade. The text recalls the annual International Day of Remembrance on 25 March and the educational purpose behind the memorial.

The Assembly notes that the design 'Ark of Return' has been selected and construction is under way. It decides the memorial will sit within the Headquarters campus. It says leftover trust-fund money will support its upkeep. It thanks contributors and urges further voluntary donations. It asks for annual commemorative activities and public-awareness work. It asks for reports on outreach and on the fund at the seventieth session. The memorial was meant to make remembrance a permanent physical presence at the United Nations, not only an annual observance.
un-sc-res-119:
Resolution 119 is short, but it marks a turning point in UN history. Adopted on 31 October 1956, during the Suez Crisis, it notes that action taken against Egypt had created a grave situation. France and Britain, both permanent members, had blocked the Council from acting at two earlier meetings.

Because its permanent members could not agree, the Council could not do its main job of keeping peace and security. So it decided to call an emergency special session of the General Assembly, using the route set out in Assembly Resolution 377 A (V) of 1950. That move let the wider UN membership take up the crisis when the Council was stuck.
un-sc-res-1319:
Murdered aid workers in West Timor forced the Council's hand on 8 September 2000. A militia-led mob had killed three United Nations refugee staff on 6 September. Attacks in Betun the next day reportedly killed refugees as well. Two UNTAET peacekeepers had also been murdered in East Timor. Indonesia's president wrote on 7 September promising a full inquiry and firm steps against the guilty.

The Council insisted that Indonesia take further steps. The militia had to be disarmed and broken up, law and order restored in West Timor, and safety secured in the refugee camps. Those behind the attacks on international staff had to face justice. Indonesia was called to stop militia raids across the border into East Timor. Its plan to send more troops was noted. UNTAET, for its part, had to answer the militia threat with force. The Secretary-General owed the Council a report within a week.
un-sc-res-1419: Security Council business produced Resolution 1419, catalogued in this library as a 2002 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1519: Resolution 1519 belongs to the Council's 2003 output, preserved here from the official record via English Wikisource. Fifteen ambassadors vote on every such text at UN headquarters in New York. What they pass becomes the world's formal position on the matter at hand, which is why the untouched wording, kept whole here, matters.
un-sc-res-1619: Resolution 1619, adopted in 2005, is preserved here through English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. The Security Council's decisions carry weight because member states accept its authority on peace and security in the UN Charter. This entry keeps one such decision entire, so its demands and authorizations can be checked against the source.
un-sc-res-1719: Kept under the number 1719, a formal Security Council resolution survives through a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The genre is consistent across decades: preamble, then operative paragraphs, then the usual request for the Secretary-General to report. This entry follows the genre faithfully and is preserved whole for readers who need the exact text.
un-sc-res-1819:
Liberia's expert watchers were renewed on 18 June 2008. The government had made steady progress since January 2006 in rebuilding the country. Timber measures had been dropped after the 2006 forestry reform law, and the diamond measures had ended too. Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process and set up its internal controls. UNMIL still helped the state hold the diamond and timber regions and the borders.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to renew the Panel of Experts on Liberia to 20 December 2008. Its task was to check the remaining sanctions, above all the arms embargo and the asset freeze on listed persons. All states and Liberia's government had to cooperate with the panel. The government was encouraged to apply the Kimberley Process advice and to keep its forest reforms working. UNMIL's help to the government, and the Côte d'Ivoire mission's watch on the shared border, were both reaffirmed.
un-sc-res-19: Ships struck mines in the Corfu Channel in 1946, and Security Council Resolution 19, passed on 27 February 1947, starts the fact hunt. Britain and Albania stood in dispute over the blasts, which had wrecked British warships in the strait. As a first step, the Council names a team of three of its members. The team must sift all the proof at hand and report the facts of the case by 10 March 1947. Both states are asked to aid the team's work in full.
un-sc-res-1919:
Sudan moved through the Council as Resolution 1919, adopted on 29 April 2010. National elections had just been held that April, the first in decades. A referendum on southern self-rule was due in January 2011. Local violence inside Southern Sudan kept flaring despite the 2005 peace deal.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2011. The mission should take the lead in helping prepare the referendums, including advice on security. It must build a mission-wide plan to shield civilians and boost its presence where clashes loom. Both sides are told to honor the peace deal in full. Reports come every three months.
un-sc-res-219:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed at the end of 1965, in a pattern that had become familiar. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 10 December, said the force was still needed on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay beyond 26 December 1965. Resolution 219 was adopted unanimously on 17 December 1965.

The Council reaffirmed its line of Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The force's stationing was extended once again. This time the extension ran for three months, ending on 26 March 1966. The Council also thanked the Secretary-General for his efforts on Cyprus. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place through the 1960s. Each one bought a few more months of quiet while a settlement stayed out of reach.
un-sc-res-319:
Namibia diplomacy moved slowly through 1972, and the Council kept it alive. The Secretary-General had reported on his contacts with the parties. On 1 August 1972 the Council thanked him for that work. It restated the Namibian people's right to self-determination and independence. It also restated the territory's unity and wholeness. South Africa still ran Namibia in defiance of the United Nations.

The Secretary-General had to continue his contacts with all concerned. A small group of Council members would work with him. Their aim was to create the conditions for Namibians to choose freely. The text builds on resolution 309 of that February. The effort stalled the next year, but the legal position never moved.
un-sc-res-419:
Benin's mercenary invaders were pursued through paperwork on 24 November 1977. Mercenaries had attacked Benin on 16 January 1977, flying into Cotonou at dawn. A Council mission had reported on the raid, and a damage assessment now lay in document S/12415. The Council judged such fighters a danger to all states, above all the small.

The Council restated resolution 405 (1977), which had condemned the armed aggression against Benin in the strongest terms. All states were called to work closely together to gather every fact about the mercenaries who took part in the January attack. Benin's wish to see those men face due process of law was noted. States and aid bodies were appealed to for help rebuilding what the raid had damaged. The Secretary-General had to give Benin the help needed and watch over the text's working, reporting back to the Council as required.
un-sc-res-619: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 619, catalogued for 1988. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 119 was adopted on 31 October 1956, by 7 votes to 2, with 2 abstentions. It addresses the grave situation created by the military action taken against Egypt in the Suez crisis. Disagreement among its permanent members at two earlier meetings had stopped the Council from carrying out its main responsibility for peace and security. Noting that, it decides to call an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The session is under the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution 377 A (V). The Assembly can then make appropriate recommendations.

Murdered aid workers in West Timor drive Resolution 1319, adopted on 8 September 2000. Two days earlier a militia-led mob had killed three United Nations refugee workers at Atambua, and more attacks followed at Betun. The killings landed during the UN Millennium Summit, where the Secretary-General and several heads of government voiced outrage in the hall.

The Council condemned the killings as an outrageous act against unarmed staff who were helping East Timorese refugees. It demanded that Indonesia disarm and disband the militias in the camps, make the area safe for refugees and aid workers, and bring those responsible to justice. Refugee intimidation, it insisted, had to end so people could choose freely whether to go home.

A milestone in Afghanistan's recovery, the Emergency Loya Jirga, is welcomed on 26 June 2002. The grand assembly had met from 11 to 19 June under the Bonn Agreement. The Council noted with special satisfaction the large share of women taking part and the presence of all ethnic and religious communities.

The Afghan people are commended, and all groups are urged to work with the new Transitional Authority to finish the Bonn process. The Authority is pressed to fight the poppy crop, advance the welfare of women and children, and provide schooling for girls and boys alike. Far greater aid is also called for, so refugees and displaced Afghans can return home.

A new monitoring team for the Somalia arms embargo is set up on 16 December 2003. The embargo, in place since 1992, kept being broken, most recently tracked by a panel whose work was ending. Peace talks for Somalia were under way in Kenya under regional sponsorship.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish a Monitoring Group of up to four experts, based in Nairobi for six months. Its focus is ongoing embargo violations, including transfers of ammunition, single-use weapons, and small arms. Somali and regional parties, officials, and states are all told to cooperate fully with the group, and any refusal is to be reported through the sanctions committee.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for another twelve months on 11 August 2005. The mission had been created in August 2003 and renewed a year later. The national dialogue UNAMI supports is stressed as crucial to Iraq's political stability and unity.

The extension runs twelve months from adoption, and the mandate would be reviewed within that time, or sooner if Iraq's government asked. The United Nations' leading role in helping Iraqis build institutions for representative government is restated. The Secretary-General's August letter on the mission, which informed the decision to keep UNAMI in place, is also noted.

A new United Nations office for Burundi is created on 25 October 2006, as the peacekeeping operation there winds down. Burundi's transition had ended with an elected government. A Comprehensive Ceasefire Agreement with the last rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, had been signed in Dar es Salaam in September 2006.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish a United Nations Integrated Office in Burundi, BINUB, to succeed the peacekeeping operation. The office would back peacebuilding, security reform, justice, and development under Burundian ownership, with special attention to women's rights and gender questions. Burundian actors are urged to pursue the remaining reforms and to investigate reported abuses fully.

Resolution 1819, passed on 18 June 2008, keeps the expert team on Liberia's bans in place. The Council had let the ban on Liberian wood lapse by choice. It had ended the ban on rough gems the year before. Liberia had joined the world gem-check scheme and passed a woods law in 2006. Work stayed undone on land rights, on saving wild woods and beasts, and on fair deals for logging firms.

The expert team won a fresh span of work. It would track Liberia's gains and weigh what the last bans still did. The Council stressed that the UN force still counted for safety across the land. The state had to plant its writ in the gem and wood zones most of all.

The Corfu Channel dispute between the United Kingdom and Albania takes a first step on 27 February 1947. Incidents in the channel had brought the two countries before the Council. Before judging the case, the Council wanted the facts established from the evidence available.

A sub-committee of three of its members is appointed to examine all the evidence on the incidents. The sub-committee had to report on the facts by 10 March 1947. It could ask the two governments for more information, and both were told to give it every assistance. The dispute later went to the International Court of Justice, in one of that court's earliest cases.

Sudan's mission is extended into the referendum countdown in Resolution 1919, adopted on 29 April 2010. Nationwide elections had just been held in April. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement was at a critical stage. The 2011 referenda on South Sudan's future and the popular consultations lay ahead. Localized violence, especially in the south, and Lord's Resistance Army activity threatened civilians.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2011. UNMIS must be ready to help prepare the 2011 referenda. It must support the Abyei arbitration outcome, north-south border demarcation, and wealth sharing. It must apply a mission-wide strategy to protect civilians, including refugees, displaced people, and returnees. Quarterly Secretary-General reports must detail referendum support plans, post-referendum issues, and planning for the UN presence after the interim period. The Council also asks UNMIS to coordinate with other regional missions against the LRA threat.

Late in 1965, the Council renewed the Cyprus force once more. On 17 December, it adopted Resolution 219 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report said the force was still needed on the island. The Cyprus government agreed it should stay past late December.

The text restates the whole chain of earlier Cyprus decisions. The chain starts with Resolution 186 of 1964. It then extends the posting by three months, to 26 March 1966. Short renewals like this turned an emergency mission into a fixture. The island's two peoples stayed split, and no deal was in reach. Each renewal bought quiet, not a cure.

Namibia's fate still hung on talks in 1972. South Africa ruled the land in defiance of the UN. A fresh push for contact had begun that February. The chief had met the sides and sent in word. Resolution 319 passed on 1 August 1972 by fourteen votes to none.

The Council thanked the chief for his work. It restated Namibia's right to rule itself. The land had to stay whole and one. The chief was told to keep up his contacts. He would work with a small Council group. A named aide could join the effort to help him. The aim was stark: let the people choose their fate as free and equal men and women. A progress note was due by 15 November.

Resolution 419, adopted on 24 November 1977, follows up an attack on the People's Republic of Benin by foreign mercenaries on 16 January 1977. A Council mission had already looked into the raid, and Benin's representative warned of more threats. Members said hired fighters from abroad were a danger to all states, above all small ones.

The Council backs its earlier Resolution 405, which condemned the attack and all outside meddling in a country's own affairs. It takes note of a report on the damage done and calls on states to share what they know about the mercenaries involved. It notes Benin's wish to see the attackers face due process in court. It also appeals for help to repair the damage and asks the Secretary-General to support Benin and report by 20 September 1978.

The long war between Iran and Iraq was ending in 1988, and its cease-fire needed watchers. Resolution 598 of 1987 had demanded that cease-fire. The Secretary-General had now reported on how to put the demand into effect. Resolution 619 was adopted on 9 August 1988.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report. It set up a United Nations Iran-Iraq Military Observer Group, called UNIIMOG, at once and under its own authority. The group was established for a period of six months, unless the Council decided otherwise. The Secretary-General was told to take the steps needed to put the plan into practice. He also had to keep the Council fully informed of further developments. The observers would watch the cease-fire on the ground while the two countries moved toward a settlement.
us-amendment-19:
Women gained a clear shield for the ballot when the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. Congress had passed it in 1919, after a long campaign by suffrage groups across the country. The amendment says the right to vote cannot be denied because of sex.

Its single sentence doubled the pool of people who could take part in elections. Women had won the vote in some states earlier, but now the rule held nationwide. The change closed a fight that had lasted more than seventy years. It still stands as a landmark step toward equal citizenship in the United States.
veblen-place-of-science-1919:
Thorstein Veblen collected his essays as The Place of Science in Modern Civilisation in 1919. Veblen, the Norwegian-American economist who had coined the phrase conspicuous consumption, was the most original American social thinker of his age. The title essay asks why science flourishes in some ages and starves in others.

His answer credits idle curiosity, the disinterested wish to know, working against the practical and pecuniary habits of business culture. Other essays turn his irony on universities, which he treats as businesses in caps and gowns, and on the learned professions. Veblen's method is deadpan: he describes modern institutions as an anthropologist might describe a strange tribe. The volume shows him at his most characteristic. Readers who finish it tend to see their own institutions through his cold, amused eyes forever after.
veblen-vested-interests-1919:
Veblen published The Vested Interests and the Common Man in 1919, as the First World War ended and the peace was being made. The old iconoclast turned his irony into open anger for this short book. Its target is absentee ownership, the holding of industry by men who profit from it without working in it.

Veblen argues that owners keep prices high by holding back production, a kind of legal sabotage of the common good. Against them he sets the engineers and technicians who actually run the machines, and who might run them for use instead of profit. The book fed the brief vogue for technocracy that followed. It is Veblen's angriest work, written as the world remade itself and he hoped, in vain, for a different peace. The prophet of the engineers' republic speaks here without his usual smile.
vega-fuenteovejuna-1619:
Lope de Vega wrote Fuenteovejuna around 1619, a Spanish play based on a true revolt from the 1400s. A cruel commander abuses the people of the village of Fuenteovejuna. He seizes women and rules by fear. The villagers at last rise together and kill him.

Royal judges arrive to find who struck the blows. Under torture, old and young give one answer: Fuenteovejuna did it. The king must pardon the whole town or punish it as one. The play praises unity and justice against tyranny. Its famous reply has become a lasting symbol of a people standing together.
waley-li-po-1919:
Li Po drank, wandered, and wrote the freest verse of Tang China, and Arthur Waley's The Poet Li Po of 1919 gave him to English readers. The study joins a biography of Li Bai, who lived from 701 to 762, with thirty translated poems. Waley drew on Chinese sources to build the first substantial English account of the poet.

Mountains, rivers, moonlight, and partings fill the poems, rendered in Waley's clear, quiet English. The life matches the verse: court favor, exile, and endless roads. Readers meet here the poet China itself ranks among its greatest, in the version that first carried his name west.
weimar-constitution-1919:
Germany's National Assembly adopted the Weimar Constitution in 1919, meeting in the town of Weimar because Berlin was in turmoil. The empire had collapsed in defeat and revolution, and the assembly had to found a republic on the ruins. Hugo Preuss drafted much of the text, aiming at the most democratic law of its day.

The charter gives the vote to all adults, women included, with seats shared by proportion of votes. It promises a full list of basic rights, from free speech to welfare duties of the state. It also arms the president with emergency powers, later used to rule by decree. The republic it founded lived only fourteen years before Hitler destroyed it. The noblest and most ill-fated founding law of modern Europe still teaches how democracies die.
whitehead-principles-natural-knowledge-1:
An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Natural Knowledge, published in 1919, is Whitehead's first book in the philosophy of nature. After Principia Mathematica he turned to physics itself, asking how science builds its world of points, instants, and particles.

His method of extensive abstraction derives those ideal entities from what we actually perceive: durations, events, and their overlaps. The aim is to found physics on experience without fictions. The book is technical and demanding, the start of Whitehead's long second career in philosophy. Readers of his later metaphysics will find its roots here, in the problem of how nature is known.
wilson-complete-dictionary-of-astrology-:
James Wilson was a London astrologer whose Complete Dictionary of Astrology appeared in 1819. The book defines the terms of the art from aspect to zodiac in alphabetical order. It became the reference work of the early astrological revival.

Wilson explains each term plainly, often with a working example drawn from a real chart or a past master. He is frank about where authors disagree, letting the reader see the art's unsettled corners. Practitioners kept the dictionary at hand because no English book had gathered the vocabulary in one place before. It assumes a reader with a chart in hand and a question to answer.
woolf-night-and-day-1919:
Virginia Woolf published Night and Day in 1919, her second novel. Woolf wrote it in a more traditional shape than her later books, with a full plot and clear chapters. Readers sometimes use it to see where her famous experimental style began.

Katharine Hilbery, granddaughter of a famous poet, spends her days helping with his biography and her nights secretly studying mathematics. She becomes engaged to the earnest William Rodney, then finds herself drawn to the less polished Ralph Denham. A second couple, Mary Datchet and her suffrage work, mirrors the main story. Woolf quietly questions marriage, family fame, and women's work. The comedy is gentle and the intelligence constant.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol19:
Volume XIX of the Journal of Discourses came from Liverpool in 1878, the first volume printed after Brigham Young's death. His sermons still appear, drawn from the record, alongside talks by the leaders who followed him. The Twelve Apostles now carry the church, and their voices grow stronger in the set.

The transition shows in the preaching: old doctrines restated by new mouths, counsel fitted to fresh troubles. The Journal kept its form through the change, shorthand to print as before. Volume XIX lets readers watch a movement pass its first great succession without breaking stride.
